Uniform title: Kāmaratnatantra Editor: Hemachandra Goswami Tattabhusan Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski.
Revision 0: September 18, 2011 Publisher: Assam Government Press Year of Publication: 1928
Place of publication: Shilong;
Country of publication: India. || Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. ||
Now begins the first instruction of the *Kāmaratna*, adorned with a Hindi commentary.
I bow to that Śaṅkara, the remover of all suffering, whose stainless lotus-feet are served by the bee-like wise ones, and who is filled with the group of eight qualities indicative of liberation.
The Goddess said:
"By your grace, I have understood how the bondage of time arises from the essence of mantra; now, tell me the remedy."
Indeed, there are many medicinal herbs for the benefit of human beings;
however, tell me directly about that which was previously mentioned by you. (1)
Īśvara said:
This wonderful Kāmaratna has been extracted by me from the various oceans of tantras,
beginning with the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*) and ending with the practice of mantras for the *yakṣiṇīs*.
The physician should perform the extraction and uprooting [of the affliction] using mantras, according to the lunar day, the asterism, the day of the week, and the specific divisions of the seasons.
By taking medicine at the proper time, one attains supreme strength; O Goddess, in the autumn and early winter, one should collect the bark and roots.
In the cool season, one should properly gather fruit along with roots and the essence;
in spring, flowers and leaves; and in summer, fruits and seeds.

Just as trees, though always strong during their own season, lose half their strength when their roots are dried up in the rains; so too is the case for a physician regarding [the patient's] humors such as *mala*.
This [process] occurs during the summer and rainy seasons, and the fullness of autumn; likewise, trees and other plants produce fruit and seed according to their own proper season.
For these fruits, flowers, and creepers are strong in their own season;
those born of the forest possess potency at night, while those born of the water are strong by day.
The wise proclaim the six rites to be those ending with killing: pacification, subjugation, immobilization, as well as inciting hatred and expulsion. (1)
O Dear One, one should employ rites of subjugation and attraction during the spring;
one should perform the rite of inciting enmity in the summer, and likewise, the rite of immobilization during the rainy season.
Killing rites should be performed in the winter, while pacifying rites are prescribed for autumn;
one skilled in the aforementioned rituals should perform enriching rites during the early winter.

Spring is said to be in the forenoon, summer at midday; the rainy season is known to be in the afternoon, and likewise, the cool season (śiśira) at dusk. Autumn occurs at midnight, and the dewy season (hemanta) is said to be at dawn.
Indeed, all these seasons have been described here in their proper order;
devoid of them, [the rites] do not succeed, even for one who performs them with great effort.
For they certainly achieve success through undivided devotion; it is not otherwise.
Thus ends the determination of the seasons;
now follows the determination of lunar days (tithis):
a wise person should accomplish rites of subjugation on the seventh lunar day.
On the third and likewise on the thirteenth day, one should indeed perform the rite of attraction.
One should perform the rite of eradication (uccāṭana) on the second and the sixth lunar days;
likewise, the rite of immobilization (stambhana) on the fourteenth, the fourth, and the first lunar days.
One should employ delusion on the ninth and likewise on the eighth;
and similarly, one should employ killing on the twelfth as well as on the eleventh.
On the fifth and on the full moon day, one should perform rites for pacification and so forth;
these lunar days have been declared in sequence for the sake of accomplishing all vidyās.
Thus concludes the determination of the lunar days (tithis). Now, regarding the days of the week:
on Friday there is prosperity, on Saturday subjugation, and on Sunday the rite of killing.
Uccāṭana (expulsion) is auspicious on Wednesday and Bhauma (Tuesday), as are rites such as vidveṣa (enmity). || 1 ||
Stambhana, mohana, and the supreme vaśīkaraṇa—
know that these should be performed here in the Māhendra and Vāruṇa [yantras].
One should perform the rites of inciting enmity and eradication through the conjunction of fire and air.
Jyeṣṭhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Anurādhā,
and Rohiṇī are said to be situated within the Maṇḍala of Mahendra and are bestowers of success in one's undertakings.
Uttarābhādrapadā, Mūlā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvābhādrapadā, and Āśleṣā should be known as situated in the middle of Vāruṇa;
and Pūrvāṣāḍhā is remembered by Śambhu as bestowing success in those rites. || 4 ||
Svātī, Hasta, Mṛgaśiras, Citrā, Uttaraphālgunī,
Puṣya, and Punarvasu are proclaimed to be situated within the circle of fire.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śravaṇa, Maghā,
Viśākhā, Kṛttikā, Pūrvāphālgunī, and likewise Revatī—
situated within the sphere of Vāyu, these grant success in their respective undertakings.
Thus concludes the determination regarding the Māhendra and other [deities].
[There are] indeed the rites of pacification (śāntika), nourishment (pauṣṭika), and malevolent magic (abhicārika). || 7 ||
The wise one should diligently perform the sequence mounted upon the index finger and the others;
likewise, both [fingers] mounted upon the thumb are for all ritual acts.
Thus ends the determination of the fingers.
Now follows the consideration of the relative strength of medicinal herbs:
a medicine accompanied by the proper ritual and mantras shall be fruitful.
But medicine devoid of ritual and mantras becomes like mere wood.
When that medicinal herb remains in a secluded and auspicious forest, it accomplishes its purpose; indeed, it possesses potency therein.
Herbs that grow by chance in anthills, hollows, streets, at the foot of trees, in temples, or in cremation grounds, though prescribed by ritual injunction, shall not grant success.

Physicians declare that a medicinal substance which has been soaked in water, scorched by fire, grown out of season, or whose body is infested with worms— whether it be deficient or excessive— is no longer a fit substance for use.
Thus concludes the consideration of the relative strength and weakness of medicinal herbs. Now follows the procedure for collecting root-herbs:
having worshipped Girīśa (Śiva) at dawn, accompanied by [the recitation of] the *bhūta* mantras and other rites, those who have risen early [should proceed].
All medicinal herbs should be gathered, whether they have been worshipped by those observing the ancestral rites (śrāddha) or not.
Thus, the ritual procedure and the mantra for all roots are declared.
First, having gone to the root of a tree, one should consecrate it with the mantra.
Oṃ! May the vetālas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and reptiles—all of them—depart from this tree by the command of Śiva. 3.
Then the salutation:
Oṃ, salutations to you, who are born of nectar and who increase strength and vigor;
grant me strength and long life, and protect me from sin from afar. || 4 ||
Then [there is] the digging by which Brahmā digs you, by which Bhṛgu digs you,
by which Indra and Varuṇa likewise approached you. || 5 ||
Therefore, I shall dig with my hand purified by mantras;
do not fall, lest these [seeds] fall, and lest your splendor be diminished.
Stay right here, O auspicious lady; be one who carries out my work. Once my task is accomplished and completed, you shall then go to heaven.

The mantra for uprooting: With this mantra, on a Sunday, under the Puṣya asterism, or during the conjunction of Puṣya and the Sun, one should uproot all medicinal herbs. *Oṃ hrīṃ kṣauṃ phaṭ svāhā*. With this, one should cut the root. This is the procedure for taking the roots.
*Oṃ hrīṃ caṇḍe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. *Oṃ hrīṃ kṣauṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Oṃ hrīṃ caṇḍe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā— this is the procedure for taking the root-plant (mūlikā).
Now follows the procedure for taking the *bandā* plant.
The mantra: Oṃ vanadaṇḍe mahādaṇḍāya svāhā | Oṃ śūdrī (sūtrī)kapālamālinī svāhā.
Having recited [the mantra] seven times for each [deity], the *bandā* (garland) should be taken; from that, the accomplishment of the task follows.
This is the procedure for taking the *bandā*.
Thus is the determination of time for the sake of accomplishing all vidyās.
And herein has been explained with diligence the extraction of the roots and so forth.
Now, regarding subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*):
therein, the subjugation of all people is the supreme among the castes, as is the station of the mantra.
And also Oṃkāraśiras, and then Oṃkāraśiras again. || 1 ||
Having placed the letter *ra* at the lower part, one should extract the mantra;
it should be recited while consuming food that is free from meat. || 2 ||
By this mantra— *kroṃ proṃ vroṃ*—
even kings who are otherwise difficult to subdue, as well as sons, friends, kinsmen,
those born of my lineage, and all animals everywhere [shall be brought under control]. (3)
All those who are to be accomplished—
whether they have been questioned, seen, or whose names have been taken there— come under one's control by reciting [the mantra] five hundred times.
Then, all mantras beginning with these should be received with devotion from the guru;
thus all undertakings are accomplished, for otherwise one shall not attain success.
The mantra is:
*Oṃ namaḥ kaṭavikaṭaghorarūpiṇī svāhā*. By means of this mantra, a ball of food consecrated seven times, when eaten for seven days in the name of someone, that person certainly becomes submissive.
Oṃ namaḥ kaṭavikaṭaghorarūpiṇī svāhā. The mantra:
Oṃ vaśyamukhī rājamukhī svāhā. By rinsing the mouth with this, all become submissive.
The mantra verse is:

*Oṃ rājamukhi vaśyamukhi svāhā*. Having placed oil in the left hand, one should consecrate it three times with the ring finger; then, having recited the root mantra three times, one should stand upon the bed at dawn and smear [the oil] on the face, hair, and so forth. By doing so, all people become submissive, and even a tiger will not devour [one].
The mantra is:
Oṃ cāmuṇḍe jaya jaya stambhaya stambhaya jambhaya jambhaya mohaya mohaya sarvasattvān namaḥ svāhā. Having consecrated flowers with this, whoever they are given to becomes submissive.
Oṃ Cāmuṇḍe, victory! Victory! Paralyze, paralyze! Render unconscious, render unconscious! Delude, delude all sentient beings! Svāhā!
The practitioner, remaining with a one-pointed mind, should recite this mantra thirty thousand times;
thereafter, the adept causes the worlds to tremble by his mere sight.
One should grind the root of the banyan tree known as Bhūtākhyavaṭa with water; when combined with sacred ash and the mantra, this tilaka brings the world under one's control.

Having bound the root of *punarnavā* to one's hand on the day of the Puṣya asterism after it has been consecrated seven times with the mantra, one shall be honored everywhere; the mantra for this is stated right here: *aiṃ rauṃ ḍaṃ kṣobhaya bhagavati tvaṃ svāhā*. For this aforementioned yoga, one should first recite the mantra twenty thousand times. 8.
One should grind the root of the Apāmārga plant with gallstone (rocanā) and apply it as a tilaka on the forehead; thus one shall bring the three worlds under one's control.
Oṃ aiṃ rauṃ ḍaṃ, O Blessed One, cause agitation, svāhā!

Oṃ, salutation to you, the garlanded one who possesses a net of arrows of Kandarpa, O you who bring all worlds under control, svāhā! Having recited this mantra-conjoined yoga one thousand and eight times, success [will follow].
Oṃ, homage to her who wears a garland of the clusters of arrows of Kandarpa, the subduer of all worlds, svāhā!
On the fourteenth or the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
having fasted and offered a bali-oblation, one should uproot the sahadevī plant and grind it into powder.
That powder, when given with betel-leaf, certainly brings about subjugation;
that powder should also be employed in bathing and as an unguent, and it will become a means of subjugation.
A forehead mark (tilaka) made from rocanā and sahadevī brings the world under one's control;
one should wear that powder on the head, for it brings subjugation everywhere.
Having placed its root in her mouth and tied it around her waist, one should desire whichever woman; she shall become submissive through this mantra-yoga, as it is taught.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Lady Mātaṅgeśvarī, the delighter of all faces, O Great Illusionist of all, Mātaṅgī, Kumārikā, you whose tongue is *lahalahaja*, the subduer of all worlds, svāhā! Having recited this a thousand times, there is success in the aforementioned yogas. 12.

The root of the white *parājitā* plant, uprooted while the moon is eclipsed, enables a man whose eyes are colored with it to bring the three worlds under his control; likewise, that same root, when combined with *rocanā* and applied as a forehead mark (*tilaka*), brings the world under one's power. (13)

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Mistress of the Mātaṅgas, who delights the faces of all; O Great Illusion, Mātaṅgī, O Maiden, O you with the lolling tongue, O you who bring all the world under your power, svāhā!
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should take white guñjā and its root;
these should be administered with betel-leaf to bring all the world under one's control. || 14 ||

When a tilaka is made with stone-paste, yellow pigment (rocanā), and betel leaf mixed with water, it brings all people under one's control through mere conversation; this is the supreme method of subjugation.
If that same mixture is encased in gold and used for a tilaka, [the result is even greater]. || 15 ||
Upon merely being seen, whether she be a woman or even a man, she comes under one's control.
Oṃ vajrakiraṇe śive rakṣa bhava imam ādya amṛtaṃ kuru kuru svāhā.
Then, by reciting this mantra one thousand times according to the prescribed yoga, success is attained. 16.

Oṃ vajrakiraṇe śive rakṣa bhava imam ādya amṛtaṃ kuru kuru svāhā. One should place the impurities of the heart, feet, eyes, and nose into betel nut. Whoever eats that betel nut shall remain under one's control for as long as they live. || 17 ||
Having consecrated the root of the *daṇḍendīvara* with mantras,
and having rubbed it with *rocanā* in a copper vessel, [one should apply it] as collyrium to both eyes.
He becomes beloved to all at the mere sight of him; of this there is no doubt. || 18 ||
That root, combined with honey, should be applied as a tilaka on the forehead or placed in betel leaf; it is an excellent means of subjugation.
One should grind the root of that plant—or a root arising from *rañjana*—and apply it;
when given with betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) to one who has eaten, it will certainly bring about subjugation (*vaśya*).
Having consecrated [the materials] with this mantra, "Oṃ piṅgalāyai namaḥ," one should accomplish the aforementioned yogas. || 20 ||
Oṃ, salutation to Piṅgalā.
Having taken both eyes of a red vulture, or one eye of a black peacock, or having taken a black female peacock, [one should prepare] a lamp with its oil. (21)
Having prepared a wick and smeared it with honey for the purpose of producing collyrium,
one should apply that as eye-salve and bring the three worlds under one's control.
A wise man should have a pill made from *devadālī* and *siddhārtha*;
by placing it in his mouth, he becomes beloved by all—there is no other way. (23)
By placing the root of the *bhṛṅga* plant in one's mouth, one shall be honored by all.
Having gathered the *vaṭavandāka* plant under the asterism of Rohiṇī, one should wear it on the hand;
this brings everything under one's control, as spoken by Viśvāmitra. (24)
Equal parts of saffron, tagara, and kuṣṭha, along with yellow orpiment— these three, applied as a tilaka with blood from the ring finger, bring the world under one's control.
Having ground together *viṣṇukrāntā*, auspicious *bhṛṅgī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and *mūlarocanā*,
and having formed them into a pill, a tilaka made from this is the supreme means for subjugation.
A wise person should prepare a pill from the root of Śvetabhānu, uprooted during the Puṣya asterism, with goat urine; by means of a tilaka-mark made from it, the world is brought under control.
On a Friday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, a wise man should grind that root with goat's blood;
having extracted the collyrium, a person should apply it to his eyes.
The three worlds come under one's control merely by being seen; of this there is no doubt. || 28 ||
If one takes the root of the piṇḍītagara plant under the asterism of Śravaṇā and wears it, it brings the entire world under one's control. || 29 ||
Having uprooted the root of the *kṛṣṇāparājitā* under the asterism of Puṣya, one should grind it into powder;
mixing it with cow’s ghee, the wise man should apply it as collyrium.
By merely anointing oneself with that very [substance], one shall bring the three worlds under one's control. || 30 ||
A man who applies a tilaka made from the leaf of the putrajīvaka tree combined with yellow pigment (rocanā) upon his forehead becomes beloved by all. (31)
Having applied a tilaka mark at the tip of the nose with the root of white Aparājitā as well as the tips of white Javā flowers, one will bring others under control; of this there is no doubt.

By applying a tilaka on the forehead made from mañjiṣṭhā, yavakṣāra, vacā, śitasūryamūla, one’s own blood, and kuṣṭha in equal parts, the grateful one brings the three worlds under his control in a mere instant. || 33 ||
Water from the Śambhu-vessel, madhuka, kṛtāñjali,
and sacrificial oblation (havya)— these, mixed equally with the impurity of one's own body,
are used for the rites of anointing and eating, or when applying a tilaka.
This very yoga brings the worlds under one's control. || 34 ||
The roots of jaṭā, tagara, and meṣaviṣāṇikā,
along with the five parts [of these] and one's own bodily excrement,
should likewise be combined with honey on a Tuesday.
By means of the curved tilaka, they bring the worlds under their control. || 35 ||
The pair of wings of a bhr̥ṅga bee combined with the flesh of a parrot, one's own ring-finger blood and earwax, and one's own seed—
these, by means of the method of anointing or by consumption, [achieve the desired result].
They bring even the entire world under their control instantaneously. || 36 ||
Having applied a wick made of *tālīśa*, *kuṣṭha*, and *tagara* together with *siddhārtha* oil and wrapped in a firm cloth,
[one should apply it] to the surface of a man's skull.
By that collyrium, it is said, the world comes under one's control. || 37 ||
Having combined yellow orpiment, lotus petals, priyaṅgu, and red sandalwood, one should apply it as collyrium to the eyes; whoever one looks upon shall become submissive. || 38 ||

The impurities of the nose and eyes, along with the impurities of the feet, mixed with betel nut and consecrated with mantras— if these are given to someone, that person will certainly become submissive.
Oṃ, obeisance to Piṅgalā. Now follows the method for subjugating kings:
saffron, sandalwood, and gorocanā mixed with the excrement of a rabbit.
An ornamental mark made with cow's milk certainly brings the king under one's control.
Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ, bring such-and-such a person under my control, svāhā!
Having first recited this mantra one thousand times, one should apply a tilaka consecrated seven times with it.
Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ, bring [the person named] so-and-so under my control, svāhā!
Having carefully tied a sprig of the *caṃpaka* tree in one's hand, one should grasp it according to the prescribed rite during the asterism of Bharaṇī or Puṣya. (2)
At that very moment, a person shall bring the king under their control; by binding the root of the Sudarśanā plant upon the hand, one shall become beloved by the king.
Thus ends the subjugation of kings.
Now, for the subjugation of women: having gathered a flower under the asterism Puṣya, and likewise a fruit under Bharaṇī;
One should likewise offer a branch under Viśākhā, and similarly a leaf under Hasta. || 1 ||
Having uprooted the root of the *kṛṣṇonmatta* plant from its base,
one should then grind it together with camphor, saffron, and equal parts of *rocanā*.
By means of this forehead mark (tilaka), even a woman as steadfast as Arundhatī herself comes under one's control.
Kākajaṅghā, vacā, and kuṣṭha, mixed with semen and blood—if these are placed in her food, a young girl will weep constantly in the cremation ground.
*Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya cāmuṇḍe amukīṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*. This is the mantra for all the aforementioned applications. (3)
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord Rudra; Oṃ, Cāmuṇḍā, bring [the woman] named so-and-so under my control, svāhā!
Having washed one's face in the morning, if one drinks water consecrated seven times with this mantra while uttering the name of a woman, that woman will certainly become submissive. (4)
Oṃ, homage to Kṣiprakāminī! Bring so-and-so under my control, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Kṣiprakāminī! Bring so-and-so under my control, svāhā! || 4 ||
One should give the root of *kṛṣṇāparājitā* combined with betel leaf to a woman who is unwilling; she will certainly become submissive, and not otherwise.
Oṃ hūṃ svāhā. Having consecrated [it] with this, one should give it. || 5 ||
Having performed seven recitations over a flower while designating it with the names of the person to be won over and the practitioner, whoever is given that flower will certainly become submissive.
For when this mantra is well-accomplished, it necessarily bestows its fruit;
therefore, one should accomplish this supreme mantra with diligent effort. (7)
Oṃ hūṃ svāhā!
One should collect vandāka during the asterism Viśākhā and under the influence of Maṅgala;
having tied it on the hand, one brings a choice woman under one's control. || 8 ||
Oṃ pāte vajrāya svāhā!
Black utpala, a pair of wings from a bee, the root of tagara, and white kākajaṅghā—when this powder is applied to the head of a young woman, she will instantly become a slave; how wonderful! (9)

She whose left foot a playful woman suddenly smears with the semen from her own source at the conclusion of dalliance using her lotus-like right hand—she alone becomes his mistress; of this there is no doubt. (10)
Having ground together rock salt, honey, and *pottamala*, one should smear it upon the penis and enjoy a young newly-wed bride;
she will certainly not go to another man even in her mind, and with a charming, divine form, she will surely become a devoted servant. (11)

Having smeared the banner with gorocanā, the seeds of Śiśiradīdhiti and Śambhu, combined with saffron, sandalwood, and liquid gold, a man who sports with whichever woman he desires becomes like a crest-jewel upon her heart. (12)
Under the Puṣya asterism, a wise person should cause the root of Rudrajaṭā to be placed in the mouth;
it should be given with betel and other such items, and she will certainly become submissive. 13.
In the same way, the root of *pāṭalā* combined with betel-leaf acts as a subjugator.
Having ground the root of the three-leaved *bhaṇṭikā*, one should apply it to the body;
by a mere drop, she instantly comes under one's control. (14)
Taking his own desire, he should again meditate upon Kāmadeva;
by that which is placed in the heart of a young woman, she becomes submissive at that very moment. (15)
If a woman finds delight after swallowing even a little mercury, she will not abandon that man even at the end of her life. (16)
If one recites [the mantra] at night for half a month with a mind overcome by desire,
the delighted servant of the universe will certainly bring about subjugation.

Aiṃ piṃ sthāṃ klīṃ! O Kāmapiśācinī, quickly seize, seize [the woman] named so-and-so; with passion, tear her apart with your nails, tear her apart with your nails; put her to flight, put her to flight; bind her with affection, bind her! Śrīṃ phaṭ!
Success is achieved with twenty thousand [recitations]. || 17 ||
The best of those who know mantras should grind together nāgāpuṣpa, priyaṅgu, tagara, padmakeśara, jaṭāmāṃsī, and nimba in equal proportions.

Aiṃ piṃ sthāṃ klīṃ! O Kāmapiśācinī, quickly seize, seize [the woman] named so-and-so! With passion, tear her with your nails, tear her with your nails! Put her to flight, put her to flight! Bind her with affection, bind her! Śrīṃ phaṭ!
By fumigating one’s own body with this, women will serve one like lovers.
This is the incense mantra.
Oṃ mūlī mūlī mahāmūlī, agitate, agitate all these calamities, svāhā! Thus.
Having offered seven handfuls of water and recited this vidyā, a man obtains an adorned maiden within the span of a single month. (19)
Oṃ, the Gandharva named Viśvāvasu is the lord of maidens; grant me a maiden of beautiful form, well-adorned! Homage to that Viśvāvasu, svāhā!
One should cast a piece of *śāla* wood eleven finger-breadths long into the house of the maiden.
And he who bestows that maiden under the constellation of Pūrvaphālgunī— || 20 ||
Now, for the subjugation of a husband: one should grind the flesh of a wagtail together with honey. By applying this as an ointment to the vagina, the husband will certainly become a slave.
Having ground the five parts of a pomegranate together with white mustard seeds, even an unfortunate woman makes her husband a slave by applying it to the vagina. (1)
Camphor and *devadāru* wood, together with honey, yield the same result as before.
[The mantra is: *oṃ kāmakāmamālini patiṃ me vaśamānaya ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*.
Success in the aforementioned applications is achieved when [the substance] has been consecrated seven times with this mantra. || 2 ||

Oṃ, O garlanded one who fulfills desires, bring my husband under my control! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ. Having ground together yellow pigment (rocanā) and fish gall, when this is applied as a tilaka on the little finger of the left hand, the husband will certainly become a servant.
A tilaka made from one's own blood mixed with gorocana brings the husband under control.
One should have the flowers of the *citraka* tree prepared with honey;
this should be given for consumption and drink, and it will bring the husband under one's control.
Furthermore, by applying *bhūrja* bark mixed with honey to the vagina, the husband becomes submissive.
One should place the powder of snails, conch shells, and the like into the mouth of the leeches.
Having collected that powder and combined it with betel leaf, it should be given to the master to eat; thus he becomes submissive, and not otherwise. || 5 ||
One who always applies a tilaka made from that [substance] infused with gorocanā, nalada, and kuṅkuma attains power over others;
this was revealed by Vātsyāyana in many ways at the time of performing rites for the good fortune of women. (6)

At the conclusion of sexual enjoyment, whichever passionate woman touches her own husband's penis with her left lotus-foot, her husband immediately becomes her servant; this is indeed declared by the Son of the Donkey as the "King of Yogas."
Thus ends the subjugation of the husband; this is the first instruction, titled "Subjugation," in the *Kāmaratna* composed by the illustrious Nityanātha. || 1 ||
The second instruction: now, regarding attraction— having drawn forth the fourth letter situated within the second group [of consonants].
Having placed three *hāṃ*s ending with *hāṃ*, [one should place] the second *he* at the end of that.
Having placed the syllable *aṃ* at the head, one should recite the mantra syllable by syllable:
*jhāṃ jhāṃ jhāṃ hāṃ hāṃ hāṃ heṃ heṃ*.
By reciting it five hundred times, the eternal fruit is attained. || 2 ||
O lady of beautiful limbs, humans, asuras, and gods, along with yakṣas, nāgas, and rākṣasas— both the stationary and the moving— have been drawn forth by you.
Oṃ jhāṃ jhāṃ jhāṃ hāṃ hāṃ hāṃ heṃ heṃ.
Having taken the letter *ra* at the end of *hā*, and especially the letter *ya*,
one should divide that triad of syllables into two parts and emanate them.
Having personally prepared the edible substance, one should perform the visualization with the mantra.
O auspicious lady, whatever food is given to all living beings,
they all go at that very moment to wherever they are led.
One should consecrate the noose with the syllable *hrīṃ* and likewise the goad with the syllable *hūṃ*.
Holding the three-fold noose in the left hand and the blazing goad in the right hand,
the practitioner of mantra should then recite this mantra.

The mantra is: *Oṃ hrīṃ rakṣa rakṣa cāmuṇḍe turu turu [name] ākarṣaya [name] ākarṣaya hrīṃ*. One should first recite this mantra ten thousand times (*ayuta*); thereafter, success (*siddhi*) is attained. *Oṃ cāmuṇḍe jvala jvala prajvala prajvala svāhā*. Upon seeing a woman, one should recite this mantra; at that very moment, that woman will come from behind. One should first recite it ten thousand times; thereafter, success is attained. (7)
Oṃ, protect, protect, O Cāmuṇḍā! Turu turu! Summon so-and-so, summon so-and-so! Hrīḥ!
Oṃ, Cāmuṇḍā, blaze, blaze, blaze forth, blaze forth, svāhā!
Having gathered a cluster of arjuna flowers under the constellation Āśleṣā...
Having ground [the substance] with goat’s urine, one should cause it to be applied to the head of women;
for men or animals, one should throw it [upon them], and there will be attraction.
Then, one should fetch that clay from a place where a female lizard has been killed;
thereafter, one should have an image fashioned from it using the blood of a chameleon.
One should write that syllable of the Sādhyas within her heart with red [pigment].
One should always bury it in the place where urine is voided and void one's urine right there;
by this, one may attract that woman even if she is situated a hundred yojanas away.
On the fifth lunar day, a wise man should cause the root of the sūryāvarta plant to be seized;
he should offer it together with betel leaf, and she herself will arrive at that very moment.
The two hands engaged in the act of pleasure should be carefully grasped by the wise as two bees;
having separated them, one should burn them with the wood of the funeral pyre.
One should bind the ashes separately into two small effigies with a cloth;
having firmly tied one of them to the horn of a goat, one should test it.
Whichever female sheep she follows, that one is separately seized by the wise.
That ash, when placed upon the head, will attract women in an instant.
Furthermore, it should be kept on the garment; otherwise, the amorous woman will not come. (15)
Oṃ, svāhā to the one of black complexion! One should first recite this mantra ten thousand times. Then, having consecrated the aforementioned yoga [substance] with it, success is attained. || 16 ||
Thus ends the second instruction, titled "Attraction," in the *Kāmaratna* composed by the illustrious Nityanātha. || 2 ||
The Third Instruction:
Now, as for victory:
the letter *ha* joined with a vowel, well-honored by the letter *u*.
Having worshipped with the syllable *oṃ*, one should apply *phaṭ* at the beginning;
by reciting "oṃ huṃ phaṭ" a hundred times before the one to be conquered, he is surely defeated, and not otherwise. || 1 ||
Having placed that which was to be conquered within his heart, closing his eyes,
and touching it while reciting the mantra, he conquered it in that very instant.
Either *gojihvā* or the root of *śikhimūlī*, when placed in the mouth or on the head,
secured under the asterism of Puṣya, brings victory in all debates.
On the full moon day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should extract the root of the Śikhī plant;
by wearing it on the arm or the head, one shall be victorious in debate.
One should collect girikarṇī, śamī, and white guñjā;
combined with sandalwood, one becomes victorious by means of this tilaka. || 5 ||
Kanakārka, vaṭa, vahni, vidruma, and likewise pañcama—
he who applies the tilaka with these shall see his enemy in five ways.
In the skull of a black cobra, provided with fat and clay, one should plant white guñjā seeds; from that, one should collect the root.
Then the enemy, having seen him with the tilaka mark applied, would perceive himself as being overwhelmed.
While he was being devoured by packs of dogs and had fallen upon the ground,
an herb named Siṃhikā rubbed him with its great essence.
It should be placed between a *siṃhī* plant and a cowrie shell, accompanied by its root;
then, having covered its opening with beeswax.
When that [mark] is situated crookedly, however, a man is known to be like a lion;
he remains undefeated in battle, in the royal court, at gambling, and in dispute.
At the mere sight of him, even an elephant intoxicated with rut turns its face away. (11)
Mercury, rubbed with the juice of *vyāghrī* and combined with its root, should be processed as before; and likewise, the fruit of *vyāghrī* should be prepared in that same manner. (12)
Having tied the root of the Sudarśanā plant in his hand, one is victorious in the royal court;
the root of the Jayā plant, placed in the mouth, bestows victory in the royal court.
Under the constellation Ārdrā, one becomes invincible by tying a sprig of the *vaṭa* tree in one's hand;
under that same asterism, one should take a sprig of the mango tree and hold it in the hand.
One attains victory in battle; by remembering Jayā, one shall become victorious. || 14 ||
One should wrap the left eye of a *kokā* bird with molten lead;
by placing it in one's mouth, a man shall be victorious in all debate. (15)
If Kṛttikā and Viśākhā are conjoined with a Tuesday,
a weapon forged on that day will grant victory in battle.
Whatever weapons are smeared with the juice of Apāmārga will certainly become as hard as adamant in battle. (17)
One should consecrate all of those with the King of Mantras mentioned previously;
for you, the accomplishment of all the aforementioned yogas will certainly come to pass.
If one holds in the hand the root of the *arka-lāṅgalī* plant consecrated with the root mantra,
then by rubbing with its powder, a wrestler can bewilder many other wrestlers.

Mantra: Oṃ, homage to you of great strength and prowess, expert in the science of weapons, Śārada! Bind, bind the arm-strength of [Name]! Paralyze, paralyze his sight! Shake, shake his limbs! Cast him down, cast him down upon the surface of the earth! Hūṃ! 19.

Oṃ, homage to the one of great strength and prowess, skilled in the science of weapons! O Śārada, bind, bind the arm-strength of [Name]! Paralyze, paralyze his sight! Shake, shake his limbs! Cast him down, cast him down upon the surface of the earth! Hūṃ! 18–19.
Thus ends the section on victory.
Now, the procedure for securing good fortune:
the root of white Arka (Calotropis gigantea) extracted under the Puṣya asterism [should be applied] to the right arm.
Having tied it, even she who is unfortunate attains good fortune from her husband. (20)
The root of red *citraka*, uprooted during a lunar eclipse, should be ground with honey and made into pills; by applying these as a tilaka, even an unfortunate woman becomes beautiful.
Having written someone's name with saffron, gorocanā, and lacquer, if one places it in the midst of honey, good fortune arises. || 22 ||
Having written someone's name on a bilva leaf with saffron and lac-dye, if one places it in the midst of honey, that person becomes fortunate within seven days. || 23 ||
Thus ends the procedure for bringing about good fortune.
Now follows the pacification of the wrath of Īśvara and others (the rite for quelling the anger of Īśvara).
Oṃ, peaceful, perfectly peaceful, pacifier of all anger, svāhā!
By reciting this mantra twenty-one times and wiping the face with it, the pacification of anger occurs; one becomes devoted to serenity. 24.
Oṃ, peaceful, thoroughly pacified, allanger-subduer, svāhā!
Having written the name on a palm leaf with a thorn, one should place it in the mud;
the angry person becomes appeased. 25.
Having written someone's name with *gorocanā* on birch bark, if one places it in the midst of milk, an angry person becomes pacified. || 26 ||
Thus ends the pacification of anger.
Now, for the warding off of elephants:
having captured a muskrat under an auspicious lunar mansion, one should grind it into powder.
By means of that ointment, the elephant indeed goes far away from the front. || 27 ||
The powder of bilva flowers mixed with an equal amount of chuchundarī [root]—upon seeing a man whose limbs are smeared with this, even an elephant flees from afar. (28)
The root of the markaṭavallī plant, when tied to the arm or on the head, removes even a wicked elephant; it moves far away and becomes a wondrous sight.
The root of white aparājitā held in the hand will ward off an elephant;
the root of triśūlī placed in the mouth certainly brings an elephant under control. (30)
Thus ends the warding off of elephants.
Now, the warding off of tigers:
The root of the *bṛhatī* plant held in the mouth, or held in the hand, overcomes the fear of tigers. (31)

Reciting the eight-syllable mantra—*hrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ drauṃ drauṃ hi* or *krīṃ hrīṃ oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ*—one should recite it over a clod of earth and throw it; then [the opponent] will not move their mouth and will be unable to go.
Hrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ drauṃ drauṃ hi eti, or alternatively,
krīṃ hrīṃ oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should take the root of the lāṅgalī plant.
It is proclaimed that [this mantra], held in the hand, removes the fear of tigers, lions, and other such creatures.
Thus ends the third instruction, titled "The Warding Off of Victorious Tigers and Other Such Creatures," in the *Kāmaratna* composed by Śrī Nityanātha. 3.
The Fourth Instruction:
Now, the paralyzing of the mouths of enemies:
the root of the *meghanāda* plant, encircled by a *tāra*, should be placed in the mouth.
The opponent adversary shall either become mute or depart for the ends of the earth. || 1 ||
The root arising from the white guñjā plant, when placed in the mouth, conquers those with large beaks.
Oṃ hrīṃ, protect me, O Cāmuṇḍā! Turu turu! Bring such-and-such a person under my control, svāhā!
This is the mantra of Cāmuṇḍā, which brings success in the two aforementioned yogas. || 2 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ! Protect, O Cāmuṇḍā! Turu turu! Bring so-and-so under my control, svāhā!
On a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, a wise person should take a madhuvandāka flower and cast it [into the assembly];
then, in the midst of the assembly, the mouths of everyone become paralyzed.

Having written someone's name with the juice of yellow orpiment on an Arka leaf, if one places it in the northeast corner of a garden, the binding of that person's mouth occurs—that is, their speech is paralyzed. || 4 ||
Thus ends the suppression of speech.
Now, for the suppression of sleep:
one should prepare a nasal medication by grinding the root of *bṛhatī* and *madhuka*.
This indeed is the suppression of sleep, as spoken by Mūladeva.
Thus ends the method for paralyzing sleep. Now, for the method of paralyzing a boat:
on the day of the Bharaṇī asterism, one should drive a five-finger-long stake made of *kṣīrikā* wood [into the water].
Then, in the midst of the ship, the mooring of the vessel will certainly take place.
Thus ends the method for paralyzing a boat;
now follows the method for paralyzing weapons:
aṅgulī, jaṭā, pāṭhā, viṣṇukrāntā, and pāṭalī.
The white Aparājitā, together with the goddess Kākajaṅghikā, [should be used] by men. || 7 ||
Having been extracted under the Puṣya asterism, she remains situated upon the crooked head;
she alone indeed wards off the multitude of weapons in the clash of men.
Having tied [it], one shall conquer the fear of tigers, kings, thieves, and enemies;
the root of the *jātī* flower placed in the mouth is the supreme means for paralyzing an enemy.
During an eclipse of the sun or the moon, one should take the root of either the Puṅkhā or the Pāṭalā plant;
it removes [the affliction] when held in the mouth, as if struck by a shaft or weapon.
On the day of Kṛttikā, one should extract the Vandāka plant from a Kapittha tree;
that very plant, when positioned crookedly, becomes a supreme means for paralyzing a sword.
Having bound the root of the *sudarśana* to the hand, there shall be a paralysis of weapons;
the tip of the *ketakī* placed on the eyes, and the root of the *tāla* situated in the mouth.
And when holding a date-palm fruit in the hand during battle, it becomes a pillar of swords. || 12 ||
One should drink these three roots ground together with clarified butter for three nights; thereafter, one is never afflicted by them for as long as one lives. || 13 ||
Kumbhakarṇa becomes propitious for all these aforementioned yogas;
he shall ward off the approaching army and its multitude of weapons.

*Oṃ aho? Kumbhakarṇa, great rākṣasa, born from the womb of Kaikasī, paralyze the enemy army! The Great Blessed Lord Rudra commands this, svāhā!* One should recite this one hundred and eight times for all the yogas to achieve success. || 14 ||
Oṃ! Aho, Kumbhakarṇa, great rākṣasa born from the womb of Kaikasī! Paralyze the enemy army! The Great Blessed Lord Rudra commands this: svāhā! || 13-14 ||
Bearing a hook, a discus, a thunderbolt, a trident, and likewise a mace,
she resides within the bodies of men in battle, warding off all weapons.
If the root of the Apāmārga plant is taken under an auspicious lunar mansion,
it serves as a protection against all weapons for heroes by its mere application as an ointment.
The date palm held in the middle of the mouth, the ketaka flower tied at the waist, and the sun-disk resting upon the staff-like arms—this constitutes the warding off of all weapons. (17)
If one uproots the white guñjā plant during the Puṣya asterism and wears its stalk on the hand,
there shall never be any fear in battle.
Having encased the mercury, combined with vajra and mica, within three metals, it wards off all weapons when held in the mouth or held in the hand. (19)
Brahmadaṇḍī, Kaumārī, Īśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Vajriṇī, Cāndrī, and likewise Mahālakṣmī. || 20 ||
These are divine medicinal herbs, and they are likewise known as the Mothers;
by remembering them and binding them upon one's hand, they ward off all weapons.
Thus ends the immobilization of weapons.
Now, the immobilization of fire: Oṃ Śaṅkara Hara Hara, immobilize the fire, immobilize it!
By blowing upon the fire with this [mantra], one paralyzes the fire.
Oṃ śaṃkara hara-hara, paralyze the fire, paralyze it!
Having recited this over the matted locks of the goddess Tārā, the slayer of Mahiṣa, a man who enters into the midst of acacia embers is not burned. 22.

Oṃ, O you who are dense with the destruction of my hips, O you who are to be meditated upon as the hips, O you who are like the ocean of the venerable Alipya, having scattered [the enemy] into the lower realms, O Mantrin, krīṃ phaṭ! || 1 ||
Oṃ krīṃ! O you who ride upon a buffalo, paralyze, paralyze; delude, delude; shatter, shatter; obstruct the fire, obstruct it! Ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ! || 2 ||
Having ground kumārī and śūraṇa, a man whose hands are smeared with it will not be burned by glowing coals when he uses iron implements accompanied by mantras. (23)
Having ground the juice of the kumārī plant,
a man whose hands are smeared with it will not be burned by glowing coals or heated metals, provided he employs the mantra.
The mantra, however, is as before. || 24 ||
By binding the root of the *sudarśana* plant to the hand, the immobilization of fire occurs;
here, the drawing of the mantra is as before. (25)
Thus ends the suppression of fire.
Now, for the suppression of water:
one should prepare a fine powder of the substance known as *padmaka*.
One should cast [the image] into ponds, wells, or tanks, or bind it within water.
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Rudra! Paralyze the water, paralyze it! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ!
Within half a moment he shall break the jar, yet the water remains right there. || 27 ||
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Rudra! Paralyze the water, paralyze it! Ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ!
One should smear the roots of *devadālī* combined with the juice of a frog upon the hands and feet; this is the supreme method for paralyzing water. (28)
One should fashion a pair of sandals from the ground powder of the Śleṣmāntaka plant;
having bound them with the skin of a monitor lizard, one may mount them and walk upon the water. (29)
Having ground the fruit of the Śleṣmāntaka tree into powder, one should smear it upon a jar to a thickness of one finger-breadth;
once dried, one should fill it with water.
Having taken the root of a śirīṣa tree on a Sunday,
one should rub it with water and apply it as a tilaka-mark upon the forehead.
Thus ends the immobilization of water.
Now, the immobilization of the divine:
likewise, in the ordeal by heated [metal], one is liberated from the fault of every deed.
One should take the root of Meghanāda facing north;
by eating it or wearing it with one's garments, it is supreme for producing divine pillars.
The root arising from the white guñjā plant should be taken under the constellation Uttarabhādrapadā, facing north; when placed in the mouth, it produces divine paralysis.
Having ground the root of *bhṛṅgī* and *rocanā*, one should smear it upon the hand;
by making a tilaka-mark on the forehead with this, one becomes victorious in heated divine contests. || 34 ||
If one has committed an offense using divine rice-grains produced from the sun, one is liberated by chewing and swallowing marīca, māgadhī, and elā. || 35 ||
Having drunk clarified butter with sugar and having chewed ginger and *vacā*, one should thereafter lick heated iron; thus, having expelled the impurities, one is liberated.
A man whose hands are smeared with the roots of *lajjā* (mimosa pudica) ground together with the juice of frogs becomes purified in the ordeal of heated metal, provided he speaks the truth. (37)
The mantra for the immobilization of metallic substances:
Oṃ agnīdahaṃtī kodharai maidharo jātīnābhāvāchuchi nidadodivyapatitastambhe īśvaro maheśaḥ.
By this, immobilization [is achieved]. This is the command of Śrī Mahādevakī.
One should recite this mantra ten thousand times, and divine accomplishment (*divyasiddhi*) arises.
Oṃ, Agnīda, Hantī, Kodhara, Medhara, Jātīnābhāva, Chuchinida, Divyapātita, Stambha, Īśvara, Maheśa.
Oṃ, Lohā, Prajvala, Ko-ilāke, Bhānuha, Caṇḍakedārakāpaḍī, Lohāpaḍī, Tuṣāra.
Thus ends the divine immobilization (divyastambhana).
Now, for the immobilization of elephants, cows, buffaloes, and so forth:
one should certainly bury the bone from the jaw of a camel in the four directions upon the ground;
this will immobilize cows, horses, rams, buffaloes, and even female elephants.
Thus ends the immobilization of elephants, cows, buffaloes, and so forth. Now follows the immobilization of humans:
*Kālī Karālī, immobilize [name], svāhā!*
By holding the name of the person to be acted upon in one's heart or by touching them while reciting this mantra, they are quickly paralyzed through the mere sight [of the practitioner]. || 39 ||
The yantras for paralyzing humans: "Kālī Kaṅkālī, paralyze so-and-so, svāhā!
Thus ends the paralysis of humans.
Now, for the immobilization of the mind:
having taken earth from the pits of a leather-worker and likewise from those of a dyer,
and having extracted filth from a pit, as well as the menstrual garment of a *caṇḍālī*.
The wise man should tie a *poṭalī* and place it before whomsoever [he intends to act];
there shall be paralysis in that person's rising—this is declared as the *siddhayoga*. (40)
Thus ends the immobilization of the mind.
Now, for the immobilization of the seat:
one should sow the fruit of white *guñjā* along with earth in a human skull.
On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should remain awake there for three days.
One should constantly sprinkle it with water and perform its worship with mantras;
its branches and creepers should be taken during an auspicious lunar mansion (nakṣatra) while reciting one's own mantra.
If one hurls it at another's seat, that person will certainly be paralyzed at that very moment.
Oṃ, homage to the Rudras! Oṃ, to the one whose form is the vajra, who possesses vajra rays, O Śivā, protect existence; make it nectar, make it nectar, svāhā! This is the mantra for worship.
Thus ends the immobilization of the seat.
Regarding the immobilization of the intellect of all beings: *bhṛṅgarāja*, *apāmārga*, *siddhārtha*, and *sahadevikā*.
One should collect equal amounts of each of these substances, including vacā and śvetā.
Having cast it into an iron vessel, one should extract it at the end of two days;
by means of this mark (tilaka), one becomes a paralyzer of the intellect of all beings.
Thus ends the immobilization of the intellect of all beings. Now follows the immobilization of the intellect of enemies:
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, homage to Viśvāmitra! To the two All-Faces, to Viśvāmitra, Viśāmitra commands: come by your power, come, svāhā! This is the mantra for the aforementioned yoga.

Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, obeisance to Viśvāmitra! To the two Sarvamukhīs, to Viśvāmitra, Viśvāmitra commands: come, come by means of your power, svāhā! Oṃ, Aṅgulīlā, threefold intention, come, svāhā! Having entered a river with this mantra, one should offer one hundred and eight handfuls of water (añjali). Thereupon, the intellect of enemies becomes paralyzed. Having written the name [of the enemy] upon charcoal from a funeral pyre with camphor, one should place earth over it; thereby, the mouth of the enemy is bound.
Thus ends the immobilization of the enemy's intellect.
Now, the immobilization of the thief’s movement:
*Oṃ namo brahmadveṣiṇī śive rakṣa rakṣa ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*. By means of this mantra...
Having taken seven pieces of stone from a cremation ground, one should bind three to the waist and hold the others in the fists; thus, the movement of thieves will be paralyzed. So it is said.
Oṃ, homage to the one who hates Brahmā, O Śivā! Protect, protect! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ!
This is the immobilization of the movement of thieves; now follows the immobilization of the womb.
Having taken the root of thorn-apple on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and tying it around his waist, he may enjoy his beloved; she shall never conceive.
By means of the "liberated" [substance], one obtains conception, as previously stated by Nāgārjuna;
however, if the powder of its root is placed in the womb, conception will never occur. (46)
If a woman binds the root of the Siddhārtha plant upon her head and enjoys sexual union with her beloved, she shall not conceive; however, if it is released, she may conceive again.
Thus ends the method for arresting conception.
Now, for the method of arresting semen:
one should, while naked, uproot the root of *indravāruṇī* under the constellation Puṣya.
Having mixed the three pungents with cow’s milk and formed them into balls, they should be dried in the shade; kept in the mouth, this causes the retention of semen in men. (48)
Having tied the root of indigo found in a cremation ground around his waist, he becomes possessed of virility.
One should apply a plaster made from the root of *kṛṣṇonmatta* ground with honey to the penis;
then a man will enjoy his beloved twice as much as by his own nature.
Take two guñjas each of bhṛṅgī-viṣa and mercury;
by adding a drop of varāṭākṣa, it becomes stable when held upon the head.
On a Monday, one should invoke the red root of the Apāmārga plant;
having uprooted it on a Tuesday morning and tied it around the waist, one becomes possessed of virility.
One should procure a black-colored snake named Dundubhi;
by wearing its bone upon the waist, a man does not emit his semen.
When it is emitted, he emits [it] [only] through liberation; this is declared as the Siddhi-yoga. || 53 ||
Having taken the nails and bones of a white cat and the tip of the tail of a chameleon, one should fashion a ring from them using the threads of a corpse.
When worn on the little finger with a cord, a man does not lose his virility. || 55 ||

The seed of the white *pikākṣa* tree, extracted during the Puṣya asterism and tied with a red thread around the waist, prevents the emission of semen during sexual intercourse; indeed, this is always renowned as the "King of Elixirs" (*yogarāja*).
The white fruits of the tree known as upuṣṭā, ground with milk and placed inside the seeds of the karañja, when held in the mouth, arrest the semen even within the body of a banyan tree.
By placing the seed of a seven-leafed tree (*saptaparṇa*) uprooted on a Sunday into his mouth,
a man may conquer women at the onset of sexual union, even those whose passion is driven by the intense force of love.
A wise man should consume one karṣa of nāgakeśara with cow’s ghee;
having eaten it, he may enjoy a woman, and then his vital essence (bindu) will become firm. || 58 ||

Taking the feather from the shaft of a white arrow and binding it to a man's waist with a thread spun by a virgin during the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism and the Sun, the seed of the mind quickly conquers.
The seed of the *īśvaraliṅga* plant, along with a scorpion’s sting, should be mixed;
one should throw a betel nut (*pūgaphala*) into this and encase it with the three metals.
When that is placed upon the tongue, a man does not emit his semen.
By applying a plaster made by mixing the root of *sahadevī* with lotus filaments, along with honey and clarified butter, a man does not lose his virility. (61)
The filaments of the blue lotus and the white lotus, as well as honey and sugar.
With these and by means of an ointment for the navel, the lover enjoys for a long time. || 63 ||
Having taken the root of the *kṛṣṇetara-kākajaṅghā* plant and the filaments of a white lotus, and having ground them with honey, one should smear the navel; thus the semen of a man will be arrested.
One should grind the root of *lajjā* with goat’s or sheep’s milk and apply it as a paste;
[by doing so], the semen will never flow from the heart or the feet.
Alternatively, by applying the root of *śvetapuṅkhā* mixed with honey to the navel,
or likewise by applying the seed of a lotus with honey, one maintains one's virility.
One should saturate the root of *indravāruṇikā* seven times with the urine of a mad goat; by applying it as an ointment to the penis, one becomes possessed of virility. (67)
One should grind the root of the vānarī plant with the urine of a mad goat;
by smearing this upon his penis, a man does not discharge his semen for a long time. (68)
Having ground together camphor, borax, mercury, an equal amount of munirasa, and honey,
one should smear the liṅga and remain thus for one watch (yāma).
Then one should wash the liṅga and enjoy the woman as is appropriate;
this, correctly proclaimed by Nāgārjuna, brings about the retention of semen for men. (70)
By anointing the feet with safflower oil, one who possesses mature virility may sport at will;
furthermore, by applying a paste of *punarnavā* powder, he never loses his seed. (71)
By applying camphor, saṃpāka, and the seeds of Maheśa together with the seed of a man upon the navel and the hips of a beloved woman,
O lovely one, his semen shall never again flow downwards.
By applying a paste of *bhūlatā*, beeswax, and safflower oil to the feet, one gains virility; likewise, by applying the paste of the *taṭaka* stalk, one attains the same. (73)
One should not touch a bed or one's feet with fresh butter.
Having ground the seeds of *śleṣmāntaka*, *kuraṇṭaka*, and *kārañjaka* with the milk of a *bheḍī* goat, one who eats a *karṣa* of that mixture will possess virility.
One should grind the root of *sudarśana* together with betel leaves;
by consuming it with effort while avoiding ghee, this is the supreme method for the immobilization of semen (*śukrastambhana*). (75)
A wick made from the cotton-wool of the white Arka plant, with a lamp fueled by the fat of a boar—so long as this lamp burns, one does not lose virility. (76)
One should grind the root of Varāhakrāntā with goat’s milk;
by applying this as an ointment to the penis, it will cause the semen to be arrested.
The root of the white-horse-āra plant, extracted under the Puṣya asterism, when bound to the region of the hips, causes the semen to remain steady; however, upon release, it flows out again.
One should cause the mercury from the curved vessel to be caught in a vessel placed above it while the sun shines.
Having ground it, one should form it into pills, dry them, and then store them. By smearing that with one's own urine at the base of the penis, one becomes possessed of virility. (79)
Having ground the seeds of the *pūtīkarañja* and the roots of the white *bandhūka* and *maṇḍa*, one should apply them together with sandalwood paste to the tip of the *liṅga*.
Likewise, one should place it on the palm of the left hand; thus the drop (bindu) becomes stable. || 81 ||
Having ground bhaṭikā, the root of *lajjālu*, in a copper vessel and prepared an ointment with it, one should apply it; thus, one shall remain steady until midnight. (82)
One should invite the great deity Mahākāla, who is dark and cunning, on Saturdays; having brought him on Sundays, one should worship him with offerings made by an ungiven woman.
Having carefully tied it with threads representing the three qualities (guṇas) on the left hand,
one should then sit upon a seat for three watches (yāmas) divided into three sections;
thereby the drop (bindu) attains stability, and when released, it slips away in that very instant.
The seed of black dhattūra is equal to gold-colored collyrium. || 85 ||
Having ground the seeds of *kuberākṣa* with the milky sap of the banyan tree (*vaṭa*) and placed that in the mouth, it will cause the retention of semen. (86)
Thus ends the fourth instruction, titled "The Description of the Paralysing of Enemies' Mouths and Other Rites," in the *Kāmaratna* composed by the venerable Nityanātha. 4.

The Fifth Instruction: Now, regarding the delusion [of the mind] in the case of a maiden and a suitor, in the union of young women, in the sight of men, in the presence of a king, or in buying and selling, and so forth.
In the ritual of wisdom, in every rite, or in any festive ceremony, incense should always be employed by those who are skillful. || 1 ||

Having taken equal parts of śṛṅgī, vacā, analada, sarjarasa, truṭi, and malayaja—these six—one who constantly fumigates her own house, clothing, and body with this incense will find that people fall into a state of infatuation toward her like a slave. (2)
Bhṛṅgarāja, Keśarāja, Lajjā, and Sahadevikā—
by applying a tilaka made from these, a man shall enchant the three worlds.

A man who, with palms joined in reverence, offers a three-petaled flower of the thorn-apple (dhattūra) and applies a forehead mark (tilaka) made from bhr̥ṅgarāja mixed with clarified butter, shall enchant others.

A wise man should prepare a pill from equal parts of talaka, kunaṭī, and the wing of a blue jay, along with the flower of black unmadaka; by applying a tilaka-mark with that very mixture, a man can enchant the three worlds.
At the beginning, the seven vowels are to be taken, joined with the syllable *huṃ* at the end;
having placed the syllable *oṃ* at the head, one should assign *phaṭ* at the end.
The mantra is: Oṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ hūṃ phaṭ. || 5-6 ||
Having prepared the betel-leaf with this very mantra,
when it is placed in the mouth of the target, he falls into a state of delusion at that very moment.
Oṃ bhīṃ kṣāṃ bhīṃ, delude, delude! Oṃ, salutations to the pollen of the lotus feet of the Blessed Lady! By reciting this mantra three times, people fall into a state of delusion. || 8 ||
Oṃ bhīṃ kṣāṃ bhīṃ, delude, delude!
Oṃ, homage to the pollen of the Blessed Lady’s lotus feet. 7–8.
Having ground together the root of the *śubhā* plant, seeds produced from red sandalwood,
and equal amounts of *truṭi* seeds, one should apply it to betel and other such items.
One should give with one's own hand so that the master may eat; if he falls into delusion, [the merit is lost]. || 10 ||
Incense made from the powder produced from scorpions deludes men. || 11 ||
A fumigation consisting of poison, the five parts of the *dhūrta* plant, buffalo blood, *kaṇā*, and *niśā*,
combined with *guggulu*, causes delusion at night.
Incense prepared with equal parts of halinī, viṣa, dhattūra, śikhin, and bird droppings will certainly cause delusion. 13.
A musk-rat, a snake’s head, a scorpion’s sting,
and yellow orpiment— this incense, when used in equal parts, shall delude all men.
Now, for the delusion of enemies: a mark made from the combination of adhaḥpuṣpī, śikhā, white girikarṇikā, and gorocana causes the delusion of enemies. (15)
One should cause the seeds of *tālaka-unmatta* to be given in a drink to an enemy;
at that very moment, he falls into delusion and the man becomes insane. || 16 ||
A person who is healthy will become free from delusion by drinking white lotuses together with honey. || 17 ||
Thus [is] the deluding of enemies; now,
regarding the pleasing,
therein is the pleasing of the body.

In this matter, body-unguents (aṅgarāga) should be applied by a man upon his limbs for the sake of the pleasure of sexual union with a woman; therefore, I shall first describe the entire procedure for perfumes for the sake of the elegant man.
Harītakī, lodhra, leaves of mariṣṭa, saptacchada, and the bark of pomegranate—this is declared by the lords of poets to be an ointment that removes bodily foul odors for a woman. (19)
Harītakī, śrīphala, musta, ciñcā, triphalā, and the seeds of pūtikarañja quickly destroy even abundant body odor from the armpits and other areas during the summer season. (20)

By means of an ointment made from equal parts of *harītakī*, sandalwood, *musta*, *nāgara*, *uśīra*, *lodhra*, and *amaya-rātri*, the sweat and body odor of both men and women is quickly destroyed. (21)
The leaf of the Kadamba, Lodhra, and the flower of the Arjuna tree. || 22 ||
By grinding it and using it as a body rub, even foul odors are destroyed. || 23 ||
A woman, having anointed her body with sandalwood, uśīra, karañja leaves, the marrow of kola and akṣa fruits, along with aguru and nāga, destroys the odor of one who has long been pregnant.

A paste made from equal parts of the bark of the *sadāḍima*, honey, *lodhra*, and *padma*, ground together with *picumarda*, when applied to the body by a young woman during the summer heat, destroys the accumulation of foul-smelling perspiration. (25)
By anointing the body with the powdered mixture of sakeśara, uśīra, śirīṣa, and lodhra, King Bhoja declared that men’s bodies shall never experience the loss of moisture during the summer. (26)
When the body is rubbed with sesame, mustard, the two types of *rajanī*, *dūrvā*, *gorocanā*, and *kuṣṭha*,
ground together with goat’s urine and buttermilk, it becomes incomparable.
With parts of *harītakī* and *toyada* equal in measure, and a fourth part of *vaneruha*,
with half that portion of *nakha*— this is said to be the fragrance known as *madanaprakāśa*.

Cardamom, *śaṭī*, cinnamon leaves, sandalwood, water-lily, *abhayā*, *śigru*, and *ghanasāra*—this fragrant scent, worthy of the king of the gods, is renowned as "Naramohana" (the Deluder of Men). || 29 ||

Having ground together dhattūra, saffron, thick water (musta), iron, turmeric, and usīra in equal parts, this beloved ointment was proclaimed by the wise lords among poets of old as dear to gods and men alike. (30)
Having ground together ushira, black aguru, and sandalwood in equal parts with water infused with leaves,
this mixture produces upon the bodies of graceful women a fragrance equal to that of śrīkhaṇḍa.
Thus ends the beautification of the body.
Now, the beautification of the face:
the essence of the heart of *rasāla* and *jambū* fruits, together with *karkaṭa* and mixed with honey.
Situated at the edge of a man's mouth at night, it provides the desired fragrance for the mouths of men.
A small pill (kṣudravaṭī) should be prepared with jaggery, cinnamon, cardamom, nakha, nutmeg, śigru, and gold;
placed inside a betel leaf, it provides men with a desirable fragrance for their mouth by day and by night.
The woman who daily licks at dawn and dusk a powder made of *murā*, saffron, and *kuṣṭha* will, within even half a month, possess a fragrance of the mouth that is fully equal to that of camphor. (34)

He who daily eats the powder of *kuṣṭha* combined with the seeds of *pikākṣa*, along with honey and ghee, for the duration of one month, his mouth will acquire a fragrance equal to the scent of the *ketaka* flower. (35)
Pathyā boiled with cow’s urine and combined with miśi, kuṣṭha, and kaṇā, when practiced regularly, destroys foul odors of the mouth. (36)
Having chewed sesame, nutmeg, and betel nut, one should afterwards drink half a *pala* of cold water; this destroys bad breath from the mouth.
One should consume a small amount of ghee and sour gruel as a mouth-rinse on all sides;
when done in this manner, the foul odor in the mouth will be destroyed. (38)
One should boil kuṣṭha, bālaka, and harītakī with cow’s urine;
having ground everything together, one should make pills that destroy foul odors from the mouth. (39)
It is no wonder that a tooth-stick which is pungent, bitter, and astringent constantly destroys bad odor; nor is it surprising that a powder of kuṣṭha with honey does the same.
By applying a paste made of *sindhūttha*, *siddhārthaka*, *sārivā*, and cinnamon bark, the foul odor of the mouth of both men and women is forcibly destroyed, even in their youth. (41)
Having ground lentils with thick sour gruel and repeatedly smearing the face with it, the boils and pustules that have grown on the faces of beautiful women vanish within half a month. (42)
If one grinds the thorns of the *śālmali* tree with milk and applies them as a paste to the cheeks for eight days, the pustules of a slender woman will vanish in three days. (43)
Having ground together equal parts of grain, *vacā*, and *sāvara*, one should thoroughly smear it upon the face;
by this means, the pustules arising on the faces of men due to youth will surely vanish in due course. (44)

Having ground two seeds of *siddhārtha* and sesame with alkaline salt and smeared it upon the face, one destroys black stains on the lips situated in the mouth within just seven days; thus says Rantideva. (45)
For two nights, one should apply geru (red ochre), red lac-sticks, lotus stalks, water, Indra-yava, and excellent barley;
by using this for three times the duration of a night, the face becomes equal to the moon.
Having ground black pepper together with yellow pigment (rocanā), one should smear it on the face;
all pustules arising on the face of a young woman will vanish. || 47 ||
On the limbs, either the bark of the arjuna tree or mañjiṣṭhā mixed with honey should be applied;
when rubbed for three days, the face becomes like a lotus.
A paste made from the root of *mātuluṅga*, clarified butter, *śilājatu*, and the liquid from cow dung produces radiance on the face and overcomes pimples, moles, and dark spots. (49)
Red sandalwood, mañjiṣṭhā, kuṣṭha, lodhra, priyaṅgu, banyan sprouts, and masūra beans destroy freckles and bestow beauty upon the face. (50)
One should cook one *kuḍava* of oil with these ingredients— mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, lākṣā, and mātuluṅga mixed with clarified butter— each weighing one *karṣa*.
One should slowly cook that double amount of goat's milk with fire until it becomes soft.
It destroys dark spots, pimples, and freckles simply by being massaged;
it is beneficial even for those with a clear complexion, provided it is free from blue tints and coarseness. (53)
Through its use for seven nights, [the body] becomes like gold;
here, because it is mentioned twice, there are two karṣas of yaṣṭīmadhuka as well.
Realgar, lodhra, the two types of turmeric, and mustard seeds in equal parts,
ground with water, form a beneficial paste that, when applied to the face, removes dark spots.
When a paste of turmeric and red sandalwood, combined with buffalo milk, is applied, it quickly destroys the dark discoloration residing on the face. (56)
Both types of turmeric, madder, ghee, white mustard seeds, and red ochre—these should be ground together and cooked with goat’s milk. || 57 ||
By this very [mixture], the face shall become radiant like the rising sun;
[the ingredients are] vacā, lodhra, uśīra, ghee, sarjarasa, and milk. (58)
One should grind yellow *vaṭa* leaves together with turmeric;
this ointment, when applied to the face and feet, makes them exceedingly beautiful like lotuses. (59)
Having ground lentils together with honey, one should rub the face with them;
by practicing this for seven nights, the complexion becomes like the luster of a lotus petal.
Thus ends the adornment of the face. Now follows the adornment of the hair: garlands, perfumes, incense, garments, and ornaments do not grace those whose hair has turned white.
Therefore, one should practice the cultivation of passion for the hair on the crown of the head, just as one does with collyrium and ornaments.
Oil extracted from mango seeds, powdered magnetite (kāntapāṣāṇa),
and the black fruit of kākatuṇḍī should be diligently ground together.
Having cast it into a heap of grain, after a month one should apply it to the head as a nasal drop (nasya) for three days; by this, the hair becomes dyed,
remaining black like the collyrium of a bee for half a year.
Triphalā, iron powder, nīlī, and the entire root of bhṛṅgī. || 64 ||
One should let this powder soak for one day in cow dung and urine;
by rubbing with that very substance on the head, it is colored like a bee.
One should take the powder of guñjā seeds, kuṣṭha, elā,
and devadāru in equal parts, and macerate that powder for one day with the juice of bhṛṅgarāja.
One should cook it in oil four times the quantity of the powder over a gentle fire;
by anointing with that, the hair becomes thick and attains a color like that of a bee.
By grinding equal parts of burnt elephant tusk and an equal amount of mercury with goat’s milk and applying it as an ointment, the hair is dyed.

One should place the powder of triphalā and iron, along with the juice of sugarcane and bhṛṅgarāja, together with black earth inside a vessel and seal it for one month. By applying that as an ointment, the hair will be dyed and will remain stable for four months. (69)
Having ground iron filings, hibiscus flowers, and āmalaka fruits in equal parts, one should apply it to the head for three days; this results in the coloring of the hair for two months.
One prastha of the juice of Bhṛṅgarāja and an equal amount of oil from black sesame seeds; || 71 ||
One should grind the juice of *nīlikā* with oil for one hour;
by applying that ointment for three days, it will become a hair-dye.
A powder made of Sarja-yavakṣāra, Siddhārtha, and Āranālaka,
along with Nāgapuṣpa, applied as a paste at midday, results in the coloring of the hair.
Then, one should take equal parts of *kākamācī* seeds and black sesame seeds; having extracted that oil in a press, one should apply it for the purpose of dyeing the hair.
Cow’s ghee, the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, and *mayūraśikhā* should be cooked over a gentle fire; one should apply that for the purpose of blackening the hair.
Then, one should take equal parts of *kākamācī* seeds and black sesame seeds, along with the juice of *japā* flowers and a *karṣa* of honey, and apply them.
One should dye the hair for seven days; this is the procedure for all [hair types].
One should grind equal parts of triphalā and iron powder with water;
then one should cook them for a moment over a gentle fire with an amount of oil equal to the weight of those two combined. (77)
One should cook the juice of *bhṛṅga* equal to the oil until it becomes as oily as the oil itself;
once it has become unctuous, it should be placed in a vessel, set on the ground, and after one month, it should be removed.

One should apply [the paste] for seven days; having applied it, one should place the head upon a plantain leaf in a windless place, subsist on a milk diet, and wash [the head] with water decocted with triphalā.
Indeed, this should always be performed; within seven days, the hair will become dyed.
For as long as one lives, there is no doubt that the hair will be like the color of a black bee.
The seeds of Mahākāla are equal to the seeds of Vākucī. || 81 ||
One should then saturate the powder with the juices of *nirguṇḍī* and *japā* flowers for four days,
and subsequently [process it] in a *pātālayantra*.
The oil should be extracted from that; having applied it as an ointment, one should wrap the head with castor leaves, subsist on a milk diet, and avoid wind and sunlight. (83)
In this manner, one should apply the plaster for seven days and hold rice grains in the mouth;
they will turn black, and this occurs every day.
Having cast the fierce delusion into the mire, one should extract it after six months;
that [substance] quickly becomes black, and one karṣa of it should be placed upon the head.
The hair grows black, resembling a swarm of female bees;
it is known as "the dyeing of the skull," which lasts for as long as one lives—of this there is no doubt. (86)
Having smeared the hair with *sanīlikā* mixed with rock salt (*saindhava*) and long pepper (*pippalī*), followed by an application of ghee,
the hair quickly becomes black like a conch shell and attains a deep, lustrous blackness.
One who has received the traditional instruction should cook a *piṇḍāraka* flower from a mango tree that bears fruit, or one that is pale and dark-blue in color,
along with a measure of a *prastha* of sesame oil.
And if, in the midst of that, a swan’s wing feather of deep blue color should be found, then its ripening must be performed by men; it is renowned on earth as "Blue Oil" (nīlataila).

This grey hair of men, entirely white like a conch shell and free from oil for three nights, brings about auspicious results; it has been observed that such a practice leads to long-lasting prosperity. (90)
Śatāvarī mixed with black sesame, along with gorocanā and that which is called kākamukhā—by smearing [the hair] with these, one makes even fair-haired persons black. (91)
This sesame oil, prepared with the juice and paste of *madantikā*, completely destroys premature graying, roughness, and the brittleness of the hair in men. (92)
Moth, mustard seed, and likewise uśīra, together with a decoction of harītakī and an equal amount of āmalakī—[these should be used]. 93.
Having smeared the root of the hair, the hair shall become like a cloud.
Thus ends the procedure for dyeing the hair.
Now, for the fragrant substances used for bathing:
[one should use] small cardamom, *jīmūta*, and *nakha*, together with mangoes, and combined with *svarṇa*, *āmalaka*, and leaves.
Indeed, by bathing there, a person always obtains the fragrance and beauty of his hair. (95)
By applying an ointment consisting of gold, ambuda, uśīra, and nakhī, combined with pathyā,
a man who has bathed attains a fragrance of his hair for half a month.
Having bathed, a man who applies a paste made of *āmalakī* fruits ending with *pathyā*, combined with *jīmūta-rasa* and *māṃsī*, attains fragrance and beauty. (97)
Thus ends the section on fragrant substances for bathing.
Now, regarding the prevention of lice, nits, and the like: this pungent oil (kaṭutaila) is prepared with cow’s urine and a paste of viḍaṅga and fragrant blue lotus (gandhotpala).
By means of this application as an oil massage, it destroys the accumulation of lice, nits, and other parasites on the hair. || 98 ||
An ointment made from cow’s urine and the root of sārivā wards off lice.
One should rub one niṣka of mercury with the juices of black dhattūra.
Alternatively, one should smear a piece of cloth with the juices of the *nāgavallī* plant;
having wrapped that cloth around the head, it should be worn for three watches (yāmas).
Then lice fall away from the head entirely—of this there is no doubt. (100)
By applying a plaster of two parts butter and one part curd from the crown of the head down to the knees, [the body becomes radiant]. || 101 ||
Having ground together blue lotus, sesame, liquorice, mustard, nāgakeśara,
and dhātrī fruit in equal parts, this ointment destroys lice.
Night-blooming jasmine, sulphur, cow’s urine, viḍaṅga, and mustard oil—having ground these together with an equal amount of mercury, this ointment destroys lice. (103)
Lac, marking-nut, nut-grass, asafoetida, bdellium, mustard seeds, and equal parts of embelia— this fumigation applied as an ointment wards off lice.
The root of the *bilva* tree mixed with cow urine, when applied as an ointment, destroys lice.
Thus ends the prevention of lice, nits, and the like. Now follows the prevention of hair loss, such as *indralupta* and other ailments:
having smeared the entire area of the head with *guñjā* fruits mixed with honey, [one cures] all forms of *indralupta*.
By this yoga, black, curly, and abundant hair always grows. || 106 ||

Having prepared ink from the tusk of an elephant, finely ground to the consistency of white collyrium, one should smear with this very substance that which has been lost by Mahendra; thus, even hair grows back as if in the palm of one's hand.
Having ground saffron together with black pepper, one should apply it with oil;
this quickly destroys *indralupta* (alopecia), or alternatively, with the juice of *jambīra* fruit.
Having thoroughly burnt elephant tusks, goat's milk, and *rasāñjana*, and having ground them together, hair grows even upon the palms of the hands through the application of this ointment. (109)
Jātī flowers, petals, and roots, ground with the urine of a black cow—
this ointment, applied for seven nights, is supreme for making the hair firm.

Having made equal fine powders of śṛṅgāṭa, triphalā, bhṛṅgī, nīlotpala, and iron filings (mayūrarajas), one should cook them in four times the amount of oil. By anointing [the hair] with that, even curly hairs become firm and straight. 111.
One should rub a spot where hair has been eaten by insects with gold until it reaches a state of intense heat; during that time, apply this ointment.
Bhallātaka, bṛhatī, and the root and fruit of guñjā,
when applied as an ointment with honey, destroy wind-disorders, consumption, and urinary calculi.
Bhallātaka, black sesame, and the fruit of Kaṇṭakārī in equal parts, ground with rice-water—this ointment shall destroy that [condition]. (114)
One should destroy that [defect] with hibiscus flowers by means of an application of black cow's urine. (115)
Sesame flowers ground together with *gokṣura*, salt, and cow’s ghee, when applied as a paste to the head for just seven days, cause the hair to become long and abundant. (116)
The roots of the śālmalī, tāla, and mūlī, along with that produced from the lotus,
should be ground together with goat’s milk and applied as an ointment to the shaved head.
One should consume that for three days; it is the best means for promoting the growth of hair.
Thus ends the prevention of hair loss, such as *indralupta*, and so forth.
Now, for the whitening of the hair:
one should saturate sesame seeds with the remaining milk of the *vajrī* plant for seven days.
And the hair, when smeared with that oil, will become white; of this there is no doubt. (118)
One should saturate the powder of *roga* and *āmalaka* seven times with the milk of a *vajrī* cow;
by applying its paste, the hairs of the head turn white. (119)
One should saturate the fruit of *abhayā* with goat’s milk for seven days;
when applied as a paste with that powder mixed with oil, [the hair] indeed becomes white.
