Thus ends the fifth instruction, titled "The Description of Enchantment and Other [Rites]," in the *Kāmaratna* composed by the illustrious Nityanātha. || 5 ||
The Sixth Instruction:
Now, on aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*).
A woman is satisfied by strength; for one who lacks virility, there is never happiness.
Therefore, for the sake of strength, I shall first describe the methods for aphrodisiacs for one who is addicted to pleasure. || 1 ||
Having drunk the *vaṭavṛndāka* under the asterism Aśvinī with milk, one becomes possessed of great strength;
one should diligently drink the root of the white *arka* plant uprooted under Puṣya.
By taking it with cow’s milk for seven nights, even an old man becomes like a youth.

Having consumed the powder of vidārī, processed with its own fresh juice and dried by the network of the sun’s rays, mixed with honey and clarified butter, one may approach ten women without hesitation. (3)

He who, at the onset of night, repeatedly consumes the powder of the *āmalaka* fruit mixed with its own juice, along with sugar, clarified butter, and honey, will surely attain youth even if he is old.

Having licked one *karṣa* measure of Madhuka powder mixed with honey and clarified butter, and followed it with a draught of milk, one enjoys [sexual vigor] for as long as this remains within the stomach of men. (5)
He who daily licks the seeds of the white *pikata* tree together with rice and *yaṣṭikā*, combined with ghee and honey,
remains charming to women even while his body is emaciated, until it undergoes digestion within the cavity of his stomach.
One should drink the juice of the root of the old *śālmali* tree with sugar;

Having drunk the root of the *laghuśālmalī* mixed with the powder of *tālamūlī*, along with clarified butter and milk, one will become like a sparrow during sexual union.
Having repeatedly processed them with ghee for a month until they are well-refined, dried in the sun,
and prepared with milk, he who eats them becomes possessed of fierce virility and approaches a hundred women.
The meat of the vartakī, lāvaka, and piñjala birds, as well as that of the domestic fowl, when prepared with sacrificial ghee and rock salt, will bring great strength to one who consumes it. (10)
If a person eats a paste of vidārīkanda equal in size to an udumbara fruit, along with ghee and milk, even an old man becomes like a youth. (11)
He who eats the testicles of a goat, prepared with milk and ghee and combined with the juice of long pepper (pippalī), may approach a hundred women.
A man who eats sesame seeds that have been repeatedly soaked in milk prepared with goat testicles would approach a hundred women as if they were virgins.
Gokṣuraka, kṣuraka, śatamūlī, vānarī, nāgabalā, and atibalā—this powder should be drunk with milk at night by one who has a hundred women in his house. (14)
Having drunk milk prepared with the fruit, root, bark, and sprouts of the *aśvattha* tree, along with sugar and honey, a man rejoices like King Kaliṅga. (15)
One should cook ghee containing śatāvarī with four times as much milk;
when combined with sugar, pippalī, and honey, it is declared to be aphrodisiac. (16)
One *prastha* each of *nṛsiṃhacūrṇa*, the powder of *śatāvarī*, and *gokṣuraka*;
twenty *palas* of *vārāhī* and twenty-five *palas* of *guḍūcī*. (17)
One should give thirty-two *bhallātaka* fruits, ten *citraka* roots, and one *prastha* of dehusked sesame seeds, all well-ground into a fine powder. (18)
Eight palas of triphalā, seventy palas of sugar, half as much honey as the sugar, and indeed half as much ghee as the honey. (19)
Powder derived from the root-tuber of vidārī should be given in a quantity equal to that of śatāvarī;
this powder, having been mixed together, should be placed in a vessel that has been lubricated with oil.
One should wear half a pala of it as a medicinal paste; its food may be taken according to one's desire.
By using it for one month, it destroys old age as well as diseases. (21)
It destroys wrinkles, graying hair, baldness, jaundice, and chronic nasal catarrh; it also cures the eighteen types of leprosy as well as the eight kinds of tumors.
Fistula-in-ano, dysuria, sciatica along with jaundice, consumption as a great disease, and the five most dreadful types of cough; || 23 ||
Eighty types of diseases born of wind (vāta), forty born of bile (pitta), twenty subtle diseases, and those arising from the combination of all three humors (sānnipātika). || 24 ||
It shall destroy all hemorrhoids and diseases, just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree. || 25 ||
Shining like gold and possessing the prowess of the king of beasts, he pursues his horse with speed;
yet he traverses more than a hundred joyful and robust women, moving as swiftly as a bird.
Likewise, a wise man shall produce sons resembling Narasiṃha;
this Nārasiṃha powder removes all diseases of men. (27)
Thus ends the *Nṛsiṃhacūrṇa*. As for *Madanamodaka*:
take the leaf of *Trailokyavijayā* along with its seeds, fried in clarified butter.
The three pungents, the three myrobalans, kuṣṭha, bhṛṅgī, rock salt, and coriander. || 28 ||
Cavya, tālīśapatra, kaṭphala, nāgakeśara, ajamodā, yavānī, and yaṣṭimadhu; || 29 ||
Take methī and the two types of jīraka in equal parts;
these powders fall [into the mixture], and that medicine is prepared at that very moment.
Having ground it on a smooth stone slab, one should reduce it to an extremely fine paste;
sugar should be added only until the mixture reaches a state of cohesion.
One should prepare a sweetmeat (modaka) mixed with ghee and honey;
one should place powdered sesame seeds fried in ghee on top of the sweetmeat.
One should place the glorious Madanamodaka, combined with the three aromatics and perfumed with camphor, inside a vessel of ghee.
Having risen in the morning, one should consume it; it removes the fear of wind and phlegm, increases the digestive fire, and kindles even a weak digestion. (33)
For those who are emaciated and excessively dry, oleation is the cause of corpulence.
It cures cough, destroys all types of colic, and eliminates āmavāta;
indeed, it removes all diseases and cures saṃgraha and grahaṇī.
Through the constant practice of this, even an old man becomes like a youth. (36)
Having heard this from the mouth of Brahmā regarding Vāsudeva, the Lord of the universe, it was revealed by Nārada for the sake of increasing Kāma’s power,
by means of which the Joy of the Yadus took delight with hundreds of thousands of excellent women. (37)
Thus ends Madanamodaka.
As for Kāmakalārasa:
[one should take] mercury, mica, and gold, along with the juices of vājigandhā and vacā.
One should grind it for a day with the juices of *muśalī* and the root of the plantain (*kadalī*).
One should cook it with small lac-encased packets and rub it with the aforementioned liquids;
a packet should be applied again and it should be rubbed—thus one should cook it with eight such packets.
For four months, one should consume the extracts produced from the Śālmalī tree;
thereafter, one should cook half a pala of the seeds of the Markaṭī with cow's milk.
This essence, known as Kāmakalā, delights with thousands of women;
one should perform an ointment for all the limbs using its own juices and the juices of the śālmalī tree. (41)
Thus ends the *Kāmakalārasa*.
As for the *Anaṅgasundarīvaṭikā*:
take mercury equal in weight to purified sulfur and [mix it] for three days with the juices of white water-lilies (*kahlāra*).
Having been ground, one should cook it for one watch (yāma) in a sand-press while enclosed in a sealed crucible (saṃpuṭa).
One should quickly soak [the substance] for one day with the red juices of the Agastya plant;
then one may eat food as much as desired and enjoy a hundred women at will.
Two palas each of pure mercury and likewise sulfur, one karṣa of dead gold, and one pala of dead mica; 44.
One should cook four niṣkas of mercury and copper together with all five nectars (pañcāmṛta) for one day using the Rudra-gajapuṭa method; at the end of that day, one should take it out.
Having ground [the ingredients] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should make pills the size of jujube fruits;
by eating this Anaṅgasundarī, one may enjoy three hundred women.
One should eat a powder of the root of the Śālmalī tree and one pala of the root of Bhṛṅgarāja with sugar along with food; thus one may desire a hundred women.
Thus ends the Anaṅgasundarī Vaṭī.
Now, for the Mahākāmeśvara Rasa:
one should grind one part of mercury (sūtapāda) and copper powder together in a mortar.
Having placed it in the root of a plantain tree, one should smear it again with cow dung.
One should cook it dry using elephant-puṭas and then place it back into the bulb;
in this manner, one should cook it with seven puṭas, placing each bulb separately within another bulb.
Having added ghee and powder there, one should cook it after binding it in a cloth;
then, joined with a *dolāyantra*, one should cook it again in goat's milk.
Then with *gūḍūcī*, *śatāvarī*, *vānarī*, and *gokṣura*, as well as *gajapippalī*, parched grain (*lāja*), *kadalī*, and *kokilākṣaka*. || 51 ||
One should cook it with white [sugar] over a mild fire for double the time;
having removed it, one should powder it and consume four *guñjā* seeds of the clear [preparation].
This Mahākāmeśvara elixir, combined with sugar, should always be consumed;
it can agitate a thousand women in the space of a single moment.
Gokṣura, vānarabīja, guḍūcī, gajapippalī, the seeds of kokilākṣa, its fruit, and śatāvarī. (54)
One should grind together karkaśā, bīja, and majjā in equal parts.
An amount of sugar equal to the powder should be added, and the resulting mass should be licked with honey.
Half a pala should be taken as a dose, followed by a small amount of cow’s milk to drink. || 55 ||
Thus ends the Mahākāmeśvara-rasa. Now follows the Madanodaya-rasa:
take mercury equal in quantity to pure sulfur, along with the juice of red lotus petals.
Furthermore, one should cast the fragrant substance for one watch, or half of the previous amount. || 56 ||
One should rub the body [of the crucible] with those juices and rub the previously mentioned fragrant substances;
having sealed it within a glass vessel for one day with the previous juices, [one should proceed]. (57)
Having extracted the medicine cooked for one day in a sand-vessel (vālukāyantra), one should consume it;
this elixir, Madanodaya, consists of five guñjas along with half a portion of sugar.
The seeds of *kokilākṣa* and *musalī*, equal in measure to sugar, should be drunk with cow’s milk; half a *pala* of this should be taken as a post-drink tonic. (59)
Thus ends the Madanodaya-rasa. Now, for the Kāmāṅga-nāyaka-cūrṇa:
take equal parts of the seeds of Vānarī and Kokilākṣa, and black sesame.
One should prepare a dried powder from the roots of gokṣura and āsā.
Dead mica (abhraka) equal in weight to the powder, with sugar equal to the total amount, should be drunk with one karṣa of cow’s milk; this is the lord of the limbs of desire. (61)
If one eats a sparrow cooked in oil before a meal and drinks milk at the end of the meal, he shall enjoy a hundred women. 62.
Thus ends the "Powder of the Hero of Love's Limbs";
now follows the "Amrita of Love" formulation:
Aśvagandhā, Vahni-mūla, Śālmalī, and Śatāvarī.
Vidārī, the root of muśalī, and the seeds of kokilākṣa. || 63 ||
One should prepare a fine powder of the seeds of *vānarī* equal to that [quantity];
the mercury (*mṛta-abhra*) should be equal to the powder, and there should be sugar equal to the total amount.
One should drink one *karṣa* with cow's milk; it enables one to enjoy the company of a hundred women. (64)
One should eat the meat of the horse-crab and drink milk;

Thus ends the Kāmāmṛta-yoga.

One should eat one *pala* daily and drink white sugar-water afterwards;
by the power of the *dhātrī* iron, one may constantly enjoy the company of a hundred women. (68)
Thus ends the section on *dhātrīloha*.

take the dehusked powder of *vānarī* seeds and mix it with powdered *māṣa* beans.

One should add twenty parts of processed abhra for every twenty parts of the flour;

Having drunk milk mixed with sugar, a beautiful woman shall delight for a hundred years;

Yaṣṭī, nāgabalā, kacūra, madana, jātīphala, and saindhava. || 74 ||

Sūtaka, marica, kuṣṭha, nāgara, kaṇṭakārikā, aśvagandhā, sesame, honey, rock salt, and white mustard seeds; || 37 ||

Having ground together sūtaka, aśvagandhā, rajanī, and gajapippalī with sugar and water, one should then apply that [mixture] as an ointment for one month. (49)

It has been observed that by applying a plaster made from the marrow of the fat of a horse, a snake, and a peacock, along with vacā, balā, bhārgī, and rasāñjana,
the penis of men instantly becomes like iron.
The root of the *kṛṣṇāparājitā* plant should be taken together with stakes of *khadira* wood;

The juice of *devadālī* and *dhātrī*, with the penis stabilized by drinking milk—
thus has the King of Mantras been declared by Śiva for all these formulations.
Having consecrated [the substance] with this, one should then apply it as an ointment for one month.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Uḍḍāmareśvara! Move, move! Cause to move! Act, act! Svāhā! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ!
The strengthening, however, should be performed without a mantra.

Now, for the enlargement of the breasts and the elevation of the bosom,
*mātaṅga*, *kṛṣṇā*, *apyadhavā*, *jagandhā*, and *vacā*, combined with water that has stood overnight [should be used].
Through the application of butter from the wife of Hayāri, they make the pair of jar-like breasts full.
Oil prepared with a paste of *vaca* and pomegranate, when applied as an ointment, makes the breasts of a woman exceedingly beautiful and full; this excellent formulation is thus prescribed. (56)
The juice of śrīparṇikā, when prepared with the excellent oil derived from sesame seeds, is prescribed as a medicinal application;

If, during the first period of menstruation, a young woman drinks rice-water mixed with *nasya* (nasal medication) while observing the prescribed restraints,

One karṣa of rice-grain that yields śāli rice should be administered as nasal drops through both the left and right nostrils.
One should boil ten palas of muṇḍī powder with four times as much water;

One should cook the remaining oil and administer it as both nasal drops and a drink;

One should boil equal parts of śyāmā, niśā, balā, parched grain (lāja), and salt together;

Having taken castor oil, fish oil, and likewise the juice of the unripe bilva fruit, one should rub them together with the upward-pointing hand; then the breast will indeed become newly fallen.

Having added equal parts of the fresh juice of gambhārī leaves and sesame oil,

likewise, one should take the leaf of *peṭārikā* combined with powdered *māṣa*. (49)
Having wrapped it with plantain leaves, one should burn it with great care;
by merely consuming it, there is indeed a cessation of excessive redness.

by the mere consumption of this, one removes disorders such as excessive blood. (51)
The powder of its bark mixed with the powder of fried rice, by the mere act of eating it, certainly pacifies the menstrual blood of women. (52)
One should carefully collect forty palas of the juice of the root of śatāvarī itself, having strained it through a cloth with diligence.
Milk from cows equal in number to the [number of] liquids, with twice as much ghee as milk;

One karṣa of this electuary quickly pacifies even difficult-to-cure excessive hemorrhaging,

jaundice, wind diseases, urinary calculi, and stiffness of the head. || 58 ||
Thus ends the prevention of excessive menstrual flow.
Now, regarding the conception of children for those who are barren:
there are women who are barren from birth, those who bear only one child, those whose children die at birth, and others.
In the past, Śambhu indicated this for the sake of the birth of sons for them.
Regarding the treatment for infertility:
on a Sunday, one should uproot the *sarpākṣī* plant along with its roots and leaves;
then, a maiden should grind it by hand in the milk of cows of a single color. (60)
A barren woman should drink half a *pala* of this daily during her fertile period;
she should be provided with a light diet of milk, *śāli* rice, and green gram. || 61 ||
One should perform this for seven days; thus, a barren woman becomes pregnant.
She should avoid agitation, fear, grief, and sleeping during the day. (62)
She should not perform any labor, and she should avoid cold and heat.
She should not be made to perform service for others, nor should she engage in activities as before.
Through union with her husband, conception occurs; there is no need for doubt in this matter.
But even a single rudrākṣa, the size of a sarpa-akṣi berry, [is meritorious]. || 64 ||
And as before, one should cause her to drink the milk of cows during her fertile period;
with the mantra of Mahāgaṇeśa, one should attach protection to her. || 65 ||
In this manner, one should perform the rite for seven days; thus a barren woman becomes the mother of sons.
Oṃ, O Great Gaṇapati, bestowing protection, grant me the nectar of a son. (66)

Having drunk a single leaf of the *palāśa* tree mixed with the milk of a pregnant woman, one obtains a handsome son; of this there is no doubt. One should follow the wholesome regimen as previously described for a period of seven days.
Oṃ, O Great Gaṇapati, grant protection; give my son the nectar of immortality.
One should cause him to swallow the root of *devadālī* under the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism and the Sun.
Three niṣkas [of gold] should be given along with cow's milk according to the previous sequence; even a barren woman obtains a son, and wholesome food should be provided as before. (69)
Having ground the root of the *śarapuṅkhī* plant with cold water and drinking one *karṣa* of it, one shall obtain a fetus through the previously mentioned sequential application.
One should drink equal parts of mustā, priyaṅgu, sauvīra, and lac, along with honey, using rice-water; by drinking one karṣa of this, a barren woman becomes possessed of sons.
She should drink it for seven days while following the wholesome regimen as previously described. (71)
And having gathered sahadevī with its roots under the asterism Puṣya and during the sun's transit, || 72 ||
Having dried that powder in the shade, a woman who drinks it with the milk of cows of a single color as before becomes pregnant, even if she was previously barren. (73)

It is said that if a woman drinks the root or the rhizome of the *lakṣmaṇā* plant with milk for three days during her fertile period, and then eats only milk-rice according to the prescribed rule, she gives birth to a son; this is no wonder. (74)
Pippalī, keśara, and śṛṅgavera, when drunk with cow’s ghee as a digestive stimulant, enable even a barren woman to obtain a son by force; this is the yoga prescribed by the sages. (75)

Having drunk ghee prepared with water infused with *turaṅgagandhā* on the day of her ritual bath, a barren woman who observes the prescribed restraint will certainly conceive upon union with a man. (76)

Having ground the root of the Lakṣmaṇā plant, which was extracted during the conjunction of Puṣya and the Sun, as well as that of the Vajra tree, and drinking it with the milk of a single-colored cow, is known by the lords of sages to cause a woman to bear a son. (77)
Having ground a tuber-root with clarified butter during her fertile period, she shall become pregnant. || 78 ||

If a young woman drinks the powder of *lakṣmaṇā* extracted under the Puṣya asterism, ground by a man and mixed with ghee, and then consumes rice with milk, she will conceive through union with her husband; this is no wonder. (79)
A woman who has bathed after her menses, even if she is barren, will conceive a child if she drinks the root of *kṛṣṇāparājitā* mixed with goat’s milk three times.
A woman who drinks fresh powder of *nāgakeśara* with cow’s milk for seven days, and consumes her meals with ghee during that period, shall conceive a child upon union with her husband. (81)
And she who [desires a son] during her fertile period should drink milk with a single leaf of *putrajīvaka*.
Through this recitation, that woman shall truly become possessed of a son;
and by drinking its root with the milk of a single-colored cow, she shall likewise have a son.
Having drunk the two types of *kākoli*, the root of *lakṣmaṇā*, and the rice-grains of *ṣaṣṭika* with the milk of a woman of the same caste during her fertile period, she becomes pregnant. (84)
On the day of Aśvinī, a wise man should cause one to grasp a branch of the Bodhi tree;
by merely drinking it with cow’s milk, a barren woman shall become possessed of sons. (85)
Indeed, sesame oil and jaggery,
cooked with the addition of cow dung fire and the urine of a young bull mixed in a measure of one *prastha*,
when drunk seven times during the middle of the menstrual period, [achieves its purpose].
Only when she has indeed blossomed does she certainly give birth to a son. || 86 ||
One should grind equal parts of white Kadamba leaf and the root of Bṛhatī with goat’s milk. || 87 ||
One should drink this great medicine for three nights or five nights;
when it is drunk during the fertile period, a fetus will certainly be conceived. (88)
One should drink the seeds of gokṣura with the juices of nirguṇḍikā for either three nights or seven nights; thus a barren woman becomes possessed of sons. (89)
If the powder of *karkoṭa* seeds and milk of a single color are drunk during the fertile period, a pregnancy will certainly occur. (90)
If one ties the root of a banyan tree under the constellation called Bhaga or under Hasta, one shall obtain a handsome son who increases the prosperity of the family.
If a woman who has bathed after her menses drinks the well-consecrated juice of the *aśvattha* tree's tender shoots on the previous day, even a barren woman may obtain a son. (92)

Vatica laccifolia (vaṭavandāka) well-ground with the milk of a cow that is of a single color and has a calf of the same color, and then processed [with medicinal herbs], when drunk by a barren woman, will cause her to obtain a son.

Thus ends the treatment for those barren from birth. Now follows the treatment for those who have become barren after previously having sons: if a woman who formerly had children should at some point become barren...
She should be known as a "crow-barren" woman; now her medical treatment is described. || 94 ||
Having ground Viṣṇukrāntā together with its roots in buffalo milk,
she should consume it with buffalo butter during her fertile period.
In this manner, she should perform [the rite] for seven days, and follow the prescribed regimen as previously stated;
thus, even a woman who has borne only one child will conceive a most auspicious fetus.
One should cause the root of Aśvagandhā to be taken under the Puṣya asterism when the sun is shining.
One should grind [the medicine] with buffalo milk and always consume half a pala;
after seven days, even a woman barren like a crow conceives a long-lived child. 98.
Thus ends the treatment for the "barren as a crow.
Now follows the treatment for those who have lost their children: [if] the fetus has perished merely upon being conceived, after a fortnight, a month, or a year...
She whose child dies within two or three years is called a "Mṛtavatsakā" (one whose children have died);
in that case, a ritual application (yoga) should be performed as taught by Śaṅkara.
Or in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Jyeṣṭha, on the full moon day, when the house has been plastered.
One should have a new pitcher prepared, filled with fragrant water,
provided with branches and fruit, and endowed with the nine gems.
Adorned with golden threads and situated within a hexagonal mandala, one should worship the goddess renowned by the name Ekāntī in its center. 102.
One should worship with devotion using perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, incense, lamps, and food offerings, together with liquor, meat, and fish. 103.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and Indrāṇī—these are the Mothers upon the six petals. (104)
One should worship with mantra-seeds consisting of the syllables *phaṃ*, renowned by name.
The worship mantra is: *oṃ hrīṃ phaṃ ekāntidevatāyai namaḥ*.
With this mantra, worship and recitation should be performed.
And one should prepare seven funeral cakes (piṇḍas) made of curd-rice.
One should arrange six balls, corresponding in number to the six petals, separately for the Mothers;
the seventh ball, resembling a bilva fruit, one should cast outside in a clean place.
Oṃ hrīṃ phaiṃ, obeisance to the deity Ekāntidevatā.
Having partaken of that [offering], one should return home and perform the sacrifice before the wheel;
one should feed a maiden, a yoginī, and a beautiful woman along with their families. (107)
One should cause them to give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in the presence of the deity and not otherwise;
then, having dismissed the deity, that water from the pitcher should be poured into a river.
The wise one should observe the family [of deities]; by means of an auspicious [sign], he should predict an auspicious result.
Conversely, in the case of the opposite, the rite will grant complete success for as long as it is performed.
One should perform this every year; thus one shall obtain a long-lived son. || 110 ||
Facing east under the Kṛttikā constellation, one should collect the Vandhyākarkoṭakī plant;
its root should be ground with water and one should always drink one karṣa of it.
If taken for seven days during the period of menstruation, a long-lived son shall be born. || 111 ||
She who drinks a single portion of bījapūra tree root prepared with milk and mixed with clarified butter during her fertile period obtains a good husband and gives birth to a long-lived son. (112)
Thus ends the section on barren women conceiving.
Now, for the *phalaghṛta* (medicated ghee):
mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, kuṣṭha, triphalā, śarkarā, and balā.
Medā, payasyā, kākolī, the root of aśvagandha, ajamodā, the two types of haridrā, hiṅgu, and kaṭukarohiṇī. (113)
One should cook one prastha of ghee with one karṣa each of these: blue lotus (utpala), white water lily (kumuda), grapes (drākṣā), the two types of kākolī, and the two types of sandalwood (candana).
The juice of śatāvarī, milk, and four times as much ghee should be administered.
Having drunk this ghee, a man always acts like a bull among women. (115)

A woman gives birth to sons who are wise and pleasing to behold through the Priyadarśana [oblation]; likewise, she whose fetus is unstable, or the woman who gives birth to a stillborn child, [is purified by it]. (116)
It is recommended for those who have given birth to a short-lived child or a daughter, as well as in cases of defects of the womb, defects of the menses, and miscarriages. (117)
This secret is proclaimed as "Phalaghṛta" by name; it increases progeny, bestows longevity, and wards off all malevolent planets. (118)
In this rite, clarified butter is offered from a cow that has a living calf and is of a single color;
here, the flame for the fire is provided by means of wild cow-dung.
Thus ends the oil with fruits (*phalaghṛta*).
Now, regarding the protection against miscarriage: if, unexpectedly, in the first month of pregnancy, there occurs pain in the womb;
One should grind equal parts of padmaka, uśīra, and candana with cow’s milk;
if a woman drinks one pala of this, her fetus will become stable within three days.
Alternatively, having ground madhuka, dāru, and the seed of the śākavṛkṣa tree,
one should drink them with kṣīrakākolī along with cow's milk.
Blue lotus, lotus stalk, licorice, and karkaṭaśṛṅgikā—having drunk these with cow's milk on the second day, the pains are pacified. || 122 ||
Alternatively, having ground the bark of the *aśvattha* tree, black sesame, *śatāvarī*,
and *mañjiṣṭhā*, one should drink it with four times as much milk.
One suffering from pain on the third day should drink *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *tagara*, *kuṣṭha*, *mṛṇāla*, and the filaments of the lotus ground together with cold water.
Alternatively, one should drink milk after grinding kṣīrakākolī and balā.
One should drink blue lotus, lotus stalks, gokṣura, and kaśeruka with the milk of cows during the fourth month; thus the pain subsides.
Alternatively, having ground madhuka, rāsnā, śyāmā, brāhmaṇayaṣṭikā, and anantā, one should drink them with cow's milk.
In the fifth month, she should drink a decoction of punarnavā, kākolī, tagara, blue lotus (nīlotpala), and gokṣura, which removes the distress of pregnancy.
Alternatively, having ground a pair of *bṛhatī* plants— the sacrificial limb and the excellent bud—
and mixing them with cow’s ghee and milk, one should drink it on the fifth day.
One should grind white sugar and the pulp of the wood-apple (kapittha) with cold water;
in the sixth month, one should drink this with cow's milk for the removal of distress. 130.
Alternatively, in the sixth month, one should drink gokṣura, śigru, madhuka, and pṛśniparṇikā, ground together with balā and mixed with cow's milk. (131)
Having ground kaśeru, the root of the lotus (pauṣkara), śṛṅgāṭa, and the blue water-lily (nīlotpala),
and having drunk it with milk in the seventh month, [the fever] is pacified.
Alternatively, on the seventh day, one should drink madhuka, grapes, śṛṅgāṭa, kaśeruka, and lotus stalks mixed with sugar and milk.
In the eighth month, one should drink yaṣṭī, padmākṣaka, musta, keśara, gajapippalī, and nīlotpala with cow’s milk.
Alternatively, one should prepare milk with these: the root of the *bilva*, the *kapittha* fruit, the fruit of the *bṛhatī*, and the roots of the sugarcane and the *paṭola*. (135)
Having drunk that milk mixed with water, the pain in the womb is pacified. || 136 ||
One should grind *viśālā*, *bīja*, and *kaṅkola* together with honey;
by this, the pain of the ninth month shall be pacified, and not otherwise. (137)
Alternatively, on the ninth day, one who suffers from pain should drink milk prepared with madhuka, śyāmā, anantā, and kṣīrakākulī.
In the tenth month, for the sake of pacification, one should cause [the woman] to drink sugar, cow’s udder-shaped [milk], grapes, honey, and blue lotus along with the milk of cows. (139)
Alternatively, one should drink cow’s milk prepared with ginger on the tenth day;
or else, one should drink licorice and deodar wood together with milk and ginger. (140)

As a general treatment, a woman who forcibly drinks for three days a mixture of *dhātrī*, *añjana*, *sāvara*, and *yaṣṭikā* [liquorice], and continues its application for only seven days, will stabilize a displaced embryo; this is no wonder. 141.

Honey, sandalwood from the Sindhu region, and clarified butter from Mount Mahendra, well-ground with milk—this formulation, which quickly destroys the fetus as it flows out, was indeed taught by the Mūladevas. (142)
A dose of clay from a potter’s hand, mixed with cow’s milk and honey, wards off miscarriage and the pain of labor, and forcibly brings about a normal delivery. (143)
Milk prepared with kaśeru, śṛṅgāṭaka, jīraka, payasyā, eraṇḍa, and śatāvarī,
mixed with sugar, shall eliminate the pain of the womb and ensure the stabilization of the fetus.

One should drink the bulb of *kaumudaka* mixed with honey, combined with milk and ghee, for seven days; or, when the wind is provoked, one should take it with sugar and well-cooked *balā*, cooled down.
This cures miscarriage, loss of appetite, wind-related disorders, grief, the three *doṣas*, and vomiting.
It destroys every kind of colic; thus is that which is traditionally remembered.
Water boiled with *hrībera*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, and black pepper should be administered when the fetus is unstable, in cases of menorrhagia, or when there is pain in the abdomen. (146)
Having drunk the root of the *kuvalaya* plant with sesame seeds, mixed with honey and sugar, along with milk,
one will quickly stabilize a fetus that has been displaced by severe morbid humors.
Blue lotuses, lotus stalks, licorice, sugar, and sesame seeds—these are the best for stabilizing the embryo when the fetuses are beginning to dissolve. 148.
Thus ends the protection against miscarriage.
Now, for the prevention of fetal wasting:
cow’s milk mixed with sugar serves to pacify fetal wasting.
Or, for the alleviation of that [condition], a pregnant woman should drink equal parts of madhuka powder and gambhārī fruit powder with cow’s milk. (149)
Thus ends the method for preventing fetal malpresentation. Now follows the procedure for an easy delivery: one should insert the powder of the root of white *punarnavā* into the vagina.
A woman, excessively tormented by her fetus, gives birth in an instant. || 150 ||
The root of the white guñjī plant should be taken facing north;
by tying it around the waist, one will immediately obtain an unborn son.
One should extract the root of the vāsaka plant located on the northern side;
by tying it around the waist with seven threads, a woman gives birth easily.
Furthermore, by stirring some white guñjā fruit in cow's urine, one attains an easy delivery at that very moment; there is no doubt about this.
Or, if one smears the vagina with it, she gives birth with ease. (153)
Or, by applying the root of *sahadevī* to the horse's tail at the waist, she shall give birth easily. || 154 ||
One should cause a four-finger-length root of the *apāmārga* plant to be taken;
if a woman inserts it into her womb, she will give birth at that very moment. (155)
Having ground the tuber of the *lāṅgalī* plant with water, one should smear it upon the vagina and smear the navel with it; then she will certainly give birth at that very moment. (156)
She should drink half a guñjā fruit cut into pieces along with half a water-nut (pūga), or she should drink it ground with water; thus, she will give birth easily.

Having uprooted a pair of *guñjā* roots according to the prescribed rite under the asterism of Puṣya and on a Sunday, and having bound them to the waist or the head with blue threads, a woman will bring about a swift delivery. (158)
"By drinking either house-soot with house-water, a weak woman gives birth very quickly;
furthermore, the root of *alambuṣā* tied [to the body]—these two methods," so the King declared. (159)

A woman, having drunk the juice of *mātuluṅga* mixed with the powder of *madhuka*, honey, and clarified butter, will forcefully obtain a birth free from pain; there is no doubt to be entertained in this matter. (160)
In this case, the root of the citron (mātuluṅga) should be used, not the fruit; having boiled it, it should be drunk.
A woman afflicted by labor pains should drink water boiled with the ten roots (daśamūlī), combined with ghee and rock salt; she will give birth with ease. (161)
The mantra for easy delivery: *oṃ manmatha oṃ manmatha oṃ manmatha manmathavāhini lambodara muñca muñca svāhā*.
With this mantra, a person who is pure should give well-heated water to drink.
Indeed, by drinking water mixed with *abhipāna*, a pregnant woman gives birth more quickly and with ease. || 162 ||

Oṃ manmatha oṃ manmatha oṃ manmatha manmathavāhini lambodara muñca muñca svāhā! Having placed the syllable Oṃ at the head and having well-worshipped it with the syllable Haṃ and the syllable A, [one should say] "Oṃ" at the beginning and "namas trimūrtaye" at the end. || 163 ||
"Aṃ oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Threefold Form (Trimūrti).
By this very mantra, one should recite [the name] in the lying-in chamber;
she will obtain an easy delivery and will certainly receive a son. (164)
Thus concludes the procedure for a comfortable delivery.
Now follows the warding off of spirits, ghosts, and the like from infants and women in childbirth:
take the root of the *bilva*, *devadāru*, cow horn, and *priyaṅgu*.
The excrement of a cat, kuṣṭha, bamboo bark, and goat urine [are used]. || 165 ||
Having ground these, this incense quickly destroys the afflictions of planetary spirits, malevolent beings, fever, and the like.
With the mantra "Oṃ drāvitaṃ tāpe ṭhaṃ ṭhaḥ svāhā," one should offer this incense.
[It wards off] ḍākinīs, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, and brahmarākṣasas.
Fever that lasts for one day or two days is destroyed at that very moment. || 166 ||

Oṃ drāvitam tāpe ṭhaṃ ṭhaḥ svāhā. Incense made of fragrant resin (*śrīvāsa*), mustard seed, costus (*kuṣṭha*), sweet flag (*vacā*), oil, ghee, and fat should be offered for children seized by spirits, in order to pacify the seizing demons. 167.
Ghee mixed with equal parts of the leaves of *śirīṣa* and *nimba*, the bark of cow-horn, *vaca*, bamboo bark, and peacock feathers, along with *kaṅgu* grain; 168.
Incense destroys the *bālagrahas*; one should consecrate it oneself with the mantra.
The incense mantra is: *oṃ drutaṃ muñca muñca uḍḍāmareśvara ājñāpayati svāhā*. || 169 ||
An incense prepared from punarnavā, nimba leaves, mustard seeds, and ghee is said to provide constant protection for pregnant women and children. || 170 ||
Oṃ, release quickly, release! Uḍḍāmareśvara commands: svāhā!
One should gather the sprouts of a pomegranate under the Jyeṣṭhā constellation;
when tied at the door, it wards off all seizing spirits (grahas) from children. 171.
On a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, one should uproot the root of the white guñjā plant and wear it around the necks of children;
this destroys the fear of ḍākinīs.
One should prepare a nasal drop (nasya) from the juice of the two—the leaves of white Aparājitā and the leaves of Jayā; by this, the Ḍākinīs, Dānavas, and other such beings flee.

A fumigation made from snake-skin, *śikhijāriṣṭa* sprouts, turmeric, *vacā*, garlic, asafoetida, *golomī*, *śṛṅgī*, black pepper, and honey destroys all fevers; it removes the fever of children. (174)
The excrement of a muskrat, meat, turmeric, and bilva leaves. || 175 ||
Indraja mustard leaf, employed as an incense preparation, quickly stops a child's crying at night; of this there is no doubt. (176)
A wise person should saturate dried *marica* with the bile of a fish king on a Sunday; when applied as collyrium, it captivates all beings. (177)
The mantra of Narasiṃha, when uttered even once, removes ḍākinīs, grahas, and bhūtas, just as the rising sun dispels darkness. (178)
The Nṛsiṃha mantra:

Oṃ, to Narasiṃha, the tearer of the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu’s son, who pervades the three worlds, the uprooter of the families of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and ḍākinīs, the source of all pillars of power; remove, remove all defects! Disperse, disperse! Cook, cook! Strike, strike! Make tremble, make tremble! Churn, churn! Hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ phaṭ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ! Come, come! Rudra commands: svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having consecrated mustard seeds with this mantra, one should strike the afflicted person; then all the seizing spirits (grahas) will flee.
For those overcome by child-seizing spirits (bālagraha), one should diligently prepare an offering:
having cooked fish, meat, liquor, and fruit for seven days in a clean manner. (179)
At night, one should cast flowers, incense, unbroken rice, perfumes,
and a lamp toward the southern direction into a clean, new earthen bowl at a crossroads.
On a Saturday or a Tuesday, for the pacification of the defects of children. || 180 ||
The mantra for the offering of the *bali*: Oṃ, accept, accept the *bali* from all beings, svāhā!
Now follows the warding off of diseases such as those caused by snake-charmers and the like for the child.
When the moon is eclipsed, a wise man should extract the root of the *śikhī* plant according to the prescribed rite;
bound around the neck or the hips, even a child shall conquer a snake-charmer.
Having gathered the root of the white *arka* plant, one should tie it to a house pillar on a Sunday coinciding with the *puṣya* asterism; thus a child shall conquer a snake-charmer.
One should bind the root of the udumbara tree or the round fruit of the bṛhatkūṣmāṇḍa to the waist of a young child; by that means, one shall conquer snake-charmers.
Thus ends the protection of children against snake-charmers and diseases.
Now, for the protection of women during menstruation: the fruits and flowers of the *palāśa* and *rājādana* trees, as well as those of the *śālmalī* tree.
If one drinks this with clarified butter for half a month, protection will certainly be attained during the Puṣya constellation. || 184 ||

Having boiled the root of the *pāvakavṛkṣa* tree with dew-water while observing a vow, if a woman drinks it for three days at the time of her menses, she shall remain protected until the end of her life. 185.

Having drunk the fruit of the *kadamba* tree along with honey and *tuṣodaka* water—either once or for three days—at the conclusion of the ritual bath, one certainly achieves protection through the power of *haṭha* by means of this constant practice. (186)
If a woman constantly eats one *pala* measure of three-year-old treacle for half a month, her barrenness is declared by the preeminent poet to be certainly brought to an end. (187)
Two karṣas of the seed of the rākṣasa-tree and white śāli rice for seven days;
this is prescribed as a certain protection when drunk during the fertile period by a woman with eyes like a young deer. 188.
Thus ends the protection against menses for women.
Now, regarding the making of one unfortunate: if the *vandāka* plant of the *nimba* tree is placed upon a woman's body under the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, she becomes unfortunate. || 189 ||
Thus ends the rite for making [one] unfortunate.
Now, the rite for causing strife using the yantra that bestows power upon the donor.
If one places a *vibhītaka* fruit together with the root and leaf of a *śākhoṭa* tree at the door of someone's house, that person will surely experience quarrels.
Wherever in a house there is incense made from the hair of a cat, a mouse, a bird, or a naked ascetic during the lunar mansion Ārdrā, enmity indeed arises there.

Under the Viśākhā constellation, one who is naked and turns away from the tree should uproot the northern root of a neem tree and cast it into the house of someone; in that person's home, quarreling will occur every day.
One should collect the root and leaves of the śākhoṭa tree and place them together;
when they have been removed from that house, prosperity will prevail there.
Under that same lunar mansion, one should combine two seeds of the śākhoṭa and the jujube (badarī).
In whosever house one should place it, for that person there will be constant quarreling. || 192 ||
Having ground the *brahmadaṇḍī* plant together with its roots and combined with *kākamācī*,
one should repeatedly pound it with the juices of *jātī* flowers for seven nights.
This incense should be offered into the midst of the enemy clan;
for just as one smells according to the lineage, so does strife arise between a father and his sons.
Thus ends the eighth instruction, titled "From the Emasculation Rite to the Provocation of Quarrels," in the *Kāmaratna* composed by the illustrious Nityanātha. 8.
The Ninth Instruction:
Now follows the ritual for protection for the purpose of destroying all portents of death (*ariṣṭa*),
exactly as it was previously told by the Lord to the Goddess.
And [the syllable] beginning with *ka* and ending with the double *ra*, joined with a vowel, is a single syllable. || 1 ||
Having worshipped it with the letter *ī* as well, and having placed the syllable *oṃ* at its head, one who desires success should recite it, provided it is joined below with three *r*s.
"The mere recitation of this mantra for self-restraint fifty times shall bring about the destruction of all misfortunes; so said the Destroyer of Cities."
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ oṃ hrīṃ krīṃ khrīṃ vā oṃ krīṃ khrīṃ kṣīṃ oṃ ṭhrīṃ thrīṃ phrīṃ hrīṃ; likewise, the letters following ka, following ca, and similarly those following ṭha and ta.
Having taken the letter *pa* followed by the letter *ra*, it is well-adorned with the vowel *i*;
likewise, it is joined with the *adhorepha* and has the syllable *oṃ* at its head.
Mantra: KHRŪṂ CHRAṂ ṬHRAṂ THRAṂ PHRAṂ HRAM | Or:
OṂ KHRĪṂ CHRĪṂ ṬHRĪṂ THRĪṂ PHRĪṂ HRĪṂ (Pure).
O Sage, for those who always recite this great mantra with faith, there shall be,
in every way, the destruction of all misfortunes for that person.

Oṃ khrīṃ chrīṃ ṭhrīṃ thrīṃ phrīṃ hrīṃ (pure). O sinless one, having consecrated with even a hundred recitations a hand-held red flower and a strung garland, one should always offer them to the Goddess.
As long as he lives, his merit shall increase, and he shall obtain all gains day after day;
moreover, by having this written and installed, no misfortune shall befall his home.
O sinless one, having written the final letters of the alphabet five times, likewise [place] the syllable Oṃ at the head, joined with the letter 'ra' and the visarga.
It is taught that one should worship with the syllable *ha* and conclude with the syllable *phaṭ*;
likewise, one should worship with the syllable *ī* and conclude with the final syllable *phaṭ*.
[The mantra is: *oṃ kṣīṃ kṣīṃ kṣīṃ kṣīṃ phaṭ*.
This mantra is my very form, as is meditation and recitation;
it is my own heart, and one whose mind is always absorbed in it [attains me].
Oṃ kṣrīṃ kṣrīṃ kṣrīṃ kṣrīṃ kṣrīṃ phaṭ. By reciting this half-a-thousand times, there shall always be security in that person's home;
there is nothing equal to it in the three worlds, and one shall eternally obtain its fruit. (10)
O Goddess, listen to the great fruit: a living being becomes happy in another birth, and is always provided for by the king, his wife, his son, and his kinsmen.
By kinsmen, by virtuous people, and especially by enemies. || 11 ||
One should grasp the two ends, joined with the low-pitched sound (madhorepha). || 12 ||
Having joined it with the syllable Oṃ, and endowed it with the line and the bindu.
Oṃ kṣau kṣauṃ.
By this very mantra, those great people who perform recitation all attain security through its constant recitation. 14.
Having uprooted the root of the white Arka plant under the Puṣya asterism on a Sunday, one should wear it;
by means of the two arms, no diseases shall arise, and especially no portents of misfortune.
Upon seeing it, the ḍākinīs, dānavas, and others perish;
by its smoke, the pretas and other spirits certainly flee to a great distance. (16)
If one gathers vandāka produced from the śirīṣa tree under the constellation Pūrvābhādrapadā and places it upon the head, fearlessness certainly ensues. || 17 ||
The root of *viṣṇukrāntā* held in the hand conquers the fear of thieves;
when recited even once with the mantra of Narasiṃha, it removes *ḍākinīs*, seizing spirits, and ghosts, just as the rising sun dispels darkness. (18)
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ phaṭ svāhā. By remembering the Great Bhairavī, a person becomes fearless from the terror of ghosts, spirits, and demons; of this there is no doubt. (19)
Thus is the ritual for protection for the purpose of destroying all misfortunes.
Now, regarding the induction of sleep:
in cases of imprisonment or theft, one should recite the mantra three times.
And all the sentries fall under the very power of sleep. || 20 ||
The mantra:

Oṃ Kālakālikā, destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, Yoganidrāṇī, the goddess residing in the city of [Amuka], Kālikāmālā-Yoganidrāṇī, Udayapānā. Nandīkāla, holder of Māyā, Nāganidrāṇī, she who resides in the city of [Amuka] and wields the staff; she who rolls the kings about, the command of Kālikā, Gaḍāgaḍī, the command of Kālikā at the sacred seat (pīṭha).
Thus ends the worldly mantra.

Now, the mantra declared in the Nigamas (or Śāstras): *Oṃ hrīṃ caṇḍācaṇḍa ugracaṇḍārikā kālikā nidraya nidraya*. By means of this mantra, the Great Sleep (*mahānidrā*) occurs. Having recited this mantra, or having recited it at his house, one should reduce [the target] to dust and cast it away.
Oṃ hrīṃ! O Caṇḍācaṇḍā, O Ugracaṇḍārikā Kālikā! Put them to sleep, put them to sleep!

O Kālikā, through the spell of Time and Delusion, may the gods, asuras, and humans attain stability. Kālikā, the servant of the Destroyer of Time, protects the three worlds. As they awaken from their sleep, the earth becomes intoxicated with fame. By the command of Kālikā, those who were asleep are brought to wakefulness at the time of sunrise.
Having eaten betel nut and made a cavity from its remains, one should join it together and urinate therein;
when that [urine] reaches the garden, one causes sleep [in it] by means of this mantra. || 21 ||
The matted roots of *kākajaṅghā* placed upon the head produce sleep;
likewise, the root of black *kākamācī* is said to possess that same quality.
Alternatively, one should dig up *munikhaṇḍaka* greens at the place where the bed is located;
likewise, by binding the root of *karañja* to the head, the same effect is produced. (23)
The mantra for inducing sleep:
Oṃ śuddhe śuddhe mahāyogini mahānidre svāhā | Oṃ śuddhe śuddhe mahāyogini mahānidre svāhā |
Having ground blue lotus, black pepper, and the root of *nāgakeśara*, one should apply it to the eyes; one will undoubtedly fall asleep. (24)
Thus ends the method for inducing sleep.
Now, the method for destroying sleep:
having ground *kūṣmāṇḍa* and the horn of a buffalo in equal parts, [one should apply it].
If one applies [the ointment] to its right back, its sleep will be destroyed. || 25 ||
Having ground the seeds of *śobhāñjana*, a fine flower of blue lotus (*nīlotpala*),
and *samanāgeśvara*, one is freed from sleep by applying them as an ointment (*añjana*).
Having ground the ripe fruit of the bṛhatī along with madhuyaṣṭi, one should apply this as an ointment to the eyes of anyone; their sleep shall vanish.

Having ground together the root of *kanakadhuttura*, the ash of burnt clouds, and the pollen of *ketakī* flowers, one should administer this under a deceptive guise; it becomes a destroyer of sleep. || 28 ||
Thus ends the method for destroying sleep.
Now, regarding the release from bondage: on the full moon day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should extract the root of the Śikhin [plant].
By that, one is released from bondage; there is no doubt that one whose crest-lock is bound [is liberated]. || 29 ||
The mantra for releasing from bondage:

Oṃ, homage to her who is golden-pigmented, who is a portion of Rudra’s heart, who wears the bones of Rudra! Stay, stay! Move, move! Delude all, delude all! O Blessed One, born from the crest-lock, darkness, great illusion! Svāhā!
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should then bind the aforementioned medicinal herb at the crest-lock (*śikhā*); from that, success follows.
One should write the "release from bondage" using a portion of *plakṣa* wood, ending with the letter *ka*.

Oṃ, homage to her who is golden-tawny, a portion of Rudra’s heart, the bearer of Rudra’s bones! Stay, stay! Move, move! Delude, delude all! O Blessed One, born from the crest-lock, darkness, Great Illusion, svāhā!
O Piśācī named Sukhā, kill, kill so-and-so! Cook, cook! Quickly bring [him] under control, svāhā!
Now, the breaking of fetters and the like.
On a Sunday when the sun is in the Hasta constellation, one should uproot the uttaraga variety of *senduvāra*;
its touch quickly effects the severance of bonds, just like the wind.
One should feed a lizard equal parts of māṃsī and red lotus;
by the touch of a pill made from its excrement, one is certainly able to break open a lock.
Yogis should take well-baked brick or black diamond;
having reduced it to a fine powder, or likewise iron dross. (33)
Having strengthened a rope with threads and smeared it with sesame oil, one should soak that powder in it; this will thoroughly pierce even great iron.
The mantras for breaking shackles:

Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Rudra, the Lord Uḍḍāmareśvara, the one of many forms, the wearer of diverse forms; laugh, laugh! dance, dance! pierce, pierce! [obeisance] to the exhibitor of various wonders and magical illusions; ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā. By consecrating all yogas with this, success is attained. || 35 ||

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra, the Lord Uḍḍāmareśvara, the one of many forms, the wearer of various forms; laugh, laugh! dance, dance! pierce, pierce! O you who display various wonders and magical illusions! Ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā!

The army of Vāghavāhinī is in the lion; O Kālī, Kālī, you who are the mistress of all! Noble Goddess, refuge for those who recite the mantra, refuge for those who recite the mantra! Not even for a hundred Nāthis, O Mother of the Three Worlds! You who possess the sixty-four bonds, O Āpalā! Caṇḍā, Caṇḍacāmuṇḍī, Cāmuṇḍā, Vikaṭakālikā, Mādana! In front of [the deity], O you who possess the bond of such-and-such! Āpalā! O kinsman, kinsman! In the state of gain and loss, O firm one! The sixty-four-fold speech, the eternal Kālī! I cast off desire! *Huṃkāraḥ*! O you who possess the practice of the sixty-four bonds, O Bha-ilalyā! O short-haired Kālikā! This is the command! Or else: O Command, O Goddess, O you whose face is like the moon, O you who are served by the gods! Without delay, O Goddess, O Mother of the Three Worlds, O Ramā! You who possess the sixty-four bonds, O Ambelā! Caṇḍā, Caṇḍacāmuṇḍā, Vikaṭṭa, Kālikā, Mādana! In front of [the deity], O you who possess the bond of such-and-such! O you who toss about the kinsmen and the misfortunes of sin! The firm sixty-four bonds! O stainless Kālikā, I cast them off! *Huṃkāraḥ*! O you who possess the staff of the sixty-four bonds, O mountain-like bearer, O Lakṣārasvārakālikā! This is the command! Or else: *Oṃ agnimukhī pipācī amukaṃ hana hana paca paca śīghraṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*. Having first recited these two mantras one hundred and eight times, when they are recited seven times, the severing of various kinds of bonds occurs.

Oṃ Vāgha Vāhini Siddhe Pākādi Likā Lāyi! Ā-ā Jā Devī! O Cintā, speak to me; there is no destruction for Sarasvatī. O Tombidevī, you who are the delight of the three worlds in battle, you who partake in the bondage of the five-fold creation, you who have arrived—Caṇḍā, Caṇḍa-Cāmuṇḍā, Vikaṭa-Kālikā, Mādana, and the one before whom [the world] bows, the one who bestows wealth upon such-and-such a forest-dweller, you who have arrived, O Vāgha Vāgha, protect my feet! The sixty-four bonds are shattered by Kāsikā, the fish-bannered one (Māchaḍe), the syllable Hūṃ, and the sixty-four bond-breakers. Bhādri, Bhāla, Kṣāra, Svāra—this is the command of Kālikā.
Oṃ daṃ huṃ oṃ. Having recited this mantra, if a blow is struck with a finger at the door, the door becomes opened.

Āya āya ciñciṭhi ciṭhi hāṃlā Vajranandikā Kālikā. By reciting this mantra three times over white mustard seeds and a white Udumbara flower, one should throw them at the first door; all doors will be shattered. || 36 ||
Thus ends the breaking of shackles.
Now, for the warding off of domestic afflictions: one should fashion the image of a doll and smear it with *tāla* ground with buttermilk.
Having smelled it, flies go toward the house; of this there is no doubt.
White arka-milk mixed with kulmāṣa and sesame powder,
placed upon arka leaves, brings about the end of mice within the house.
One should grind together talaka, goat dung and urine, and onion;
by smearing this upon a mouse, one causes it to give up its life.
Upon seeing that [dead mouse], people indeed flee from the house out of curiosity. (39)
Having ground the excrement of a cat and the kernel of a palmyra fruit together, one should smear it [on the mouse holes].
Upon smelling that, the mice will immediately abandon their home and flee.
Having ground together sulphur, yellow orpiment, brāhmī, and the three pungents (trikaṭu) with goat’s urine,
one should smear the crucible as before.
Under the asterism Maghā, one should place a substance derived from honey within the field of Bradhnaka;
thereby, the binding of the mouths of flies and mice occurs.
The lamp that attracts mice is made from jaggery, molasses, and oil. || 43 ||

"Brahmā is bound by me in the east; Viṣṇu is bound by me in the west; Rudra is bound by me in the north; Yama is bound by me in the south; Vāsuki is bound by me in the netherworld, bound by my thousand hoods—Hrūṃ! Salutation to the thumb. Having formed a hollowed cup with the hands, one should strike three claps. Thereby, the warding off of mice and mosquitoes occurs. || 44 ||

Brahmā is bound by me in the east; Viṣṇu is bound by me in the west; Rudra is bound by me in the north; Yama is bound by me in the south; Vāsuki is bound by me in the netherworld (pātāla), bound within his thousand hoods. HŪṂ! Salutation to the thumb.
One should place a flower from the rohiṣa grass in the middle of the wick;
by the mere sight of that lamp, bedbugs are swiftly destroyed. (45)
One should prepare a wick made of *arka* cotton and soak it in your own [urine];
when a lamp is lit with that [wick] and mustard oil, bedbugs are completely eliminated. (46)
The fruit and flower of *Arjuna*, lac, *śrīvāsa* resin, *guggulu*, the root of white *aparājitā*, *bhallātaka*, and *viḍaṅga*. (47)
Incense mixed with resin (sarjarasa) should be offered in the middle of the house;
then snakes, bedbugs, mice, and scents will depart to the ten directions.
A fumigation consisting of jaggery, resin of Shorea robusta, bhallātaka, viḍaṅga, the three myrobalans (triphalā), lac-resin, and arka flowers removes the effects of scorpions and snakes. (49)
One should burn a powder of mustā, siddhārtha, bhallātaka, and the fruit of kapikacchu, along with jaggery and bhānuphala, together with an equal amount of sarjarasa.
Bedbugs, mosquitoes, snakes, rats, and venomous insects.
They flee, abandoning their homes, like cowards in battles. || 51 ||

Resin of the *sarja* tree, *śakra* (saffron), fat of the *meda* antelope, root of the *arjuna*, and *marubaka*, *ketaka*, and *nakha*—incense prepared from these removes insects, snakes, mosquitoes, flies, and the like. 52.
The fruit of the *rājavṛkṣa* tree, tied upon a bedstead, destroys bedbugs;
likewise, lac, resin, *uśīra*, mustard, and *patraka* are excellent [remedies]. (53)
Having made a wick from the tip of a sprout of the Somarāja tree, one should prepare a lamp; thus the bedbug is destroyed.
Bhallātaka, viḍaṅga, viśvaka, and likewise puṣkara, as well as jambula,
destroy mosquitoes when used as incense within the house.
Thus ends the warding off of domestic afflictions. Now follows the destruction of field calamities;
specifically, the destruction of all calamities affecting the crops of the field.
One should scatter sand and white mustard seeds in the middle of the field. || 56 ||
By the power of the knowledge of mantras, locusts, snakes, insects, boars, deer, mice, and mosquitoes do not enter there. (57)

The mantra is: *Oṃ namaḥ surebhyaḥ balajaḥ japa pari pari raja pari pari mili svāhā | Oṃ surebhyo namaḥ*. Having paid homage, one should employ this lore (*vidyā*). [One should say: "I employ this lore; may the lore be successful for me, svāhā! "I effect the binding of the mouths of all jackals, deer, hares, and other living beings, such as locusts and other creatures. If one transgresses the mantra here, one becomes defiled by the sin of being ungrateful toward that living being. *Svāhā!*
Having consecrated white mustard seeds together with sand seven times with these two mantras, one should scatter them in the middle of the field; all calamities will be destroyed.
It causes the piercing of the mouths of mice, jackals, and insects.
*Oṃ namaḥ surebhyaḥ balaja japa pari pari pari raja pari pari mili svāhā oṃ surebhyo namaḥ*.
"I employ this spell; may the spell be effective for me, svāhā!"

"I bind the mouths of all jackals, deer, rabbits, and other living beings, including locusts and other creatures"—by uttering this, one who is ungrateful toward life becomes tainted by that sin where he transgresses the mantra; *svāhā*.

Having consecrated white mustard seeds with sand seven times using these two mantras, one should scatter them in the middle of the field, and all calamities will perish. This [is the power of] the mantra of Vidyāmaṅkuśanātha or of Bhairava, which effects the piercing of the mouths of rats, jackals, and insects.

*Namo nagaranāthāya hayahara-haraśila hayahara-haraśila, bind the mouths of all living beings, *kuru kuru* hruṃ phaṭ svāhā! O Bhairava of the city of Ujjayinī, O Mahādeva of the treasury, O Flower-Speaker, with Hanumān as witness: *asti astu*. With this mantra, one should consecrate sandalwood seven times and cast it into the middle of the garden. All flowers and fruits will become free from harm. || 58 ||
Oṃ, homage to the Lord of the City! Haya, hara-hara, śila-śila! Bind the mouths of all living beings! Kuru kuru hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

The city of Ujjayinī is the speech of Bhairava; Mahādeva is the treasury; the flower is the speech; Hanumān is the witness. Let it be, let it be! A wise person should have a pill made from *devadālī* and white mustard seeds.
Having cast it into the middle of the field, one shall remove all fear of birds.
If one casts a vandā plant grown from a *vibhītaka* tree under the asterism named Pūrvāṣāḍhā into the midst of the grain, the increase of the grain will certainly occur.
Thus ends the method for destroying afflictions of the field.
Now, the method for increasing the milk of cows, buffaloes, and others:
*Oṃ huṃkāriṇīprasava oṃ śītala*. By consecrating grass and other fodder seven times with this mantra and giving it to them to eat, they will yield abundant milk. (61)
Oṃ huṃkāriṇīprasava oṃ śītalam.
Thus [is] the increase of the milk of cows, buffaloes, and so forth.

Thus ends the ninth instruction, titled "The Destruction of Calamities and Other Crop-Plagues, and the Increase of the Milk of Cows, Buffaloes, and So Forth," in the *Kāmaratna* composed by Śrī Nityanātha. 9.
Now begins the tenth instruction:

Next, regarding the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), on a Tuesday night, one should take charcoal from a cremation ground, wrap it in a black cloth, encircle it with a red thread, and cast it upon the house of the person [targeted]; within seven days, that person's eradication occurs.
One should take a five-fingered peg of *citraka* wood during the asterism of Punarvasu, empower it seven times with mantras, and bury it in the house; [the result] will be expulsion (*uccāṭana*).
For this, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one thousand and eight recitations of: *oṃ lohitamukhe svāhā*. || 1 ||
If one buries a single finger-breadth of an owl’s bone pin, consecrated seven times with the *bharaṇī* [mantra], the person [targeted] will be driven away.
The mantra is: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ dahadaha halahala svāhā. || 2 ||
By offering one hundred and eight wings of a crow and an owl while reciting the mantra over the name of the target, the total eradication of that person occurs.

Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Rudra, whose fangs are terrifying; kill, kill [so-and-so] together with his sons and kinsmen! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Quickly expel, expel! Huṃ phaṭ svāhā! Ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ! || 3 ||

Oṃ daha daha hala hala svāhā | Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra, the one with terrifying fangs; [strike] so-and-so, together with his sons and kinsmen, kill kill, burn burn, cook cook, quickly expel expel, huṃ phaṭ svāhā ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ || 2-3 ||
Oṃ tāre tāre oṃ ture svāhā. One should smear a stake made from *aṅgula* wood with crow’s bile; by burying it in someone’s house, that person’s eradication (*uccāṭana*) shall occur.
Oṃ hrīṃ, O staff-bearer, O staff-bearer, O great staff-bearer, homage be to you! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ. || 4 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ, O Staff-bearer, O Staff-bearer, O Great Staff-bearer, homage be to you! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ. || 4 ||
One should drive a human-bone stake four finger-widths deep into the door;
when accompanied by the mantra at the enemy's door, this will truly effect eradication.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra! Seize, seize so-and-so; cook, cook; terrify, terrify; rend, rend; destroy, destroy! Paśupati commands: ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ! || 5 ||
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra! Seize, seize so-and-so! Cook, cook! Terrify, terrify! Rend, rend! Destroy, destroy! Paśupati commands: ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ! || 5 ||

Having taken the discarded offerings and even the garment of a deceased man from a cemetery for the departed, one should cause them to be deposited in the house of that person [against whom one seeks harm].
On the eighth and the fourteenth [lunar days], there shall be the eradication of that very person.
This yoga has been declared by me; it succeeds even without a mantra.
Once it has been extracted, peace is attained. || 6 ||
If one places the root of white lāṅgalikā in someone's house or buries it there,
that person's immediate expulsion will certainly occur.

If a wise person buries the remains of offerings made to Śiva (śivanirmālya) in someone's house for the sake of accomplishing a goal, that person will be driven away; however, once it is removed, he becomes happy again.
Having gathered [the ashes] from the tree, one should burn that dwelling of the crow;
O beautiful woman, the ashes of the enemy given from the funeral pyre should be placed upon the head.
O Goddess, listen to this unsurpassed yoga which causes him to be expelled;
his expulsion occurs [by this], and once he is removed, he becomes happy again.
A four-finger-long *audumbara* stake, consecrated with the *śinī* mantra—whosoever has such a stake buried in their house, for that person alone there shall be expulsion (*uccāṭana*). || 10 ||
Oṃ śini śini svāhā. Now he describes another method for expulsion:
"I shall explain the procedure for expulsion as it is taught in the Śrīmatottara."
One should write the name on a nimba leaf using the dung of a buffalo and a horse;
immediately thereafter, it should be written with a pen made from a crow's wing.
The mantra, however, is as follows:
Oṃ, O Goddess with a face as white as a crow’s beak, uproot so-and-so, uproot so-and-so! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! || 11 ||
O Great Goddess, having written this mantra with the aforementioned substances,
one should then dig up the entire crow’s nest situated in a neem tree.
Then, having brought the fire from a cremation ground, it should be kindled with wood from the *dhattūra* plant.
Having prepared a fire with great oils or pungent substances,
one should perform its oblation according to the prescribed rite using the previously mentioned mantra.
Oṃ, O Goddess with a face as white as a crow’s beak, uproot so-and-so, uproot so-and-so! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Having worshipped Dhavalāmukhī with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), one should then scatter that ash upon the house of the enemy.
He shall be driven away, along with his sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
One should meditate upon the Great Goddess, who is white in complexion yet smoky-hued, three-eyed, and crowned with the moon;
she is endowed with a mass of matted hair and draped in a tiger skin.
And [she holds] a slender-limbed woman, a garland of bones, a small knife, and likewise a lotus.

Having meditated within one's heart upon her who has eyes like hollows, fearsome fangs, and an abdomen resembling the netherworld (pātāla), a person intent on yogic meditation should indeed worship her;
this is the renowned method of yoga for Maheśvarī in the Vīra-tantra. 15.
Thus ends the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*).
Now, for the rite of inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*):
one should grind together monkey hair, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *dārvī*, and donkey skin into a powder.

That powder, consecrated with mantras and interwoven with the names [of the two persons] and their actions, should be recited three thousand times. By means of that, even two who are affectionate toward one another will become intensely hostile, even though they were previously close, through the use of incense.
One should write the mantra, interwoven with the name and the ritual action (*nāmakarma*), upon a palm leaf;
having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of life-force) and recited it three thousand times,
one should split it in two after smearing it with poison and bury it on the bank of the Indus.
Even between Umā and Īśāna, who are naturally affectionate toward one another, there would quickly arise mutual enmity.
On one hand [of the child] he should place a crow's wing-feather, and likewise on the other, an owl's;
having consecrated them with mantras and joined their tips together, he should bind them with a black thread.
One should offer libations with the palms of the hands while with joined palms (añjali) over water;
one should perform this for seven days and recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Therein, a state of mutual hatred arises, which is a great wonder and a marvel.
Oṃ, svāhā to Devadatta and Yajñadatta!
May there be between Devadatta and Yajñadatta such enmity as exists between the crow and the owl, svāhā!
A doll has been fashioned from the excrement of a cat and a mouse, intended for the purpose of subjugation.
Having wrapped [the object] in blue cloth and empowered it one hundred times with the mantra,
enmity arises there between the two brothers, the father’s sons.
The mantra:
Oṃ, homage to Mahābhairava and to the one who dwells in the cremation ground; create enmity between [Name] and [Name], create it! Krūṃ Phaṭ! || 20 ||

Oṃ, homage to Mahābhairava and to the Dweller in the Cremation Ground! Cause [the two], so-and-so and so-and-so, to hate each other! Kruṃ Phaṭ! Oṃ, homage to Mahābhairava and to the Dweller in the Cremation Ground! Cause [the two], so-and-so and so-and-so, to hate each other! Kruṃ Phaṭ! And in one hand [place] a crow’s wing, and likewise in the other, an owl’s.
One should carefully offer three handfuls of water for twenty-one days using a blade of *darbha* grass;
each handful of water should be accompanied by a single flower of the red *aśvamāra* and the recitation of the mantra. (21)
One thousand and eight [mantras] should be offered daily and daily;
mutual hatred shall arise—this is declared as the Siddhayoga.
Oṃ, salutation to Kaṭīṭanī, Pramoṭanī, Gaurī, Gaurī! [Perform] for [Name] together with [Name], like a crow and an owl; perform, perform! Svāhā! This is the rite of inciting enmity (vidveṣaṇa).
Now, the rite for causing disease (vyādhikaraṇa).

And for its prevention, one should offer oblations of the three pungent spices (trikaṭu) smeared with mustard oil while reciting this mantra: "Oṃ, kill [so-and-so], kill [so-and-so], svāhā! Then the enemy becomes deaf. || 23 ||
One should make *guñjā* seeds into a very fine powder using the juices of *bhallātaka*;
by applying this to the body, leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) arises, and one becomes happy by drinking sugar with milk.
Oṃ, kill [Name], kill, svāhā!
If one throws the hairs of a female monkey, poison, the powder of *bhallātaka*,
and *guñjā* onto a person's body, that person will be afflicted with the pain of *lūtā* (spider-bite).
One should grind uśīra, candana, priyaṅgu, raktacandana, and tagara with water; by applying this as an ointment, spiders and other such pests are destroyed.
Thus ends the section on discordant substrates (*vyādhikaraṇa*).
Now, the method for inducing fever:

*Oṃ cāmuṇḍe hana hana daha daha paca paca matha matha calha calha amukaṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa svāhā*. If neem leaves smeared with pungent oil are offered as oblations while reciting this mantra along with the name of a person, fever will quickly afflict that person. If one offers a thousand *citraka* flowers, a quartan fever (*cāturthika-jvara*) occurs. If one offers salt one thousand and eight times, a burning fever (*dāha-jvara*) occurs. || 26 ||

Oṃ cāmuṇḍe, kill, kill! burn, burn! cook, cook! seize, seize so-and-so! svāhā! With this mantra, one should offer oblations of neem leaves and pungent oil while uttering the name of the person targeted; he will be seized by fever. With this [mantra], one should offer eight thousand oblations of salt; he will be seized by colic. || 27 ||
Oṃ cāmuṇḍe hana hana daha daha paca paca amukaṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa svāhā.
With this very mantra, one should offer eight thousand oblations of cane leaves; he [the victim] will be seized by quartan fever.
Having written the name of the person on birch bark with the juice of red flowers and *citraka*...
If one places it on an Arka branch, that person will be seized by a burning fever.
The mantra:
Oṃ, salutations to the glorious Lord Nṛsiṃha, the enemy of the Danujas; salutations to Kṛṣṇa. || 28 ||
By applying a plaster of snuhī-payaḥ (milk of Euphorbia) and by drinking it, one cures white leprosy (*śvetakuṣṭha*).
By placing *indragopa* (the cochineal insect) in betel leaf, one conquers white leprosy.
Having drunk [the remedy], one should diligently consume *somarājī* as before.

Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Rudra, the Lord Uḍḍāmareśvara! Seize, seize so-and-so with disease; cook, cook; strike, strike; moisten, moisten! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ! This is the mantra for the aforementioned yogas. || 29 ||
Oṃ, salutations to the glorious Lord Nṛsiṃha, the enemy of the demons; salutations to Kṛṣṇa.
Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed Rudra, the Lord Uḍḍāmareśvara: seize, seize [so-and-so] with disease! Cook, cook! Strike, strike! Saturate, saturate! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ!
One should cast a stake made of *tintika* wood under the asterism Mṛgaśiras.
If [the Moon] is in the fifth house from the enemy [planet], a deficiency of digestive fire arises. || 30 ||
One should place sea salt, fire, or pure sea-born [substances] into the womb of a harlot and cook everything inside a sealed crucible (puṭa).
Thus ends the method for inducing fever.
Now, regarding the production of eye disease:
taking that [wood] from a *karavīra* tree and fresh ginger, one should grind it into a fine powder.
The eyesight of whoever offers food and drink [to such a person] perishes. || 32 ||
To paralyze his vision, [one should use] the fruit of *maricākṣa* and *vacā*.
If one offers eight thousand karavīra flowers with the uttered mantra, eye disease occurs. || 34 ||
One should take the head of an owl and fill it with salt;
placed within an earthen vessel and covered with seven cloths, one should stir it with a stick of *akṣa* wood.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra, Uḍḍāmareśvara! Seize, seize so-and-so with disease; cook, cook; strike, strike; moisten, moisten! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Thus is the production of eye disease. Now follows the bewildering of enemies.
If one places an ashvattha peg ten finger-breadths long in the house under the asterism Aśvinī, even for him there will be a long journey; of this there is no doubt. (36)
A four-finger-long bone-stake of a jackal should be planted in the house of an enemy under the lunar mansion of Soma; indeed, for him there shall be a long journey abroad.
Thus ends the "Confounding of Enemies.
Now follows the "Causing Insanity":
one should consume a fine powder of *tālaka* (orpiment) and *dhūrtabīja* (datura seeds).
Having given [it], the enemy becomes intoxicated; by means of white milk, however, he becomes happy again. (38)
If talaka and garlic are placed on the head by a piśāca, it brings comfort through the consumption of liquor, meat, sugar, and milk. (39)
Having ground golden pyrite with honey and clarified butter, one should prepare a collyrium from it;
when this is applied as an ointment to the eyes of anyone, that person becomes insane.
Cow's ghee, rock salt in equal measure, and the bile of a boar, combined with goat's milk and taken as a drink, destroys madness. (41)
The excrement of peacocks, pigeons, and roosters, along with gold and *tāla*, should be taken;
when applied to the head, it acts like a *piśāca* and causes the hair to fall off, leaving the head shaven.
Equal parts of jaggery, karañja seeds, and thick powder should be administered at the end of the fruit; from eating this, one becomes insane.
Drinking sugar, *śatapuṣpā*, ghee, and milk brings about ease.
Oṃ, salutation to the knowledge-mantra that causes madness, ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ. This very mantra is for the aforementioned yogas. 44.
Oṃ, homage to the vidyā that causes madness, ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ!
Thus ends the rite for causing madness. Now follows the rite for killing.
One should take a human bone pin four finger-breadths long under the Puṣya asterism;
if one buries it in someone's house, that person's lineage shall perish.
Oṃ hrūṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā!
One should bury a horse-bone kīla four finger-widths deep under the Aśvinī constellation;
it swiftly destroys the family and the entire lineage of enemies within the enemy's house.
"Huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā"—if one buries [an object] consecrated seven times with this mantra at the enemy's house, his lineage will go to ruin. || 46 ||

Oṃ hrūṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ ḍaṃ ḍāṃ ḍiṃ ḍīṃ ḍuṃ ḍūṃ ḍeṃ ḍaiṃ ḍoṃ ḍauṃ ḍaṃ ḍaḥ, seize, seize so-and-so! Huṃ huṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ! With this [mantra], a kīla made of human bone, consecrated one thousand times, should be buried in the midst of a funeral pyre; he shall perish from fever.
Oṃ ṇaṃ ṇāṃ ṇiṃ ṇīṃ ṇuṃ ṇūṃ ṇeṃ ṇaiṃ ṇoṃ ṇauṃ ṇaṃ ṇaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ Oṃ sureśvarāya svāhā.
One finger-breadth of snake-bone [should be placed] in the house of the enemy under the constellation Āśleṣā.
Having recited [the mantra] seven times over it, one should bury it; this shall destroy the lineage of the enemy. || 47 ||
Oṃ sīṃ śoṣaṇe svāhā!
One should take *nimba*, *ṣaḍbinduka*, poison, cinnamon (*tvak*), and the fruit of *vānarī*.
This powder should be applied to the bed, seat, and other belongings of the enemy.
Severe boils arise, and death occurs within ten days. || 48 ||
Oṃ, svāhā to the Lord of the Gods!
One should cast the earth from the bathing ground and the urinal ground into the mouth of the serpent. 49.
One should wrap it with a black thread, facing downwards in the middle of the path.
By burying [the image], the enemy dies; by raising it up, one becomes happy. || 50 ||
One should take the left tooth of a crab from its lower part;
one should fashion an arrowhead and a blade for the bow using various types of wood.
Having fashioned a bowstring from cow sinews and a clay image of the enemy, the foe shall die at that very moment by means of an arrow produced therefrom. || 52 ||
Under the constellation Ārdrā, one should bury nimba-vandāka (Azadirachta indica shoots) in the enemy's bedchamber;
the enemy will die, but upon its removal, he becomes well again.
Likewise, one should take the Śirīṣa-vandāka plant with the previously mentioned constellation;
having placed it in the enemy's house, the destruction of the foe will come to pass.

Having applied a tilaka on the forehead with red earth from a black bull together with clay from the Gaṅgā, one should honor him; [if] pierced, [the victim] would die at that very moment, but if it is wiped away, there will be well-being.
One should remove the hair situated on the hoof of a black goat with horse-like feet.
The four wings of a black cock and crow should be taken;
having burnt them all inside a vessel, that ash is then mixed with water.
Having applied a tilaka on the forehead with the little finger of the left hand, the piercing of whichever head it is bent toward will certainly occur. (58)

If one sprinkles the powder upon the body of a spider, one marked with six dots, or a black scorpion that possesses equal proportions, pustules will appear within seven days; however, by grinding peacock feathers and blue lotuses and applying them as a paste, relief is brought.
Having dug up the constellation of the enemy and Scorpio, one should bury them in the ground.
Then, having covered it with an upper garment, one should throw earth upon its back;
by the obstruction of the impurity, the person dies, and once it is removed, he becomes happy again.

Oṃ hrīṃ kṣaḥ [Name] kṣam! By means of this mantra, through a thousand oblations of black mustard seeds, salt, and the remains of offerings to Śiva (śivanirmālya) mixed with pungent oil, the death of the enemy occurs. || 62 ||
