Oṃ hrīṃ kṣaḥ, [name], kṣam. Thus is the rite of killing. Now follows the rite for destroying horses.
A horse anointed with the powder of black cumin does not see;
by washing its eyes with buttermilk, the horse becomes sound again.
If musk-deer powder is placed in the nostrils, a horse falls down;
it becomes healthy again by drinking sandalwood water or by receiving it as a nasal drop—of this there is no doubt. (64)
Furthermore, one should fashion a horse-bone peg seven finger-breadths long under the constellation Aśvinī;
by burying it in the stable, one surely causes the horses to die.
By reciting the mantra dedicated to Bharaṇī, one should bury an eight-finger-long stake made of funeral-pyre wood; thus, the horse stable shall perish.

The mantra: Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Rudra! Oṃ, slay the horses, slay them, svāhā! Oṃ, cook them, cook them, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Rudra! Oṃ, slay the horses, slay them, svāhā! Oṃ, cook them, cook them, svāhā!
Thus ends the method for destroying horses.
Now, for the destruction of crops: during the asterism Punarvasu, one should cast three finger-breadths deep into the ground a wooden peg from a sacrificial post.
Even grain consecrated with a hundred recitations will perish there in that field. || 67 ||
Oṃ lohitamukhe svāhā! During the constellation Ārdrā, one should drive into the middle of the enemy's field a stake made from the bone of a bear; then all the grain will perish. || 68 ||
Oṃ lohitamukhe svāhā!
During the asterism of Viśākhā, one should cast a black wooden peg eight finger-breadths long;
it shall destroy the plantain fruit in the middle of a plantain grove. (69)
Thus ends the destruction of crops.
Now, regarding the destruction of a washerman’s clothes:
when the constellation Pūrvāphālgunī is present, one should plant a stake made of *jātikāṣṭha* wood.
One should bury [the root] measuring eight finger-breadths in a washerman’s place; by that, after it has been consecrated a hundred times with mantras, one shall destroy his clothes.
Oṃ kumbhaṃ svāhā. With this, there is the destruction of the washerman’s clothes.
Now follows the destruction of the fisherman’s fish.
Having taken a peg made of jujube wood under the constellation Pūrvaphalgunī, one should bury it eight finger-breadths deep; thus, one shall destroy [the enemy] in the house of the gambler.
Oṃ jale svāhā || Oṃ matsyikā svāhā || The fruit of these two mantras is equal. [One should fashion] a seven-finger-long wooden peg from the bhallātaka tree under the Maghā constellation. || 72 ||
Having taken [the fish] to the house of a fisherman, one should destroy the fish;
under the asterism Kṛttikā, one should cast a three-finger-long wooden peg from the wood of the Arka tree into the enemy's pond, well, or similar body of water, and there the fish will perish.
Thus ends the destruction of the fisherman’s catch.
Now follows the destruction of the potter’s wares:
one should take a three-finger-long peg made from *karavīra* wood and place it in his hand.
One should bury it in the potter's workshop; it will cause the destruction of his wares.
A five-finger-long peg made of nimba wood [driven] under that same asterism yields results as previously described. || 75 ||
Gokṣura, meṣaśṛṅga, or the seed of kokilākṣaka;
or else the excrement of a pig, or the root of white guñjā—
if these are thrown into the cooking vessel of pots, they will certainly cause them to burst.
Having prepared palmyra [sap], *karañja* seeds, and combined them with borax, one should cause the vessels to burst; this is declared to be the mantra for pearls. (77)
Oṃ mada mada svāhā || Oṃ guru hara svāhā, or alternatively, oṃ damanya damanya svāhā; the fruit of these three mantras is equal.
Thus ends the destruction of the potter’s wares.
Now follows the destruction of the oil-seller’s oil:
one should plant a four-finger-long peg of Madhuka wood under the asterism Citrā.
If one buries oil in an oil-press, the oil is destroyed there. || 78 ||
Oṃ daha daha svāhā; this is to be recited one thousand times.
On the day of Citrā, one should bury a piece of Bhallātaka wood eight finger-breadths deep in an oil-presser's house; then no thief will go there.
Thus ends the destruction of the oil of the oil-presser.
Now follows the destruction of the milk of the cows belonging to cowherds: one should insert a stake made of jackal-wood under the constellation Anurādhā.
Within eight finger-breadths of the cowshed, the cow's milk perishes.
Thus ends the destruction of the cows' milk for the cowherds.
Now, regarding the destruction of betel leaves:
one should place a nine-finger-long peg made of areca nut wood within the house.
If [the moon] is in the asterism called Śatabhiṣaj in the field of a betel-grower, then his betel-nut crop will certainly perish. (81)
Thus ends the remedy for the destruction of betel leaves.
Now, for the destruction of potherbs: one should indeed throw powdered sulphur there along with water.
All other vegetables perish, and those that remain are of little strength. || 82 ||
Thus ends the destruction of the Śāka plant.
Now, for the destruction of the weaver’s thread:
under the asterism Aśvinī, one should throw a citron-wood stick into the weaver’s house.
The thread measuring twelve finger-breadths is destroyed therein. || 83 ||
Thus ends the destruction of the thread for the weaver. Now follows the destruction of the liquor for the vintner:
one should cast a piece of Arka wood, sixteen finger-breadths long, under the constellation Kṛttikā.
And in the house of the vintner, the liquor there perishes. || 84 ||
Thus ends the destruction of the liquor of the vintner.
Now follows the destruction of the iron of the blacksmith:
under the asterism Rohiṇī, one should drive an eleven-finger-long stake made of *badarī* wood.
Iron cast into a blacksmith's forge does not become heated [by its mere presence]. || 85 ||
Thus ends the mantra for the blacksmith’s destruction of iron and for liberation from bodily piercing.

In this matter, for one whose body is afflicted by piercing or cutting pains, there is no remedy other than knowledge and realization. [The mantra: "O Amukāraka! Hūṃ-kalikā-Caṇḍī! O Imāre-maśila-pāthara-paḍe! In the village of Amukāra, Nārasa-samāra has killed my daughter; pierce the Tāraka-ulaṭā-veḍha! Virūpākṣa-rivānī, pierce the Pitra-pānī-ulaṭā-veḍha! He who causes me pain, pierce him with the ularā-veḍha! O Khā-phoṭa-phokaṭaṇḍī-Virūpākṣa, by your command! Having recited this three times every morning, one should drink three mouthfuls of water. If the body should be pierced by anyone, then it must be performed by that very person at that moment. || 86 ||

O Mantra! O Amupānīrā! O Piercer and Cutter of Śambhu’s body! May the knowledge and realization of Amukāraka not fail! HŪṂ! O Kālikā Caṇḍī! I spread this stone upon the village of Amukāra; I kill the man and his son, I kill the daughter, the savior, and the one who performs the reverse piercing—Virūpākṣa, the enemy! Reverse piercing! Father and mother, those who make my funeral offering (piṇḍa)! Strike! Reverse piercing! Eat him, eat him! PHOṬA PHOṬA! The staff of Virūpākṣa’s command!
Thus ends the tenth instruction, titled "The Destruction of Metals," within the section on rites such as eradication (*uccāṭana*) in the *Kāmaratna* composed by Śrī Nityanātha. 10.
The Eleventh Instruction:
Now, regarding various curiosities—
one should have [the patient] consume the powder from the crest of a peacock for seven days.
The wealth of one whose hands are smeared with its excrement is lost at that very moment. || 1 ||
One should saturate it with sesame oil for seven days in the hot sun;
meanwhile, the powder of *aṅkoli* seeds should be added and ground again and again. (2)
One should carefully extract that oil from the press of an oil-miller;
or else, one should smear two bell-metal vessels with that paste.
Having raised them, one should place them facing each other within the vessel;
from beneath those two, one should collect the oil that has fallen into the bronze bowl.
One should apply this very finger-oil, having pierced [the tree] everywhere.
Once smeared with finger-oil, one should mark it at that moment;
the tree becomes fruitful instantly—of this there is no doubt. || 5 ||
When the powder of lotus seeds is placed in water along with *bhavya* and *aṅgulitaila*,
the appearance of a lotus at that very moment is a great marvel.
Whatever seeds there may be, whether born of water or of land,
when smeared with oil from the finger-joints, they all sprout.
Whatever part originates from the root of the stalk—be it leaf, flower, fruit, or the like—if it is smeared with oil for the fingers, it will certainly become identical in form [to the original]. (8)
One should smear a pair of sandals with a paste made from *guñjā* fruit and water;
by doing so, a man can travel one *krośa* without fatigue—of this there is no doubt.
One should smear a light wooden seat with a paste of *guñjā* seeds;
when it has dried, one sitting upon it together with water does not sink.

The seeds of the *guñjā* plant, stripped of their husks and powdered, should be infused seven times with human urine; then, wood produced from a finger [of the practitioner] should be smeared with it. (11)
Having taken oil and smeared it [on the feet], one proceeds on foot as before. || 12 ||
A lamp-wick filled with the juices of the *varti* plant, smeared with oil and placed in water, will undoubtedly burn when ignited. || 13 ||
The excrement produced by pigeons and sparrows, the root of *śikhi*, and the bones of donkeys, ground together with oil extracted from bitter *tumbī*— 14.
Having applied a tilaka on his forehead with that [substance], he appears once again as the Ten-faced one, the lord of Laṅkā, O King; of this there is no doubt. (15)
Oil extracted from *śigru* seeds, pigeon dung, and the root of a peacock, combined with the fat of a boar, [should be used] in equal parts. (16)
That person who applies a tilaka on the forehead by means of that [substance] is indeed seen as five-faced, just like Maheśvara himself in person. || 17 ||
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight at night, one should place the seeds of the *bhṛṅgī* plant into the mouth of a peacock;
then, one should sow those black seeds in black soil.
Having taken a Bhāṅgī creeper grown from that [seed], one should make a rope with it;
bound by that rope, the man appears to people as a peacock. (19)
When that [powder] is applied to the mouth of a black cat, one should place a vairaṇḍa seed—one produced from those very eraṇḍa seeds—into its single mouth.
Humans will see it as a cat; of this there is no doubt. (20)
If one should sow jackals, dogs, and rams separately on that day,
then success will be attained just as the bhārṅgī plant attains it when placed in the mouth of a peacock.
Alternatively, one should plant a red guñjā fruit in a woman’s skull and then water it;
when the fruit has grown, one should place it in the mouth, and the man will appear in the form of a woman.
The head of any living being, such as a human and so forth, should be taken while still fresh;
on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should plant it together with all types of seeds.
One should bury seeds of *bhṛṅgī*, *dhattūra*, and *guñjā* together with one *vaika* in black soil, accompanied by offerings and worship.
One should irrigate [the seed] until it reaches the stage of fruit and then collect the seeds;
when each respective seed is made crooked, that specific form will certainly manifest. (25)
Thus, the sight of things in various forms in this world is merely a curiosity;
one whose seed has been liberated becomes established in well-being—of this there is no need for further deliberation.
Yellow orpiment and powdered realgar, processed with *aṅgulī-taila* oil, cause a cloth smeared with them to appear like fire when placed upon the head. (27)
In the same way, it throbs with vāṅkola oil; of this there is no doubt. || 28 ||
Having ground together equal parts of vermilion, sulphur, orpiment, and realgar,
one who wears a cloth smeared with that mixture will appear like fire at night.
Even for people standing at a distance, there is great wonder at night when a mark made from the powder of fireflies and *bhūlatā* is applied as a tilaka on the forehead;
for at that spot, a light is seen in the night, which is indeed a marvel.
Then, having rubbed white collyrium with the juices of *muni* flowers and those flowers themselves,
a man whose eyes are thus anointed shall see the starry host at midday.
And one should sow eggplant seeds along with earth in a human skull.
Or, by placing his face upon the root of the seed born from that [tree],
a person shall see everything up to a distance of a hundred yojanas as if it were right before him.
If water mixed with a fly is given for someone to drink, it will indeed pass out through his lower wind; this is truly a marvel.
By this, there is success in the consecration of all yogas; the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred and eight recitations. || 35 ||

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra, the Lord Uḍḍāmareśvara, the one of many forms, the wearer of diverse forms; laugh, laugh! dance, dance! pierce, pierce! O you who display various wonders and magical illusions! ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā!
Thus ends the various wonders.
Now, the immobilization of the sword (*khaḍgastambhana*).

*Siddhi-vastu sumati moharamā-cāndra-suraja-mohovara-bhā-ī moho varaṃ āge kopa khāṇḍā phūṭai rakṣākara devī kālikā caṇḍī ā-ī cāndasuraja tuji malemuji phūṭai rāmera ājñā siddhi.* If one sprinkles the body with dust consecrated three times with this mantra, the edge of a sword will leave no scratch; otherwise, it shall not be so. (36)
Thus ends the eleventh instruction, titled "Various Delights," in the *Kāmaratna* composed by the illustrious Nityanātha. 11.
The Twelfth Instruction:
Now, regarding the accomplishment of desired objects—
having collected on a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism the root produced from a white *arka* tree.
One should worship his image, which is the size of a thumb. || 1 ||

And one who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya), has conquered his senses, and is devoted, should worship her who is the very form of Gaṇanātha with flowers grown from red horse-dung, as well as with perfumes and other offerings. || 2 ||
One should worship with name-mantras and their seed-syllables ending in "namaḥ";
whatever desires one prays for, they are obtained within a single month.
For the sake of accomplishing each specific desired goal, one should worship for one month.

He states the seed-mantra (bīja) of Gaṇeśa: "Pañcāntaka" is *oṃ antarikṣāya svāhā*. One should worship with this. They know the seed-mantra of Gaṇapati to be "Pañcāntaka" joined with the moon-bearer (the syllable *gaṃ*): *oṃ hrīṃ pūrvadayāṃ oṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā*. With this mantra, one should offer red *aśvamāra* flowers mixed with ghee and honey; it grants one's desire.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, homage to the one who grants success through the mind, hrīṃ namaḥ. Having recited this mantra over a single red flower and cast it into a river, and having thus recited it one hundred thousand times, the Blessed Lady, as the bestower of boons, grants one of the eight supernatural powers.
This is the accomplishment of desires. Now, the accomplishment of speech.
If one holds the vandāka plant from the snuhī tree in the hand during the asterism of Kṛttikā, his speech shall become effective; this is remembered as a great marvel.
Under the asterism Svātī, one should cause a *vandāka* fruit produced from the *badarī* tree to be grasped with a mantra;
holding that in his hand, whatever object is prayed for by men [is obtained].
Everything is attained at that very moment; the mantra for this is stated right here.
Oṃ, svāhā to the intermediate space!
Thus is the accomplishment of speech (*vāk-siddhi*).
Now, regarding the disclosure of hidden wealth, hidden dwellings, thieves, and so forth:
"Wherever the riches are located, and who those thieves and others may be," [so it is said].
The high-souled ones, lords of the Gandharvas and Yakṣiṇīs, were in disguised attire.
Living beings, the elements, trees, and so forth, which reside firmly in the mortal world—all of these arise as manifestations; listen to that with a concentrated mind.

Having ground together vandā, śākhoṭa, āmra, gokṣura, salt, and padma, and having applied it as a tilaka on the forehead with goat’s milk, [the women] come openly even while remaining hidden; of this there is no doubt at that very moment. || 10 ||
On the evening of a Saturday during the asterism Āśleṣā, one should collect the juice from the seeds of a pomegranate; then,
on the eighth day of the dark fortnight during the asterism Bharaṇī,
a wise person should prepare an ointment using black turmeric and lotus root on a Tuesday.
Everything arises as luminous as before; there is no doubt in this matter. || 11 ||
Thus ends the disclosure of hidden wealth, disguised thieves, and so forth.
Now, the science of archery (dhanurveda).

The knowledge which was previously told by Indra to Arjuna consists of twenty-seven syllables: *oṃ kālāyutā raktāghorā oṃkāra śataguṇa ādhāre ekādaśaśatasahasra indra ājñā*. Having held the arrow with this mantra and recited it nine times, one should fix the arrow upon a bow drawn back to the ear; it becomes effective a thousandfold. In the Kali age, it is tenfold. That which was told by Mahādeva to Indra consists of seventeen syllables: *cāndradhanurguṇarekhā kāṇḍabrahmajñāna oṃ oṃ oṃ*. Having recited this mantra five times, one should then discharge [the arrow] as before, and it becomes effective. || 12 ||
Kālāyutā is red and Aghorā; the syllable Oṃ is a hundredfold in the foundation (ādhāra). One thousand one hundred and ten are Indra’s command.
The bow of the moon, the string, the line, and the shaft constitute the knowledge of Brahman: Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ.
One should extract the half-measure (ardhamātra), which is like a frog swallowed by serpents.
Having cut off the snake's head, one should dry it separately in the sun.
Having ground these separately, a pill should be prepared; it is remembered as bestowing the attainment of the target.
On the target, one should apply a frog-mark, and at the tip of the arrow, a mark made from a serpent’s head.
Having applied a mark up to the ear on the bowstring, one should pierce it;
the arrow will certainly hit the mark upon the target—of this there is no doubt. (15)

*Oṃ rakte dhanurakte kāṇḍarakte halijā mā māro amukāra amuka-aṅga āmuka-ṭā-ī māro tridaśadevagaṇarudrāsākṣī amukāra māro devena rākhī arjuna kṛṣṇabhavānīra ājñā.* Having recited this mantra, one pierces whichever limb of the target one intends to kill. However, for the initial test, on a Saturday or Tuesday, one should bring the lineage of a deceased Brāhmaṇa, prepare a bow and arrow, and attach a string of the appropriate length. At that time, having placed a single flower garland upon it, broken a single living swan at the place of the grip, and washed it with the water of a single coconut, one should strike the target with three arrows and then perform the rite. When one swiftly pierces the target near the limb of the enemy with the bow and arrow, then [the rite] shall not be in vain.

Oṃ! O Raktā, Dhanuraktā, and Kāṇḍaraktā; O Halijā, do not kill me, do not kill [Name], do not kill [Name]’s limb, do not kill [Name]’s wife! With the thirty gods of the celestial host and Rudra as witnesses, do not kill [Name]! He is protected by the god; this is the command of Arjuna, Kṛṣṇa, and Bhavānī.
Thus ends the science of archery.
Now follows the method for making wealth and grain inexhaustible:
under the constellation of Pūrvaphālgunī, [one should take] that which originates from a pomegranate tree.

The *vṛkṣādanī* plant should be given during the constellation of Dhaniṣṭhā; it certainly becomes inexhaustible. As for the *vandāka*, which grows on the *bahuvāraka* tree, it should be offered in the granary; it certainly becomes inexhaustible. (16)
One should collect *vandāka* from a *śephālikā* plant under the *hasta* asterism and place it in the midst of grain; that grain shall become inexhaustible. || 17 ||
On the day of Bharaṇī, a wise man should take a vessel filled with auspicious offerings and place it there;
situated within that wealth and grain, he will certainly make it inexhaustible.
A wise person should cause a sprout of the *udumbara* tree to be seized under the asterism of Rohiṇī;
he should then establish it for the sake of accumulated wealth, and it shall always remain inexhaustible.
Having consecrated it with a mantra, the mantra for this very purpose is now stated: [Mantra follows]
Oṃ, homage to Dhanada, svāhā! || 19 ||
Thus ends the method for making wealth and grain inexhaustible.
Now follows the method for attaining the power of retaining what is heard (śrutidhara) and other such vidyās:
harītakī, pāṭhā, long pepper, dry ginger, rock salt, black pepper, and vacā.
One pala each of powdered śigru and thirty-two palas of ghee. || 20 ||
Having added four times as much milk as ghee, one should cook everything together;
once it has been removed from the heat with only the ghee remaining, one should lick it, for it bestows eloquence and intelligence. (21)
Now, for *brāhmīghṛta*:
having powdered *vacā*, *brāhmī*, *phala*, *kuṣṭha*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *tilapuṣpikā*, one should saturate them with the juices derived from *maṇḍūkī* and *brāhmī*. (22)
Then, for one day, four times the amount of ghee should be cooked with this paste;
four times the amount of ghee should be added along with *brāhmī* and milk.
Having removed it from the fire once only the ghee remains, one should lick it, which bestows eloquence and intelligence. (23)
Thus ends the Brāhmī-ghṛta.
Two types of Haridrā, Vacā, Kuṣṭha, Pippalī, Viśvabheṣaja, Ajājī, Ajamodā, and Yaṣṭīmadhuka [are combined]. (24)
One should prepare these as equal parts in a dry powder form.
This powder, taken in a dose of one *karṣa* with clarified butter as a linctus, brings about purity of speech.
If one consumes it for one month, he shall become equal to Bṛhaspati. (25)
One should consume one karṣa of the equal powder of brāhmī, muṇḍī, vacā, śuṇṭhī, and pippalī with honey; clear speech will certainly arise. (26)
Vacā, asthi, kāravī, gundrā, muśalī, madhuka, and balā, along with the five parts (pañcāṅga) of apāmārga, [yield] the same result as before when combined with honey. 27.

One should daily consume one karṣa of the equal powder of apāmārga, vacā, śuṇṭhī, viḍaṅga, śaṅkhapuṣpikā, śatāvarī, guḍūcī, and harītakī, along with ghee; by doing so, one will retain a thousand verses.
Aśvagandhā, ajamodā, pāṭhā, kuṣṭha, and the three pungents (kaṭutraya). || 29 ||
Take equal parts of śatapuṣpī, viśvabīja, and rock salt (saindhava), and half that amount of powdered vacā; this mixture, taken with honey and clarified butter, [cures ailments].
One should consume a karṣa measure [of it] at the end of digestion, followed by a meal of milk;
even one who is mute shall become a master of speech and a holder of a thousand granthas.
One should rub in jyotiṣmatī oil along with balā and vacā,
gradually and little by little, until four niṣkas have been administered.
In a windless place, one should consume honey; one should be a celibate student and become a wise sage. || 32 ||
During an eclipse of the sun or the moon, one should procure the speech [of the eclipsed body] along with its name accompanied by mantras;
having consumed it ground into powder with ghee, one will become a lord of speech within seven days.
Thus, this king of mantras has been declared by Śiva for these and other yogas;
having recited it ten thousand times, success shall be attained, and thereafter one should consume [the substances] with those very [mantras].
Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Hayaśīrṣa Vāgīśvara.
One should saturate powdered vacā with the juice of dhātrī fruits for the duration of a day;
one should then have it licked with ghee in the measure of a niṣka. This brings about purity of speech, as well as memory and intelligence. (35)
Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Hayaśīrṣa Vāgīśvara.
One should throw powdered vacā into milk, consecrated again with the mantra.
By eating śāli rice with milk for seven days, one becomes a lord of speech. (36)
In the seventh and eighth [days], one will become a direct bearer of the Vedas (*śrutidhara*).

Furthermore, if one drinks the powder of *vaca* with milk, ghee, and honey according to the procedure for seven days, it should be taken as a linctus, and the result will be as previously described. (37)

Having gathered the root of the white Arka plant during the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism and the Sun, one should dry it in the shade and reduce it to powder, consecrated with the mantra itself. (38)
Having risen at dawn, one should drink either half a *karṣa*, a *pala*, or even half a *pala* [of this], having consecrated it with this mantra:
*oṃ maheśvarāya namaḥ*. One should drink it after performing the consecration.
At the end of digestion, one should take a meal of milk with either buttermilk or clarified butter. || 39 ||
In this way, within just seven days, even a child becomes a poet.
Thus ends the procedure for the acquisition of the power of retaining what is heard (*śrutidhara*) and other such skills. Now follows the procedure for becoming a *kinnarī*:
turmeric, *vacā*, costus, long pepper, and *yavānikā*.
One should prepare a powder of black pepper, rock salt, and ginger;
having ground this powder together with honey on a stone slab.
It should be eaten continuously for exactly seven days;
then men acquire a beautiful voice and sing along with the Kinnaras.
One karṣa each of vibhītaka, kaṇā, śuṇṭhī, saindhava, and tvak, taken together with cow’s urine, causes one to sing along with the kinnaras. (43)
A paste made of cinnamon leaf, long pepper, parched grain, citron peel, and honey, when licked, produces a voice even superior to that of the Kinnaras. (44)
Devadāru, kaṇā, vyoṣa, śatāhvā, patra, niśā, vacā, saindhava, and the root of śigru—these should be ground together in equal parts. 45.
One should always lick one karṣa of this with honey and ghee for the duration of a month.
His throat shall become purified, and he shall be sung of together with the Kinnaras. || 46 ||
Ginger and sugar, combined with honey, shall result in a voice like that of a cuckoo merely by consuming the pill. (47)
One should drink one pala of powdered vacā, along with equal parts of ginger, bhṛṅga, koraṇṭa, vāsā, brāhmī, and vacā, mixed with water. (48)
Every month, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, for fourteen days, his singing was like that of a Gandharva, with a voice like that of the cuckoo. (49)
Whoever licks the powder of *nirguṇḍī* root with sesame oil will achieve purification of the throat and shall sing together with the *kinnaras*. (50)
One should drink one karṣa each of bibhītaka, kaṇā, śuṇṭhī, saindhava, and tvak, along with cow's urine; thus one is praised by the Kinnaras.
Thus ends the method for making one a Kinnarī. Now, the purification of the eyes: during the rainy season, *kākamācī* with its roots should be cooked in oil.
If one should eat [it] in summary, the eye becomes equal to the vision of a vulture.
One should always apply the root of white punarnavā rubbed with ghee as an ointment;
it quickly destroys the discharge of watery fluid from the ear. Furthermore, that same root combined with niśā (turmeric) [achieves the same].
And by using this ointment, eye diseases never occur at any time. || 53 ||
Equal parts of rock salt, the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, and long pepper), and karañjaka seed,
combined with the juice of bhṛṅgarāja, will remove cataracts and film-like opacities of the eye.
By anointing with fresh butter a conch-shell, a cowrie, or anything burnt,
dried, or powdered, one preserves a long-standing flower.
Having ground the root of the bhūdhātrī plant with goat's urine, one should prepare a medicinal wick.
Combined with fresh butter, it destroys even long-standing *puṣpa*;
it may also destroy *puṣpa* by means of collyrium, or by means of honey or *svarṇamākṣika*.
When the blood in the eyes is suppressed by the Marica [cathartic], one should apply a collyrium (varti) to cure night-blindness.
Alternatively, Jayantī or Abhayā, ground with breast milk, removes night-blindness;
it also destroys hemorrhage, cataract (carmakopa), and fleshy growths (māṃsavṛddhi). || 58 ||
And one should place long pepper and black pepper inside the meat of a black goat.
Having prepared this, one should cook it in ghee and remove it after one ghaṭikā;
when ground with equal parts of ghee and breast milk, this collyrium removes night-blindness.
One should dry the three pungents (vyoṣa) placed in goat-bile at the site of the smoke-pipe;
when rubbed with the juices of *cirabilva*, this collyrium removes night-blindness.
With ghee it cures inflammation of the eye; with honey, tearing; with oil, itching and darkness of vision; and with water, night-blindness.
Punarnavā, when used with sour gruel (kāñjika), destroys these ailments and restores the eyesight of the *netrapunarnava*.
Harītakī, vacā, kuṣṭha, pippalī, and black pepper;
the marrow of vibhītaka, conch-shell navel, and realgar. (63)
Having made all of this equal, one should grind it with cow’s milk;
it destroys cataracts, itching, films on the eye, and tumors.
Even a flower two years old he destroys in a single month;
likewise, he does not see the flesh that has grown beyond its measure, nor anything at night. (65)
A wick named Candrodayā clarifies the vision of men;
it should be made as a pill that is dried in the shade, known by the name Candrodayā-vaṭī.
He who consumes the powder of *yaṣṭimadhu* in the evening, avoiding unwholesome food, along with clarified butter and honey,
is liberated from disorders of the eyes, just as a man whose wealth has been exhausted is freed from his servants.
Thus ends the purification for clearing the eyes.
Now, regarding the removal of deafness in the ears:
sesame oil prepared with the alkaline water of *śikharī* and its medicinal paste [is used].
It removes ringing in the ears and also deafness through filling [the ears]. || 68 ||
One should cook one prastha of oil with a decoction of the ten roots;
by adding this paste, it becomes the supreme medicine for deafness. (69)
Oil prepared with the juice of *nīlī* and *bradhna*, combined with boiled sour gruel (*kāñjika*),
destroys all earworms when applied lukewarm as an ear-drop.
One should chew the root of the *nandyāvarta* and *palāśa* with one's teeth;
when that [powder] is filled into the ear, it will certainly conquer the *gomakṣikā* worm.
Having consumed betel, the wise man should cause it to be distributed there;
the worms situated therein will certainly meet their destruction. (72)

One should consume the powder of *mūṣalī* and *bākucī* for the alleviation of deafness. Furthermore, one should eat a *karṣa*-measure of the powder of *manaḥśilā* and *apāmārga* saturated with honey for the complete pacification of deafness. (73)
Having ground garlic, āmalaka, and palmyra fruit, [one should cook them] in four times the amount of oil. || 74 ||
One should boil milk four times the quantity of oil until only the oil remains;
one should then instill that oil into the ear, and it will destroy deafness.
Thus ends the removal of deafness in the ears.
Now follows the method for increasing the earlobes:
take equal parts of white mustard, *bṛhatī*, and *apāmārga*.
This ointment made with goat's milk will cause the earlobe to grow. || 76 ||

One should mix the powder of *mūṣalī* tubers with buffalo milk and stir it in a smooth vessel; then, having placed it in a heap of grain, after seven days, when it has risen, it should be applied as a plaster, and the earlobe will increase in size. (77)
Powder made from the root of the guñjā plant, combined with buffalo milk.
One should then prepare curd from that [milk] and extract butter from it;
by applying this daily to the ears, one will cause them to grow—of this there is no doubt. (79)
A paste made from equal parts of aśvagandhā, vacā, kuṣṭha, and gajapippalī, applied with buffalo butter, causes the ear to grow. (80)
An ointment made with oil extracted from a boar causes the ears to grow;
likewise, by an ointment of the blood of a bat, the ear increases in size. (81)
Thus ends the treatment for enlarging the earlobes. Now follows the method for strengthening the teeth:
[one may use] the root of *yamaciñcā*, *jayā*, or *puṅkhā*, or the root of *hayamāra*.
Teeth that are loose become firm through daily brushing of the teeth.
The powder of abhayā and honey should be cooked for a moment in a copper vessel;
having ground them, a pill should be made and held in the teeth, which will remove dental worms.
The root of the *snuhī* plant, held firmly with the teeth, effectively destroys worms;
likewise, *kāśīśa* (ferruginous earth) cooked in ghee and applied to the tooth relieves pain.
One should throw the powder of Viśālā onto heated iron;
by the touch of its smoke, insects will surely fall upon the teeth. (85)
Having risen in the morning, one should chew the leaf of the *jātikoraka* plant;
by cleansing the teeth with its wood, even loose teeth will become firm. (86)
The root of *guñjā* tied to both ears destroys tooth-worms.
One part of silver and three parts of mercury, rubbed with the juice of *jambīra*, should be placed inside a *jambīra* fruit, bound with cloths, and cooked for three days. (87)
Then, having extracted that pill from the midst of milk once more,
one should take realgar (tālaka) processed with cow’s milk and ground into a fine powder.

Having placed a pill in the middle of that [mixture], tied it in a cloth, and kept it inside a jar of honey for three days, one should subsequently extract it; when held in the mouth, it instantly makes loose teeth firm through friction. || 89 ||
One should grind talaka with the milk of a *bhānu* plant for one day; then, having combined it with mercury produced from the homa of its essence and with silver, [one should proceed]. (90)
One should cook it for three days in a swinging apparatus (dolāyantra) placed within the pulp of a citron fruit.
Having extracted [the root] into a vessel containing oil and honey, one should hold it in the mouth;
it removes all diseases of the teeth, and those teeth that have become loose through friction are made firm.
The chewing of *bakula* flowers makes loose teeth firm.
A wise person should grind the seeds of the *bakula* with lukewarm water and hold them in the mouth; this is an excellent means for making the teeth solid. 93.
One should hold a warm decoction of Bakula bark in the mouth;
within seven days, even loose teeth will become firm—of this there is no doubt. (94)
Thus concludes the strengthening of the teeth. Now follows the prevention of *gaṇḍamālā* (scrofula):
[one should apply [medicines] to the armpits, shoulders, neck, and groin in portions the size of a *karkandhu*, *kola*, or *āmalaka* fruit.
Due to fat and phlegm, characterized by slow and chronic suppuration, there occurs *gaṇḍamālā*, which consists of numerous swellings.
A decoction of *kāñcanāra* bark combined with powdered *śuṇṭhī* and enriched with honey,
or a decoction of *varuṇa* root drunk even once,
quickly destroys even long-standing *gaṇḍamālā*.
Thus ends the prevention of the *gāṇḍamālā* [disease]. Now, regarding the taking of food:
having fashioned a seat from the trunk of a *bradhnaka* tree, he remained there slowly.
He who eats his meal together with ghee, like Bhīmasena. (95)
At twilight, one should perform the consecration of an *āmra* tree;
in the morning, having gathered flowers, one should wear them as a garland upon the head.
Having completely cast aside his loincloth, he eats like Bhīmasena.
Taking up a leaf-plate with its rim turned upward and a dog-toothed ladle,
she ties both at her waist and eats like Bhīmasena.
Having taken the consecrated leaves of the *vibhītaka* tree and stepping upon his right shank, the practitioner of mantra should consume food for twenty days.
Oṃ, homage to the Lord of all beings! Devour, devour! Dry up, dry up! Bhairavī commands: svāhā! This is the mantra for the aforementioned yogas.
One should bind the lower jaw of a chameleon at the location of the crest-lock;
like the son of the Wind (Hanumān), he will undoubtedly enjoy [the fruits] of this marvel. 99.
Oṃ, by the force of the navel, Urvaśī, svāhā! Thus is the performance of eating.
Now follows the performance of fasting.
Having ground the intestines of a chameleon, marrow, and the seed of the *kārañja* tree, one should form a pill from them and encase it with the three metals (*triloha*).
Whoever wears that [amulet] on their neck, hunger and thirst do not afflict them.
*Oṃ sāṃ sāṃ, draw in the nectar of the body, svāhā!* One should cook lotus seeds and great śāli rice with goat’s milk.
Having eaten milk-rice with clarified butter for twelve days, one's hunger is dispelled.
Oṃ sāṃ sāṃ, attract the immortal body, svāhā!
Having ground together the seeds of the udumbara, jambīra, śāli, śimbī, and śirīṣa, and having eaten them with clarified butter for a fortnight, one’s hunger is dispelled. (102)
Having eaten a ripe udumbara fruit that has been saturated with iṅgudī oil for a month, one destroys hunger and thirst; of this there is no doubt. (103)
One should cook the seeds of the Apāmārga plant, excluding the bark, together with milk-rice (pāyasa) in the milk of a goat; when consumed, this removes hunger for a month.

Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Rudra, who is established in the midst of the immortal sun; bestow nectar, bestow nectar upon my body! Saḥ svāhā! This is the mantra for the aforementioned yogas. 104–105.
Thus ends the method for not taking food.
Now, as for the accomplishment of the sandals:
one should grind white mustard seeds with the oil from the joints of a horse's tail-hair.
One whose hands and feet are thus anointed can travel a hundred yojanas. || 106 ||
One should cook the root of the *aṅkola* tree with sesame oil;
having smeared [the body] from the feet up to the knees, one becomes capable of traveling long distances. (107)
Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ. Oṃ, salutation to Caṇḍikā! Shake, shake the sky; cause it to enter, hili hili! O you who flow with speed, hrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā! This very mantra is for both of the aforementioned yogas.
The heart of a crow, its eyes, its tongue, realgar, red ochre, rock salt, ajamārī, and mālatī [are the ingredients]. 108.
One should grind *rudrajaṭā* together with equal parts of *vidārī*;
by smearing that on one's feet, one may suddenly travel a thousand *yojanas*.
Free from wrinkles and gray hair, [he remains so] until the dissolution of all beings.
A celibate practitioner should wrap a crow’s tongue in molten iron;
by placing it in the mouth, one can travel a hundred yojanas.
Then those men will surely come quickly; there is no doubt about this. || 112 ||
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Rudra; obeisance to the bearer of the green mace! Terrify, terrify! Agitate, agitate! O you who move, move! Svāhā!
Having mounted a sandal made from camel hide, ground with *aṅkola* oil and smeared with white mustard seeds, one may travel a hundred [yojanas]. 113.
Thus concludes the *pādukāsādhana*.
For the warding off of drought:
*hrūṃ hrīṃ* (or alternatively) *huṃ śrīṃ huṃ*. If one enters into the midst of water and recites this mantra, then it will remove the drought; a great rain will fall.
Thus ends the twelfth instruction, titled "The Warding Off of Drought," from the *Kāmyasiddhyādi* composed by the illustrious Nityanātha. 12.
The Thirteenth Instruction:
Now, regarding the collyrium that reveals hidden treasures,
for all types of collyrium, the Aghora mantra must be accomplished.
Without mantras, even the vidyās cause destruction at every step. || 1 ||
Having resorted to the Ambikāyantra, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times;
thereafter, one may undertake all ritual procedures, which will then be easily accomplished. || 2 ||

Oṃ siddho liṃ namaḥ | Oṃ śaṃ śo liṃ namaḥ | Oṃ kaṃ ko liṃ namaḥ | Oṃ kaṃ ko liṃ namaḥ | Oṃ khida khida vinda vinda jolīnamahāna mada mada mahādharaṇavarṇane namaḥ | To the one who bestows all happiness, to Dharaṇa, Maḍa, To-romā, Dharaṇa | Oṃ hrīṃ Ambike | Oṃ hrīṃ Ambike namaḥ | Oṃ ambe ambāle ambike avatāraya ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā | Hrūṃ hrūṃ hrīṃ kṣauṃ yūṃ klīṃ.
Oṃ, I recite the name of Mahādeva, the great lord of the Vidyādharas, who possesses many forms and universal forms, and who bestows all spiritual accomplishments. || 3 ||
Oṃ, O Maheshvara, holder of knowledge, you who possess many forms and universal forms!

Oṃ, salutation to Rudra, to him whose form is Rudra; salutation to the one of many forms, salutation to the one of universal forms, salutation to the Universal Self, salutation to Tatpuruṣa, salutation to the Yakṣa, salutation to him whose form is a Yakṣa, salutation to the One, salutation to the Sole One, salutation to the Single Raurava, salutation to the Single Yakṣa, salutation to the Single-eyed One, salutation to the Yakṣa, salutation to the Giver of Boons! Pierce, pierce, svāhā!
For the purpose of causing the falling of collyrium, the fire must be maintained with great care.
It is excellent in the house of one who has been initiated (dīkṣita), especially on a funeral pyre;
it is also auspicious in the house of a washerman or in the house of a thief.

*Oṃ jvalitavidyuddhūmāya svāhā*. This is the mantra for taking the fire. Or: *Jvalitavidyute svāhā; Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya bandha bandha śrīpataye svāhā*. With this mantra, one should consecrate the wick. *Oṃ namo bhagavate siddhasādhakāya jvala jvala paca paca pātaya pātaya bandhaya bandhaya saṃhara saṃhara darśaya darśaya nidhi namaḥ*. With this, one should light the lamp. *Oṃ aiṃ mantraḥ sarvasiddhebhyo namo viśvebhyaḥ svāhā*. With this, the soot (kajjala) should be taken. *Oṃ kāli kāli mahākāli rakṣedamañjanaṃ namo viśvebhyaḥ svāhā*. With this mantra, whatever substance is to be used as collyrium (*añjana*) should be consecrated. *Oṃ sarve sarvahite klīṃ sarve sarvahite sarvauṣadhi prayāhi te | virate namo namaḥ svāhā*. With this mantra, the root suitable for the collyrium should be consecrated. First, having applied the collyrium to the eye with a pure golden probe, one should then apply the collyrium substance with that same probe. Having applied the collyrium, one should afterwards fasten seven-fold leaf-rolls (*saptadhārasya patrakam*) for each eye, ensuring they are without gaps and facing downwards. (Verse 5)

Oṃ jvalitavidyuddhūmāyā svāhā. Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva! Hold, hold! Bind, bind! To the Lord of Śrī, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Accomplished One and the Practitioner! Blaze, blaze! Cook, cook! Cast down, cast down! Bind, bind! Destroy, destroy! Reveal, reveal the treasure! Homage!
Oṃ aiṃ! Homage to all the perfected ones (siddhas), to all the universal ones, svāhā!

Oṃ Kāli Kāli Mahākāli! Protect this collyrium; homage to all the universal ones, svāhā! Oṃ! All you who are intent on the welfare of all, klīṃ! All you who are intent on the welfare of all, O beloved of all medicinal herbs, you who have withdrawn [from worldly things], homage, homage, svāhā!
Over that, one should fasten a white cloth or even one made of silk;
however, one should not anoint [the image] if it has extra or missing limbs, or if it has been bitten by a dog or scorched by fire.
Having bathed with all limbs complete and being pure, one should eat a meal of milk-rice at night for two days; then, at the end of three days, one should apply collyrium.
For one who has been anointed, the binding of the topknot (śikhābandha) should be performed; the mantra for this is now declared. || 8 ||

Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Rudra! Tula tula! Maheśvara, Māheśvara! Nujvala nujvala! Vijvala vijvala! Mijvala mijvala! Hara hara! O you who are worshipped by Yakṣas and Rākṣasas! O Yakṣakumāri Sulocanā! Svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Rudra! Oṃ nanna nanna! Mahennavihenna vihennamihenna vihennamihenna! Hara hara rakṣa! Hara hara rakṣa! O you who are worshipped! O Yakṣakumāri Sulocanā! Svāhā!
One should recite this mantra at sunrise and sunset while taking refuge in the form of the Yakṣas.
The binding of the topknot (śikhābandha), as proclaimed by Śiva, has already been fully explained.
This is to be known regarding all collyria (*añjana*):

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra! Tula tula! Maheśvara, Māheśvara! Nujvala nujvala! Vijvala vijvala! Mijvala mijvala! Hara hara! O you who are worshipped by Yakṣas and Rākṣasas! O Yakṣa-kumārī Sulocanā! Svāhā!

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra! Oṃ nanna nanna! Mahenavihenna vihennamihenna vihennamihenna! Hara hara! Rakṣa rakṣa! O you who are worshipped by Yakṣas and Rākṣasas! O Yakṣa-kumārī Sulocanā! Svāhā!
In the autumn season, one should collect red-colored earth from the ground;
having filled it with vermilion, one should wrap it in a wick made of cotton.
The wise man should collect oil from very black sesame seeds and preserve it;
then, by using that oil and a wick during the northern course of the sun (uttarāyaṇa), he should produce collyrium.
Having applied the ointment to his eyes, the practitioner sees a treasure;
he discerns its measure and takes it as desired. || 12 ||
One should take the tongue-flesh of an exceedingly black crow and wrap it with cotton from a silk-cotton tree; one should then fashion a wick from that very material.
Having lit a lamp with goat's ghee and taken the soot,
a man whose eyes are anointed with it beholds a treasure as before.
One should soak lotus fibers seven times with juices extracted from sugarcane;
having extracted them, one should light a lamp combined with finger-oil.
Collyrium obtained on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight reveals hidden treasures;
this perfected ointment is proclaimed by Śambhu to be effective for all purposes. (16)
A vessel made from a human skull should be used for the lamp and the collyrium;
this is the truth regarding all collyriums, as spoken by Śiva. (17)
Having prepared manaḥśilā with the blood of a lizard, one who has anointed his eyes with that very substance sees a treasure as before. (18)
Having taken a *vandā* leaf from a *śākhoṭa* tree under the asterism Anurādhā and grinding it together with *gorocana*, this collyrium reveals hidden treasures;
this is known as "All-Collyrium" (*sarvāñjana*), famous and spoken by Śiva. (19)
One should fashion sandals from the wood of the Agastya tree, which reveal hidden treasures;
indeed, through the application of these sandals and ointments, one becomes accomplished in the Siddha-yogas.
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Rudra, the Lord Uḍḍāmareśvara; *śili śili*, O *dhūmara*, O *nāgavetālinī*, svāhā! With this [mantra], one should consecrate the sandals. 20.
On a Saturday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, one should uproot a Tulasī root;
having then crushed it with fermented rice-water (kāñjika), one should further anoint it with honey.
At that time, whether it be a boy or a girl born with feet [turned upward], a treasure is seen there;
of this there is no doubt, even if one has gone to the netherworld (pātāla).
And as it was being dug, snakes emerged at every step. || 23 ||
Without medicine, there would be danger from them even for the mantra-practitioners;
therefore, one should conquer them by means of medicinal application through anointing the feet. (24)
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Rudra! Show, show the collyrium for smearing the eyes with lampblack! Svāhā! Ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ!
By grinding the roots of the *arka*, the *karavīra*, and the *panasa* trees and applying them as an ointment to the feet, serpents will flee to a great distance. (25)
Thus ends the collyrium for revealing hidden treasures.
Now, regarding the method of making oneself invisible: one who is pure should recite this mantra four hundred thousand times in a cremation ground.
Then, pleased by his naked conduct, the Yakṣiṇī bestows a garment.
Enveloped by that, a man moves about on the surface of the earth invisible;
he beholds and seizes treasure, and is not overcome by obstacles. || 27 ||

Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ spheṃ śmaśānavāsinī svāhā. Having meditated upon Niśācarī at night and having recited this mantra with the left hand, she bestows the vidyā that makes one invisible when it has been recited one hundred thousand times. || 28 ||
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ spheṃ śmaśānavāsinī svāhā.
On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should perform the supreme worship with offerings of bali within a cremation ground or a temple of Śiva. (29)
Then, using lamp-oil and human-finger-tissue as the wick and *arka* fibers for the threads, one should light a fire in a human skull.
Having held the soot produced therein in a vessel, one should apply it as collyrium to both eyes; thus, one will not be seen even by the gods. (30)
Oṃ, homage to the Great Maheśvara of the night-walkers! Bind, bind the eyes of all people as I wander; the Goddess commands it, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the Great Maheśvara of the night-walkers! Bind, bind the eyes of all people as I wander; the Goddess commands it, svāhā!
[This is to be done] with threads of *arka*, *śālmalī*, cotton, silk, and lotus fiber. (31)
With five wicks in five human skulls, lamps should be made with fresh butter; the soot [for the collyrium] comes from the human skull.
One should diligently cause [the disciple] to grasp it with the five [fingers] as before in the temple of Śiva.
Then, one should again unify that which has arisen from the five locations;
having consecrated it with mantras, one should anoint the eyes, and [the disciple] will not be seen even by the gods.
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Kāli, Kāli, Mahākāli, you who devour flesh and blood, O Goddess with red and black faces, do not look upon me as a mere human! Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

Success is attained by reciting this mantra ten thousand times. This very mantra is for the aforementioned applications of invisibility; through the application of finger-oil consecrated one hundred and eight times with this mantra, they become effective. 34.
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Kāli, Kāli, Mahākāli, you who devour flesh and blood, O Goddess with red and black faces, do not look upon me as a human being! Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

Barley grains soaked in oil from the finger for seven days should be encased in the three metals; one should fashion an auspicious pill from them. When placed in the mouth, it makes one invisible—of this there is no doubt. (35)
White mustard seeds soaked in oil and encased in the three metals (triloha) form a pill; when placed inside the mouth, it is considered a means of making oneself invisible.
One should grind together in equal parts the blood of a black crow, bile derived from a jackal, and the claws and beak of a raven. || 37 ||
Having prepared a wick under the asterism Punarvasu, one should apply it to the eyes;
one then quickly becomes invisible and accomplishes all tasks. || 38 ||
Having ground the tip of a black cock's tail, the remains of a funeral wreath, the eye of a crow, and black pepper with urine, one should prepare [the mixture]. (39)
Having made a pill with a measurement of half a *kalāya* bean, one should dry it thoroughly;
by anointing the eyes with that very [substance], one certainly becomes invisible. (40)
Having taken blood situated within a black cat, one should meditate upon it;
therein, [one should place] a [wick] made from a white *arka* fiber using oil of *naktamāla*.
Having lit a wick and collected the soot upon a petal of the *vajra* plant, a person who applies that collyrium certainly becomes invisible. 42.
And having killed a very black cat at a crossroads, [one should perform the rite]. || 43 ||
Having caused it to be sprinkled for twenty-five days,
one should carefully collect that [substance] and wash it with cold water.
Having worshipped Mahākālī together with yellow orpiment (gorocana), one should carefully take hold of a bone that pierces the ear and is free from fear. 45.
Having saturated it with the bile of a mongoose, one should grind it;
by merely applying this as a tilaka-mark, a man will certainly become invisible. (46)
A wise person should diligently procure human flesh and the flesh of a jackal.
And prepare a pill with the blood of a woman experiencing her first menses.
Encased in three metals, when placed in the mouth, it renders one invisible. || 47 ||
One should cause black guñjā seeds to sprout upon the shaven head of a black cat;
indeed, that fruit, when placed in the mouth, makes one invisible before one's very eyes.
One should encase the left eye of a *kokā* bird with the three metals;
that pill, when placed inside the mouth, certainly makes one invisible. (49)
One should encase the eye of a bat (divābhīta) with the three metals;
when placed in the mouth, it makes one invisible, and one may wander the earth as one desires.
And under the asterism Anurādhā, by placing a vandā plant from a rāsa-tree in one's mouth, a man shall become invisible; of this there is no doubt.
And by taking the *vandāka* plant of the *śākhoṭa* tree under the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣaka with a drinking vessel, a man becomes invisible. || 52 ||
Having gathered a bundle of cotton derived from the *vandā* plant under the asterism Bharaṇī, one should [proceed].
Having tied it to the hand, one indeed becomes invisible; or, under the asterism Svāti, one should drink [a decoction] made from the nimba tree;
under Uttarāṣāḍhā, one should drink that produced from the aśoka tree.
Then, by holding a *vandā* plant grown from a *bilva* tree under the asterism Aśvinī, or by holding a *vandāka* in his hand, a man becomes invisible. || 55 ||
Thus ends the method for becoming invisible.
Now, I shall explain in brief the science of the "Reviver of the Dead" (mṛtasañjīvanī).
Having placed the liṅga beneath an aṅkola tree, one should worship it. || 56 ||
One should worship a new water-pot right there in the vicinity of the liṅga;
one should encircle the tree, the liṅga, and the water-pot with a single thread.
Having prostrated in due order with the four practitioners, one should perform this for two days; thus, one should worship with the Aghora mantra.
Oṃ! To those who are non-terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the most terrible—to all you forms of Rudra, everywhere and in every way, homage be to you!
This is the mantra for the aforementioned yogas.
A wise person should perform the ritual practice beginning with flowers and ending with the ripening of fruits.
Having taken the ripe fruits, he should fill the jar as previously described. (59)
One should worship that jar daily with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth;
then, having removed the husks, one should stir the opening of the seeds.
Its mouth should be broad and circular; one should apply a slight amount [of paste] here and there inside the wide-mouthed portion, using a tool made from the hand of a potter.
One should smear clay there and plant those seeds with effort,
facing upwards in the form of a coiled serpent (kuṇḍalī).
That vessel, once dried, should be placed upside down upon a copper plate;
one should keep it in the sun to extract the oil and preserve it.
For half a month one should use that oil, and for half a month sesame oil;
this nasal medication (nasya) should be administered at that very moment to one who is dead from the bite of Kāla.

Alternatively, one should rub human semen, equal in quantity to mercury, with that oil; a single dose of this as nasal drops (nasya) should be administered to one who is dead or bitten by a fatal snake, and in an instant [he shall revive].
Having performed that, one truly lives even after having gone to the abode of Yama;
for one who has died from disease, untimely death, snakes, and the like, indeed lives by himself. That he returns alive is not surprising—this was spoken by Mahādeva.
One should collect the root of *guḍūcī* during the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism and the sun;
when drunk with a karṣa measure of warm water, it shall remove death even for one who is dying.
Thus ends the thirteenth instruction, titled "The Description of the Eye-salve for Seeing Treasures and the Elixir of Life," in the *Kāmaratna* composed by the illustrious Nityanātha. 13.
The Fourteenth Instruction:
Now, the neutralization of poison as briefly taught by Śambhu; poison is both stationary (sthāvara) and mobile (jaṅgama).
That which is artificial, that which is born of yoga, and that which arises from scorpions and the like.
I shall now describe their characteristics in sequence, joined with the mantras;
I shall also state the names of the poisons as they were proclaimed by Śambhu in the past.
Darada, vatsanābha, mustaka, puṣkara, viṣa, krūra, śaṭha, karmaṭha, haridra, and kālakūṭaka. (3)
Indrabīja, Citrabīja, green Gālava, Viṣa, Śṛṅgī, Karkaṭaśṛṅgī, Meṣaśṛṅgī, and Halāhala.
Śākūṭa, Raktaśṛṅgī, Añjana, Puṇḍarīka, Saṃkoca, Madhupāka, Rohiṇa, and likewise Medura. || 5 ||
Stable poison is to be known through twenty-five varieties;
among these, the Saṃkoca and Kālakūṭa are exceedingly cruel.
Bhṛṅgī, musta, vatsanābha, and the fifth, which is poison that neutralizes poison—listen now as the symptoms of these when they have entered the body are described. (7)
One should observe vomiting, fainting, diarrhea, delusion, colic,
trembling, cough, dyspnea, intense burning, and a faltering voice.
One should grind the marrow of the *putrajīva* fruit with cold water;
it removes all poisons when used in food, as an ointment for the eyes, as a drink, or as a medicinal paste.
Whether it be stationary, mobile, cruel, artificial, or produced by yoga—
if [this medicine] is taken in a dose of one niṣka, there is no doubt that even one bitten by Kāla shall live.
Śāḍvala, kaṅkaṇa, tuttha, kaṭphala, rajanī, and vacā—
by grinding each one individually with human urine, it removes poison.
Likewise, one should take sarṣākṣī with its roots and leaves, as well as devadālī,
or the root of girikaṇyā, with human urine, according to the previous procedure.
Trikaṭu and devadālī, used as a nasal drop (nasya), remove all poisons;
one should consume the root of brahmadaṇḍī with honey.

The root of the white *aṅkola* tree, when placed on the face or as a tilaka mark, removes poison; likewise, the root of the eggplant (*eraṇḍa*), dried in the shade and applied to the face, destroys poison. (14)
Tarkana and devadālī, when drunk with water, remove poison;
likewise, the tail of a blue snake and the tail of a chameleon [are effective]. (15)
Having encased it in copper, one should wear that seal-ring;
water touched by it, when drunk, removes [the effects of] both stationary and moving poisons. || 16 ||
The mantra:

Ātaratha, ākī, yātaratha, ślātohāte, upajīlo, vṛkṣamuṃcaculu, karapāpiyo, sindūrasāvāṇī, kālakūṭaviṣa, śrīgorakṣera vāṇīmukhe dile haye, amṛtavāṇī, viṣakhā-u, viṣajāro, viṣakaroti bhara, viṣahari āche tridaśara, īśvara mahādevera ājñā gorakṣera vāṇī. || 1 ||
The essence of vermilion is the speech, the body is the kālakūṭa poison, and the horse is the drink; such is the command of Śrī Gorakṣa. 2.
The heavy discipline and training for weariness are like the kālakūṭa poison swallowed by Kāṇḍena. || 3 ||

The command of Mahādeva, the word of Gorakṣa: "O Kālakūṭa poison within the body, O Hayāpānī, O Kālakūṭa poison, destroy, destroy! Oṃ Pārṇā! One should consume the poison consecrated by the mantra, having empowered it with the mantra three times. || 4 ||

*Ātarathākī*, *yātarathā*, *ilātā*, *hārata*, *upajīle*, *vṛkṣamuṃji*, *caluka*, *cijā*, *pijo*, *sindūra*, *sāraṇī*, *kālakūṭa*—these poisons have been driven out from within the body by the command of Śrī Gorakṣa. The extractor of poison, the consumer of poison, the performer of the poison-rite, the bearer of poison, and the remover of poison are present; this is the command of Mahādeva, the Lord of the Thirty-three, and the word of Gorakṣa, the essence of the vermilion. The *kālakūṭa* poison has been driven out from within the body. One should wear upon the hand a ring produced from the essence of the *bhūnāga* (subterranean serpent).
It is the truth: neither stationary (*sthāvara*) nor mobile (*jaṅgama*) poison shall overcome him.
By drinking water touched by that [mudrā], all poison is destroyed. || 17 ||
One should take a bundle of śirīṣa flowers mixed with sandalwood during the asterism of Revatī;
when that is rubbed and applied to the body, it destroys poison in one's limbs. (18)
One should grind together the bile of a boar, an iguana, a mongoose, a rabbit, and a cock, along with the fruit and root of white *girikarṇī*. (19)
When drunk, it destroys all poisons, and even one who is dead rises in an instant;
this is known by the name Amṛtayoga, spoken of old by Rudra.
One should likewise smear a small drum (paṇava) and a large drum (paṭaha) with this very [substance];
even one who has died from the application of poison awakens upon hearing the sound of the musical instrument.
Having drunk the root of white Aparājitā with milk, a person destroys immobile poison (sthāvaraviṣa) located within the stomach; of this there is no doubt. || 22 ||
Having drunk sour gruel (kāñjika) mixed with river water, one may remove stationary (sthāvara) and other types of poison.
The mantra for warding off poison: Oṃ namo bhagavate uḍḍāmareśvarāya kuñcitāmṛtamarcatajaṭāya ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā.
Thus ends the warding off of poison.
Now, regarding the neutralization of the venom of mobile snakes,
the names and forms of the mobile [snakes] are stated here:
the Brāhmaṇas are white in color, and the Kṣatriyas are red in color.
The Vaiśyas are yellow in color, and the Śūdras are black in color. || 24 ||
The mantra for neutralizing snake venom.

Oṃ meghamāle adhimāle, remove, remove the force of poison! Hā hā hā hā, O remover of water! O Mother, O Mother, O destroyer of all poisons, O Great Illusion! Hūṃ hūṃ laṃ saḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā! Jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ! This is the Vidyā named Meghamālā, the Destroyer of All Poisons. Oṃ prauṭhaḥ, svāhā to Nīlakaṇṭha! Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One! O you of red limbs, red eyes, tawny matted hair, and tawny body! O you with a *kaṭkaṭka-hakahabhañja-bhañja* trident-tip in hand! O fierce and most terrible one, O great satiator! O black one, O exceedingly black one! Having entered this human body, wander, wander, wander, wander! Cause it to wander, cause it to wander! Dance, dance, O you of many forms, O playful one, O devoted one! O black-limbed one, fulfill, fulfill! Cause to enter, cause to enter! O you of universal form, O Rudra of the red garment, he commands: Hūṃ phaṭ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ! This is the Vidyā of Svāsthāveṣā. Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, to Pārśvayakṣa! Hrīṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ! O cow, O cow! Tremble, tremble! Having seen the ancient [text], cause [the spirit] not to enter, cause not to enter! Svāhā! || 25 ||
Ananta, Kulika, Vāsuki, Śaṅkhapālaka, Takṣaka, Mahāpadma, Karkoṭa, and Padma—these indeed are the eight nāgas of the family (kulanāga); their emblems have been declared by Śiva. (26)
A white lotus is seen upon the head and the back of Ananta;
a conch shell is on the head of Śeṣa, and a blue lotus is on the back of Vāsuki.
Karkoṭa bears the mark of three eyes, while Takṣaka is marked with a hare;
on the head of Śaṅkhapāla is a flaming trident and a half-moon.
Like a royal insignia, there is an equal-sized dot behind the great lotus; and upon the back of the lotus, five intensely red dots are seen. (29)
Thus, for one who knows the names of birth and so forth as declared by Śiva to be the *bindu*,
his mantras and medicinal herbs indeed attain success, but not otherwise.
From afar, snakes and other creatures fall from him like [prey] from Garuḍa;
such is the sign called "Time" (Kālākhyā), as previously declared by Śiva.
The bite of serpents is to be known as being of ten kinds by the best of physicians:
[the snake] that is frightened, intoxicated, afflicted by hunger, attacked, or arrogant with poison; || 32 ||
The ninth is "desiring food" when afflicted by hunger, and the tenth is "protecting one's own position"; the ninth is "concluding peace with an enemy," and the tenth is designated as "time. (33)
The ten results according to the distinction of locations are as follows:
in a garden, at an old well, at a banyan tree, at a crossroads, at a square, at a withered tree, in a cremation ground, and at a Plakṣa, Śleṣmātaka, or Śigruka tree. (34)
In a temple of the gods, as well as at a Śāka tree—in these places, those men who are bitten do not survive. (35)
Between the eyebrows, on the lower lip, at the crown of the head, on the shanks, the eyes, and likewise the two brows;
on the neck, the chin, the throat, in the middle of the hands, and in the palate.
One bitten by a snake does not survive if the bite occurs at the two breasts, the joints, the belly, the penis, the testicles, the navel, or anywhere at the vital points (marmas) and joints.

One bitten by a snake on a Sunday, Tuesday, or Saturday does not survive. Indeed, the eighth, fifth, full moon, new moon, and fourteenth days are declared to be inauspicious lunar dates; one bitten by a snake on these does not live.
One does not survive under Kṛttikā, Śravaṇa, Mūla, Viśākhā, Bharaṇī, the three Pūrvās, Citrā, or Āśleṣā. (39)
At midday, during the two twilights, at midnight, and at the end of the night—
at these times of death and on the days of the week designated for death— one bitten by a serpent does not survive.
The tooth of the serpent located in the middle of the palate, which resembles a goad, releases terrible poison; for this reason, it is known as Kāla.
And the bite may be circular in shape, or it may have the appearance of a ripe jambu fruit.
Whether blue, white, or red, even a person with such [complexion] does not live;
or else, urine and feces may flow out, accompanied by heart pain, vomiting, and a burning sensation.
One should know that a voice with nasalization, or even a breaking of the euphonic junctions (*sandhi*) in speech;
eyes that are copper-colored or as dark as a crow; and separation from one's beloved—these are called the "Bite of the Gods," which falls within the noose of Death.
One whose body does not experience horripilation even when repeatedly sprinkled with cool water should be known as one who has fallen into the noose of Death.
There was pain at the base of the fang, or perhaps the bite-mark had disappeared;
immediately thereafter, there was an intense burning sensation, and he too was devoured by time. (46)
When he does not see the moon, the sun, or even a shining star, || 47 ||
If one does not see one's own face in a mirror, in water, or even in ghee or oil, despite looking for it, one has been bitten by Kāla; of this there is no doubt. (48)
Having understood both the proper and improper time, one should subsequently administer medicine;
for in the case of a snakebite, there is no poison [if treated at the right time], yet one bitten at the wrong time does not survive.
For him, medical treatment must be administered there until the end of his life;
however, through the power of mercurial and divine medicines, he shall become a conqueror of time.
For the treatment of poison: equal parts of mercury (sūtaka) and sulfur (gandhaka), along with an amount of borax (ṭaṅkaṇa) equal to the turmeric (rajanī);
having ground these with the juice of *devadālī* for one day, one should consume a *niṣka* of it.
The elixir named Kālaśailāśani removes all poisons;
if one drinks human urine after it, even one bitten by the God of Death survives.
The root of white Aparājitā and the root of Devadālīya,
ground with water and used as a nasal drop (nasya), revives even one bitten by Kāla.
Curd, honey, fresh butter, long pepper, ginger, black pepper, costus as the eighth, and rock salt.
If Takṣaka or Vāsuki were to bite me in anger while I am seated in the assembly hall, he would be brought here in that very instant.
Having drunk *kuṭakī* and the root of *muśalī* with water, one destroys poison;
by applying the root of *vīraṇa* as an ointment, one destroys all poisons, including those of scorpions.
Either borax drunk with water, or the root of the arka plant, or rock salt with human urine—each one individually destroys poison. (56)
The root of *indravāruṇī*, white *punarnavā*,
the root of *vandhyākarkoṭakī*, and the roots of *muśalī* and *śikhi*—
each of these, when drunk with rice-water, destroys poison. (57)
A decoction of cow's milk, turmeric, and kuṣṭha, when drunk, removes poison.
The root of Bhṛṅgarāja, the root of Triśūlinī, or the root of Taṇḍulī—each one taken with water will be a conqueror of poison. (59)
One should drink the powder of *somarājī* seeds, once saturated with cow’s urine;
it destroys all poisons, both mobile and immobile, and is a reviver of the dead. (60)

The fine root of the bitter gourd (kaṭutuṃbī), ground with cow's urine and dried in the shade, forms a pill that destroys poison when administered as a drink or applied as an ointment along with [cow's] urine. 61.
By merely drinking a decoction of turmeric with cow urine, human urine, or aged ghee, one destroys all poisons, whether mobile or immobile.
Ghee that is ten years old is called "ancient" (purāṇa);
by drinking it or even applying it as an ointment, it removes [poison]—of this there is no doubt—even if the poison has reached every part of the body of those afflicted by snake venom. (63)
One should drink a decoction of *añjanī* with cow’s milk to remove all poisons;
likewise, turmeric, *kuṣṭha*, honey, and ghee, when consumed together, remove all poisons. (64)
The root of white guñjā, when held in the mouth, destroys poison;
its root, uprooted during the Puṣya asterism, destroys poison when used as a nasal drop.
Its root, taken with the juice of *pāṭhā*, when drunk, overcomes the *kālakūṭa* poison;
by smearing the site of the bite with the root of the *arka* plant, it is a great antidote for poison. (66)
Likewise, by means of red *citrā* and *indragopa* insects, there is the destruction of poison;
one should also slit open the head at the tip of the tail of a green-colored snake.
The white and the black [remedies] should be applied separately as a nasal therapy (nasya) to remove all poisons.
The white [remedy] is for the white [mark] on the right side, and the black [remedy] is for the black [mark] on the left.
This is indeed the "Reviver of the Dead" (Mṛtasañjīvana); even one bitten by Kāla (the God of Death) lives.
One should drink a decoction of bitter *kośātakī* combined with honey and clarified butter; he who vomits it up at that very moment is released from the administration of poison. (69)
One should drink either *kuṭakī* or the root of the rose-apple (*jambu*) with sour buttermilk or water; one will vomit immediately and be swiftly freed from the administration of poison. (70)
One should take the bark of the rājavṛkṣa, both white and black, separately;
on the white tree, however, one should take the white portion along with twenty-four [other substances].
O Haramekhalā, it has been said that one who is addicted to drinking may, after drinking black bark along with *marica* seeds,
be rendered free from poison even if bitten.
Saffron, lac-dye, lodhra, realgar, and gorocana—
by means of a pill or an ointment made from these, one destroys all poisons, both stationary and mobile.
Two types of *haridrā*, *śilā*, *tāla*, *kuṅkuma*, and *kuṣṭha*, when ground with water and applied as a pill-ointment, most wonderfully destroy poison by mere application. (74)
Having ground the marrow of the *pūtīkarañja* seed and that produced from the *kāravella*, one should drink it with clarified butter; it destroys poison, without a doubt. (75)
One should grind long pepper, black pepper, costus, soot, realgar, orpiment, white mustard seeds, and cow-bile together. (76)
Through the use of pills, collyrium, nasal drops, drinking, ointment, or anointment,
it renders one free from poison in an instant, even if bitten by Takṣaka himself.
Pathyā, honey, black pepper, patra, hiṅgu, śilājatu, and vacā—by making a pill with these and water and administering it as a nasal drop (nasya), even one bitten by a deadly snake survives. (78)
A plaster made of aśvagandhā, meghanāda, cow’s urine, mahiṣākṣaka, and house-soot shall remove poison from the head and throat. (79)
One should grind the five parts of *aśvagandhā* with goat’s urine;
when used as an ointment or taken internally, there is no doubt that it destroys various kinds of poisons. (80)
Śilā, hiṅgu, vacā, vyoṣa, abhayā, tvak, and patrakam—when used as a nasal drop with cold water, these render one bitten by Vāsuki free from poison. (81)
One should grind the marrow of the *putrajīva* fruit with cow’s milk;
by means of an ointment, collyrium, or nasal drop, even one bitten by the God of Death returns to life. (82)
One should take one *pala* of the powder of the root of black dhattūra; having formed a pill with one *karṣa* of karañja oil, one should wear it.
By drinking it with the juices of jambīra, it wards off the poison of the *raudrī* [serpent]. (83)

Having drunk the root of *lajjālu* or the root of *nīlī* with clear water, one destroys the poison of *raudrī*; likewise, by an application of *guñjā*, *balā*, and *nata*, [the same effect is achieved]. (84)
One should drink house-soot, the two types of turmeric with their roots, and *tandulīyaka*, combined with curd and clarified butter; even those bitten by Vāsuki [would be cured]. (85)
The root of *tandulīyaka*, when drunk with rice-water, certainly renders one free from poison even if bitten by Takṣaka himself. (86)
By means of a nasal application of the root of the *kulikā* plant, even one bitten by a deadly snake survives.
*Oṃ, I am seen by the eye of the Sun; O Hara, remove the poison, svāhā!*
With this mantra, one should consecrate the aforementioned yogas.
The root of Aparājitā, when taken with ghee, destroys poison located in the skin;
with milk, it destroys that which has reached the blood; and with the powder of Kuṣṭha, it destroys that which has entered the flesh.
Oṃ! Seen by the eye of the Sun, I am seen; O Hara, remove the poison, svāhā!
[The poison] located in the bone is countered by *rajanī*; that located in the fat by *lāṅgalī*;
that located in the marrow by *pippalī* combined with the root of *caṇḍālī*.
Lauhitya destroys the [impurity] residing in the semen; therefore, Aparājitā should be given. 89.
Thus, for one whose state of being is such that this world is the very form of the Self,
even while being devoured by all manner of creatures, such as venomous insects, he is not afflicted.
For one who has been immediately bitten by a snake, an ointment made with human nasal mucus and earwax, or by sprinkling [the area] with human urine, [is effective]. 91.
By that [remedy], the poison is arrested and does not run upward into the bodily constituents;
the root of the *varāhakarṇikā* tied to the hand removes poison. 92.
White pepper, processed for seven days with the fresh juice of *śirīṣa* flowers, is beneficial when administered as a drink, nasal drop, or collyrium for those bitten by snakes. (93)
The Vidyā Svacchandabhairavī is said to be the destroyer of poison.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Svacchandabhairavī, Mahābhairavī! Shatter, shatter the Kālakūṭa poison! Expand, expand it! Devour, devour it! Cause it to descend, cause it to descend! There is no poison—whether the Hālāhala poison, artificial poison, compounded poison, or indeed most fierce poison; whether stationary (sthāvara) poison or mobile (jaṅgama) poison—the mantra of Kālacañcuyāyarā is the desired one: *taḍadarghāyaṇa ithaya ithaya oṃ kālāya mahākālāya kālamarddadevī amṛtagarbhadevī oṃ oṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. One should consecrate [the water] with this mantra. Having empowered the water seven or nine times and sprinkled [the victim] with it, one should have them drink that water, and they shall become free from poison. This is the *Svacchandabhairavī* Vidyā. Or: *Oṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ saṃsvaḥ haṃsaḥ*, or *Oṃ krūṃ krūṃ saṃsvaḥ haṃsaḥ*. By drinking water consecrated with this mantra, or by sprinkling [it], one shall become free from poison.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Sovereign Bhairavī, the Great Bhairavī! Shatter, shatter the Kālakūṭa poison! Burst asunder, burst asunder! Devour, devour! Cause it to descend, cause it to descend! There is no poison here—not the Hālāhala poison, nor artificial poison, nor compounded poison, nor even most virulent poison; neither stationary poison nor moving poison! O Kālacañcu! O Yāyarā! O Desired Mantra! O Taḍadarghāyaṇa! Go, go! Oṃ, to Kāla, to Mahākāla, to the Goddess Kālamarda, to the Goddess Amṛtagarbhā! Oṃ oṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

Oṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ saṃsvaḥ haṃsaḥ. Alternatively: Oṃ krūṃ krūṃ saṃsvah haṃsaḥ. Having ground the roots of devadāru, citraka, karavīra, arka, and lāṅgalī with water, one should drink it; this removes the bite of Death (the deadliest poison). || 94 ||
If one bitten [by a snake] does not survive despite the application of mantras and medicinal herbs,
the best of physicians should excise the site of the bite with a sharp instrument; however,
if it is a stationary poison (sthāvaraviṣa), one who is bitten by such a creature is killed by that very bite.
But that serpent, having been provoked to rage, emits smoke from its mouth; having repeatedly fed on flesh at the tip of its fangs, it has bitten him. (96)
If it cannot be cured by other means, one should treat it with poison alone. || 97 ||
One should cause the victim to drink two guñjas of poison mixed with milk, honey, and ghee;
by smearing the bite with poison, even one bitten by Kāla (the God of Death) shall live.
Known as the "Reviver of the Dead," this remedy consists of *nirguṇḍī*, *tagara*, and *viṣa*, along with the root of *piṇḍītagara*.
If these are uprooted under the asterism of Puṣya and applied to the site of the bite—even for one who is dead—the bitten person will live at that very moment. (99)
When that hero, bitten by a serpent, bites that very serpent himself, he is liberated;
the serpent dies and itself attains freedom from poison. || 100 ||
Whatever the fruit may be, he should eat it with his teeth as if it were a serpent.
Or, a man prostrating himself like a staff may bite the ground with his teeth;
of this there is no doubt that he will attain the state of a serpent, and poison shall not take effect upon him.
One who is afflicted by the pain of extreme separation from his beloved should be cast into the midst of water. || 103 ||

For one who drinks on a day of the *bhadra-yoga* the pure, well-grounded root of *pratyaṅgirā* with rice-water, from where can there be fear for him? Even if a serpent, out of sheer arrogance, should bite that person while he is possessed by delusion— [The verse continues: ...he becomes like a pillar of stone, free from all affliction. By this very method, one should drink the root of *pratyaṅgirā* at dawn; by this, one is liberated from all poison. One should drink it with water from a conch shell, or with water from a jar, or with water from a golden vessel; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a silver vessel, or with water from a copper vessel, or with water from a crystal vessel; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a pearl-oyster shell, or with water from a mother-of-pearl shell, or with water from a coral vessel; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a lapis lazuli vessel, or with water from a ruby vessel, or with water from an emerald vessel; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a diamond vessel, or with water from a sapphire vessel, or with water from a topaz vessel; by this, one is freed from all poison.
