One should drink it with water from a cat's-eye vessel, or with water from a moonstone vessel, or with water from a sunstone vessel; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a glass vessel, or with water from a lead vessel, or with water from a tin vessel; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from an iron vessel, or with water from a bronze vessel, or with water from a bell-metal vessel; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a wooden vessel, or with water from a clay vessel, or with water from a leaf-cup vessel; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a human skull, or with water from a skull of a cow, or with water from a skull of a goat; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a horse, or with water from a skull of an elephant, or with water from a skull of a lion; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a tiger, or with water from a skull of a leopard, or with water from a skull of a wolf; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a peacock, or with water from a skull of a parrot, or with water from a skull of a mynah; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a cuckoo, or with water from a skull of a pigeon, or with water from a skull of a dove; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a swan, or with water from a skull of a crane, or with water from a skull of a duck; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a goose, or with water from a skull of a ruddy sheldrake, or with water from a skull of a chakravaka; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a fish, or with water from a skull of a tortoise, or with water from a skull of a crocodile; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a snake, or with water from a skull of a lizard, or with water from a skull of a frog; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a rat, or with water from a skull of a mouse, or with water from a skull of a mongoose; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a cat, or with water from a skull of a dog, or with water from a skull of a jackal; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a boar, or with water from a skull of a buffalo, or with water from a skull of an elephant; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a lion, or with water from a skull of a tiger, or with water from a skull of a leopard; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a man, or with water from a skull of a woman, or with water from a skull of a child; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of an old man, or with water from a skull of an old woman, or with water from a skull of an old child; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a king, or with water from a skull of a queen, or with water from a skull of a prince; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a minister, or with water from a skull of a priest, or with water from a skull of a general; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a Brahmin, or with water from a skull of a Kshatriya, or with water from a skull of a Vaishya; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a Shudra, or with water from a skull of a Chandala, or with water from a skull of a Pukkasa; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a hunter, or with water from a skull of a fisherman, or with water from a skull of a thief; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a butcher, or with water from a skull of a wine-seller, or with water from a skull of a prostitute; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a courtesan, or with water from a skull of a dancer, or with water from a skull of a singer; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of an actor, or with water from a skull of a mime, or with water from a skull of a buffoon; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a jester, or with water from a skull of a clown, or with water from a skull of a fool; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a madman, or with water from a skull of a lunatic, or with water from a skull of a demented person; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a blind man, or with water from a skull of a deaf man, or with water from a skull of a mute person; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a lame man, or with water from a skull of a cripple, or with water from a skull of a hunchback; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a dwarf, or with water from a skull of a giant, or with water from a skull of a monster; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a ghost, or with water from a skull of a spirit, or with water from a skull of a demon; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a yaksha, or with water from a skull of a rakshasa, or with water from a skull of a piśāca; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a kinnara, or with water from a skull of a gandharva, or with water from a skull of a vidyadhara; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a naga, or with water from a skull of a garuda, or with water from a skull of a suparna; by this, one is freed from all poison. One should drink it with water from a skull of a mahoraga, or with water from a skull of a kimnara, or with water from a skull of a mahagandharva; by this, one is freed
In that place, he who possesses the discus (Viṣṇu) will certainly go to the abode of Yama before long.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, if one applies the root of the śirīṣa tree to the waist and drinks rice-water, no snakebite shall occur;
even if a snake bites by mistake, that snake shall perish. 105.
Under the Puṣya asterism, one should take the root of the white Arka plant and the root of the white Varṣāmbu plant.
Having collected that drink under that same constellation and bathed with rice-water, men should perform this annually for the sake of destroying the fear of serpents. (107)
One should eat [the medicine] made from the leaves of *masūra* and *nimba* when the sun has entered Aries;
for one year, there will be no fear for one afflicted by poison—of this there is no doubt.
What can Takṣaka do to him, even if he is filled with extreme rage? (108)
One should wrap the teeth of a chameleon with a white thread;
by binding it on the arm, it destroys poison, and one who has consumed poison is no longer afflicted.
It also causes the mouths of snakes, scorpions, and mice to become paralyzed. (109)
Oṃ śabarī kīrttaya sañjāva sañjāva svāhā.
Success is attained through a thousand recitations. With this mantra, one should bind [the amulet] upon the hand. 110.
Upon seeing the root of the Pātālagāruḍī hanging inside the house, snakes and other venomous insects flee far away. (111)
Oṃ śabarī kīrtaya sañjāva sañjāva svāhā | Oṃ plaḥ to the serpent family, svāhā.
Thus ends the remedy for snake venom. Now follows the remedy for scorpion venom:
the seed of the *śirīṣa*, *gomeda* gem, and the root of the pomegranate.
An incense prepared with the milk of the Arka plant destroys the poison of a scorpion.
The excrement of peacocks, pigeons, and cocks should be taken together with the roots of the *bhānu* plant.
This incense quickly destroys all four kinds of poison arising from scorpions and snakes. (113)
One should remove poison born of a scorpion by means of the incense of powdered *rajani*.

Having covered the limbs with a cloth, one should cause the patient to inhale the smoke of the incense; one should also quickly fumigate the site of the sting. This procedure applies to all types of incense. (114)
One should administer a nasal drop of ginger with water, or drink ghee mixed with rock salt;
or, for the removal of poison, the roots of *arka* and *dhattūra* may be taken as a drink. (115)
The marrow of the *putrajīva* fruit, that of the *palāśa*, and that of the *karañja*, mixed with water—this ointment destroys the poison born of a scorpion. (116)
Asafoetida, when applied as a paste with water, removes the poison arising from a scorpion;
or, by eating a portion the size of a sesame seed, or through its application as a paste, it destroys the poison. (117)
By an ointment of ghee and arka-milk, or by one fumigated with yaṣṭī, or even by an ointment of the root of bījapūraka, [the bite of] a harītakī [is neutralized]. 118.
Beeswax should be soaked seven times in the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka* plants in the sun;
when heated and touched with fire, it removes poison from the site of a sting.
An ointment made from *jātī* and molasses, or an application of turmeric, destroys the poison of a scorpion individually; of this there is no doubt. (120)
One should uproot the root of the *mātuluṅga* tree on a Sunday, facing northward and touching it while reciting the mantra *hrūṃ* (or *krūṃ*). || 121 ||

If the right [limb] is bitten on the left side, or the left is bitten on the right, one should destroy the poison along with the bite by means of wiping; this is a proven remedy. By wiping seven times, one may remove the poison born of a scorpion.
Having uprooted the root of asagandha and the root of white punarnavā on a Sunday, [one cures] the sting of a scorpion with these two. (123)

One should destroy poison by wiping it away with one's own gaze once it has been perceived; likewise, by chewing the root of the cotton plant (*karpāsa*) and blowing upon the ear, one becomes a conqueror of poison.
On Sunday, at dawn, one should take the root of *haṃsapadī* and, blowing upon it, place it in the mouth; this removes poison produced by scorpens when applied to the ear.

Oṃ kṣaḥ phaṭ svāhā! By this, one should sprinkle water [on the patient], and he becomes free from poison. [With the speed of the sun’s chariot, with the strength of Viṣṇu’s arms, and by the stroke of Garuḍa’s wings, go to the earth, O great poison!]

Oṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ | Oṃ, by the command of the venerable feet of Śrīpakṣayogin—this is the mantra. On the northern side of the Himavat mountain, there is a scorpion named Kapila. By him I have been sent as a messenger: "Go, go, O one of great venom! Klīṃ klīṃ svāhā! Ḍākinī svāhā phaṭ! Alternatively, with this Garuḍa-mantra—*śāṃkhā māṃkhā sāhīṃ khauṃhīṃ*—one should wash away [the poison] from one bitten by a scorpion using water and *karavīra* wood; he becomes free of poison.

One should consecrate [the substance] with the mantra: *oṃ jhaṃ huṃ kraṅ vaṃ vaṃ laṃ kṣaṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ haṃ haḥ* and apply it as an ointment. By consecrating a lotus stalk with the mantra *hāṃ hīṃ maṃ caṃ oṃ* and wiping [with it], the poison of a scorpion is destroyed. This yoga, spoken by Śiva, must not be treated with contempt.
Alternatively, by squeezing the bark and seeds of the *bakula* tree at the site of the sting and applying them as a plaster— once consecrated with mantras— the poison of a scorpion is removed.
Thus ends the remedy for scorpion venom.
Now follows the remedy for centipede venom:
one should apply oil from a lamp that has been extinguished as an ointment to the site of the bite.
Having offered incense made of guggulu, one should wrap it with arka leaves.
Now, regarding the neutralization of rat poison:
realgar, orpiment, and kuṣṭha should be infused with the juice of nirguṇḍī.
When administered as a drink to those bitten by rats, it removes even the most virulent poison. (128)
Having taken a house-lizard and ground it with rice-water, one destroys the poison of a rat by anointing [the bite]; or one may drink it prepared with milk. (129)
One should drink mustard seeds, saffron, buttermilk, and ghee in equal parts;
the poison of those bitten by rats will be pacified instantly.
One should lick for seven days house-soot mixed with half a pala of ciñcā fruit and aged clarified butter; this removes the poison of a rat.
Thus ends the prevention of rat poison.
Now, the prevention of dog poison:
the seed of the *śirīṣa* tree, rubbed with the milk of *snuhī*, [is effective].
O lady of excellent hips, by anointing with that [ointment], the poison born of a dog is destroyed.
A plaster of jaggery, oil, and the milk of the *arka* plant removes the poison of a dog.
Having ground one *karṣa* of the root of *apāmārga*, one should lick it with honey;
or by means of a plaster made from chicken droppings, it destroys the poison of a dog-bite. (133)
One should apply a comfortably warm medicinal bolus consisting of the fangs of a mad dog, *kumārī* leaves, and rock salt; at the end of three days, this brings about well-being.
Oṃ haḍavaḍa kuttā khaḍavaḍa dāṃta kutte kī bāṃdho | Sātauḍāḍha āvai na lohū pākai na ghāva kuttekā viṣa utara jāva | Vīra Hanumān’s couplet—Rāma-Lakṣmaṇa’s couplet—the *phura* mantra. Īśvara said:
Thus ends the prevention of dog venom.
Now, the prevention of venom from fish, frogs, and the like: one should drink milk with the bark of the *śirīṣa* fruit to remove the poison of a frog.
Tryūṣaṇa with clarified butter, as well as meghanāda, frog, and fish, remove poison.
The poison of the Śṛṅgī fish, along with sweat, ghee, and cikka, combined with piṇḍita. || 136 ||
The poison of a house lizard is destroyed by nasal drops (nasya) made from the fruit of the kāśmīrī;
one should drink [the remedy] combined with honey and sugar to remove the poison of a house lizard.
Thus ends the neutralization of the poison of fish, frogs, and others.
Now follows the neutralization of the poison of tigers:
[the remedy for] those known as wolves, tigers, jackals, bears, elephants, and horses.
One should cause blood to flow from the bite and cauterize it with an iron probe.

The root of white punarnavā, when applied as a plaster, destroys the poison of a serpent; what need is there for much speaking on this matter? It brings about the destruction of poison in that very instant.
By drinking viḍaṅga, one may remove the poison of tigers and serpents;
likewise, a powder made from the three pungent spices (trikaṭu) with the juice of dhattūra leaves [achieves the same]. 140.
An application of *karañja* oil destroys poison residing in the abdomen, whether it originates from a tiger or a serpent; it also extinguishes the inflammation caused by a tiger's claw.
Having ground gojihvāmūlikā with water and honey, this ointment indeed removes the poison from the claws and beaks of all creatures. (142)
Likewise, a plaster made of nimba, vacā, and the bark of the śamī tree,
mixed with warm water, removes the poison from nails and fangs.
Likewise, an application of dāruharidrā removes poison from the teeth. || 144 ||
Thus ends the warding off of tiger poison. Now follows the warding off of insect poison:
with clarified butter, [one should offer] the root of *taṇḍulī* or the root of *tulasī*.
By drinking rice-water, one may remove poison arising from insects.
A plaster made from the root or seed of *lāṅgalī*, or *kaṭutumbī*, or *devadāru*, or *niśā*, mixed with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), removes the poison of insects. (146)
Sesame, mustard, kuṣṭha, and the seed produced from the karañja tree—
by means of anointment or as a medicinal paste, this conquers all afflictions caused by insects.
An ointment made of karañja seeds, siddhārtha, and sesame seeds removes poison;
or an ointment of castor oil removes the poison of all insects.
Niśā, dāruniśā, mañjiṣṭhā, and nāgakeśara—a plaster made from these quickly destroys poison originating from spiders and other such creatures. (149)
Thus ends the remedy for insect poison. Now, the remedy for the poison of all creatures:
the marrow of *putrajīva* fruits ground with cold water.
By means of ointments, collyrium, or nasal drops, or by drinking a measure of one niṣka. || 150 ||
It removes the poison of tigers, mice, cows, snakes, scorpions, and the like;
it swiftly destroys even unbearable poisons and eruptive boils. || 151 ||
Having ground the root of *bandhyākarkoṭakī* with water, one should apply it as a plaster;
it removes the poison of snakes, mosquitoes, cats, scorpions, and other such creatures. (152)
Thus ends the neutralization of poison for all living beings. Now follows the neutralization of secondary poisons (*upaviṣa*) and the like:
*snuhī*, *arka*, *unmattaka*, *karavīra*, and *lāṅgalī*.
Vajrī, jaipālaka, black kuṣṭha, and likewise guñjā. || 153 ||
Mahākāla and others such as these are remembered by the wise as upaviṣas (minor poisons).
By drinking sour gruel (kāñjika) with salt (sasindhu), one removes all upaviṣas.
Harītakī taken with ghee destroys the poison of the *karavīra* plant;
likewise, neem leaves and ghee destroy [poison], as does the drinking of honey with ghee. || 155 ||
Thus ends the prevention of natural poisons. Now follows the prevention of artificial poisons:
the powder of various venomous creatures combined with natural poisons [is the remedy].
A collection of powders mixed with nails, hair, iron, and so forth. || 156 ||
Artificial poison is well known to cause affliction after a fortnight or a month;
it produces lethargy, dullness, cough, labored breathing, and loss of strength.
One should observe the discharge of blood, fever, emaciation, and yellowed eyes as its symptoms. (157)
Dead mercury, dead gold, and pure hematite—
these three should be mixed with an equal amount of sulfur and ground for one day with the juice of *kanyā*.
One should always lick that [powder] dry along with white sugar for one month;
milk combined with the root of *vahni* destroys *manuṣyagara*. (159)
Having drunk cow’s milk mixed with one niṣka of the marrow from the fruit of the putrajīva tree, one shall destroy even the most virulent poison produced by various artificial concoctions.
A drink of śaṭhī and puṣkaramūla removes the poison of liquor. || 161 ||
One should drink that with milk, which removes poison, thirst, and fever;
milk mixed with mung beans is wholesome, and śāli rice is most beneficial. (162)
Having ground house-soot with water in an amount equal to the root of *taṇḍulī*, one should add clarified butter four times the quantity of the paste and milk four times the quantity of the ghee.
One should cook all these until only the ghee remains; drinking this whole preparation removes [afflictions] from every limb. 163.
One should drink *sarpākṣī* with its roots and leaves boiled in water;
or, having ground it with human urine, one should drink it as a remedy that removes all poisons. 164.
Equal parts of cardamom, *ālīśapatra*, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), and cumin should be combined;
twice the amount of sugar should be added to the powder, and by consuming it, one becomes a destroyer of poison. (165)
One should lick one karṣa of turmeric, kuṣṭha, honey, clarified butter, soot from a house, and the root of *tandulī*, combined with milk; this removes the effects of spells.
Thus ends the remedy for artificial poison.
Now, the remedy for poison produced by yoga: poison born of yoga [is neutralized] by the combination of oil, camphor, and citron juice.
But honey and ghee in equal proportions—such a combination is poison. (167)
Coconut water and camphor, when combined, constitute a poison born of a mixture; likewise, black pepper and the root of the tumbikā plant are also a poison born of a mixture. (168)
One may obtain a son by means of *jīvaphala* alone, or with *rajanī*, *āranālaka*, *devadālī*, human urine, *sarpākṣī*, and *indravāruṇī*. (169)
Alternatively, the root of *girikarṇī* taken individually shall overcome poison;
having ground it with honey, clarified butter, and the juices of *kākajaṅghā*, one shall remove poison. (170)
By drinking girikarṇī, nāgapuṣpī, and muṇḍī, one shall remove poison.
Thus ends the remedy for poison produced by yoga. Now follows the remedy for bhallātaka poison:
from contact with bhallātaka oil, eruptions arise in men.
Having ground fresh butter with sesame seeds, one should conquer that [affliction] by applying that ointment.
One may conquer that [disease] by applying a plaster of nimba leaves, or by means of its root;
or by applying a plaster of earth from the roots of the bhallātaka tree, it certainly destroys all the disorders produced by it. (173)
Thus ends the fourteenth instruction, titled "The Warding Off of Poison," in the *Kāmaratna* composed by the illustrious Nityanātha. 14.
The Fifteenth Instruction:
Now, the sādhana of the yakṣiṇīs.
One should perform the meditation upon all the yakṣiṇīs with a concentrated mind.
She assumes the form of a sister, a mother, a daughter, or a wife, according to one's desire and in a manner that is appropriate.
One should eat food that is free from meat and avoid chewing betel; having sipped water and sat upon a deerskin or similar seat, one should not touch anyone after bathing in the morning.
Having performed his daily duties, he should recite [the mantra] in a secluded place until the Yakṣiṇīs,
who grant all desires, become manifest before him.
The sage, free from fear, should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times in a cremation ground;
having offered guggulu resin with clarified butter as a tenth part of the recitation, the Yakṣiṇī becomes pleased.
The Sādhana of Vaṭayakṣiṇī (1):
At night, at a place where there is a banyan tree on a triple-path, one should personally recite the mantra three hundred thousand times; then the goddess Vaṭayakṣiṇī becomes accomplished.
When she is pleased, she bestows upon the practitioner divine garments and ornaments, the perfection of alchemy, elixirs, and divine collyrium.
Oṃ hrīṃ, O dweller of the banyan tree, banner of the Yakṣa clan, O Yakṣiṇī of the banyan tree, come, come! Svāhā! || 5-6 ||
The Sādhana of Vaṭayakṣiṇī (2):
Having ascended the banyan tree, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Then, having consecrated it seven times with the mantra, one should wash one's face with *kāñjika* (sour gruel). 7.
If one recites [the mantra] at night for three months, the Yakṣiṇī grants a boon:
divine elixirs, rejuvenators, and manifold minor magical rites;
indeed, all undertakings are accomplished—Śaṅkara has declared it to be no other way.
Oṃ, salutation to the one who causes [the world] from the moon down to the very marrow; *klīṃ* svāhā! Or: Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Rudra, of fierce speed; svāhā!
The Sadhana of Ratipriyāyakṣiṇī:
On a cloth smeared with conch-shell paste, [one should visualize] the goddess, fair-complexioned and holding a blue lotus.
Then, having drawn her divine form adorned with all ornaments, one should worship her.
Then, with *jātī* flowers and the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times;
for seven nights, one should recite it during the three junctions of the day, and then recite it throughout the nights.
When midnight has passed, the goddess,
being pleased, approaches and gives twenty-five dīnāras every day.
Oṃ hrīṃ kanakakanaka maithunapriye ratipriye svāhā | Alternatively:
Oṃ hrīṃ ratipriye svāhā | This is the *sādhana* of the yakṣiṇī Surasundarī.
One should always worship Mahādeva at the single liṅga during the three junctions of the day;
having offered incense, one should recite the mantra three thousand times at each of the three junctions.
Then, after one month has passed, the yakṣiṇī Surasundarī arrives;
having offered the arghya, the practitioner should bow and say: "O lady, what do you desire? (13)
"O Goddess, I am consumed by poverty; become the one who destroys it for me.
Then, being pleased, she grants him wealth, long life, and vitality.
Oṃ hrīṃ āgaccha āgaccha surasundari svāhā. O beloved, I shall explain the *sādhana* of Vibhramāyakṣiṇī; first listen to the *Vibhramāsādhana*.
When she is pleased, whether in her form as Vibhramā or Prasannā, she bestows desired objects and always provides food for fifty men.

Oṃ hrīṃ vāṃ, O you of bewitching form, come, come, O Blessed One, svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ, O you of bewitching form, create bewilderment, come, come, O Blessed One, svāhā! This is the sādhana of the yakṣiṇī Anurāgiṇī.
Having drawn a woman of auspicious marks upon a birch-bark leaf with saffron,
one should then perform worship starting from the first lunar day (pratipad) and subsequently recite the mantra.

At the three junctions of the day, one should worship her three thousand times at the end of the month during the night. Having arrived at midnight, she recites [the mantra] and, being well-pleased, bestows a thousand dīnāras.
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ anurāgiṇi maithunapriye svāhā. Now follows the sādhana of Viśālāyakṣiṇī:
one who is pure should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times beneath a tamarind tree.
One should perform a fire sacrifice with flowers produced from the śatapuṣpa plant, accompanied by clarified butter.
Then Viśālā, being pleased and gracious, bestows a divine elixir (*rasāyana*); from that, all success shall come to pass. (19)
Oṃ aiṃ viśāle krīṃ hrīṃ vrīṃ klīṃ krīṃ svāhā. Having meditated upon the Sāmudrī Yakṣiṇī, one should then recite this mantra at night on the shore of the ocean, remaining pure.
When one hundred thousand recitations have been performed, the servant Sāgaraceṭaka grants success;
likewise, the three jewels and food are provided, and the gentle minister shall become happy. (20)

Oṃ, O Blessed One, Ocean, grant us jewels! O Dweller in the Waters, hrīṃ, homage be to you, svāhā! Oṃ, O Blessed One, Ocean, grant us jewels! O Dweller in the Waters, hrīṃ, homage be to you, svāhā! This is the *Mahābhayāyakṣiṇīsādhana*.
One should wear a garland made of human bones around the neck, on the hand, and on the ears;
likewise, one should possess a rosary for recitation obtained from a cremation ground.
The practitioner, pure and fearless, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
thereafter, the Yakṣī Mahābhayā bestows an elixir.
By merely consuming it, one may move all jewels;
the man shall become free from wrinkles and grey hair and live for a long time. || 23 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ trāṃ mahābhaye klīṃ svāhā. Or else: Oṃ krīṃ mahābhaye klīṃ svāhā.
Oṃ hrīṃ trāṃ mahābhaye klīṃ svāhā. Or else: Oṃ krīṃ mahābhaye klīṃ svāhā.
This is the *Sādhana* of the Yakṣiṇī Candrikā.
One should recite during the bright fortnight until the moon is clearly visible;
beginning from the first day (pratipad) until the full moon, one should perform this recitation nine hundred thousand times.
Having drunk the nectar given by Candrikā, the living being becomes immortal. || 25 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ candrike haṃ saḥ krīṃ klīṃ svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ candrike haṃ saḥ krīṃ klīṃ svāhā | The Sadhana of Candradravāyakṣiṇī.
The sādhana of the yakṣiṇī Raktakambalā: one should recite [the mantra] for three months, and she becomes propitious;
she can raise the dead and likewise cause an image to move. || 26 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ! O Great Goddess Raktakambalā, raise the dead, move the image, shake the mountains, shake them, cause them to tremble, cause them to tremble, laugh, laugh, hūṃ hūṃ!
Oṃ hrīṃ! O Great Goddess Raktakambalā, raise the dead, move the image, shake the mountains, shake them, cause them to tremble, cause them to tremble, laugh, laugh, hūṃ hūṃ!
The *Sādhana* of Karṇapiśācinī.
Having first recited the mantra ten thousand times, O Kṛṣṇa, when the girl has been consecrated with it,
by smearing it on the hands and feet, she speaks of good and evil while asleep;
she shall relate the fruit exactly as the news is in the three worlds.

Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ, homage to the Blessed One, Karṇapiśācinī, Caṇḍaveginī! Speak, speak! Svāhā! (1) Oṃ krīṃ, O Blessed One, whose power is equal to that of Brahmā, Karṇapiśācinī, Caṇḍaropinī! Speak, speak! Svāhā! (2) The Sadhana of Vidyujjihvāyakṣiṇī.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, whatever delicious food there may be,
that is offered as an oblation (bali) to her beneath a banyan tree for one month.
Then the Goddess arrives and takes the food from one's hand;
right there she grants a boon that ensures her constant presence.
She declares past and future karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
she even causes all the mountains to tremble at that very moment.
Oṃkāramukhe vidyujjihve | Oṃ hrūṃ ceṭake jaya jaya svāhā | For the sādhana of Ciñci-piśācinī, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with yellow pigment, saffron, and milk.
And on a solid birch-bark leaf, one should write the seed-syllable of Māyā on each individual petal.
Having written this mantra, one should wear it upon the head and then recite it;
having first recited it ten thousand times, one should perform it with diligence.
Then the deity speaks everything, both past and future, in a dream.
Oṃ hrīṃ ciñcipiśācini svāhā. This is the sādhana for Karṇayakṣiṇī.
[One should employ] the root of the alābu plant under the Puṣya asterism, as well as the root of the sarpākṣī plant.
One should carefully wrap the object that has been consecrated with mantras in a red thread;
having tied it to the head, even one who is asleep will speak of what is auspicious and inauspicious.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Lady Rudrā, Karṇayakṣiṇī; svāhā! Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Lady Rudrāṇī, Karṇayakṣiṇī; svāhā!
The Sadhana of Vicitrāyakṣiṇī.
Purified, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times at the foot of a banyan tree;
thereafter, [one should offer oblations] with Bandhūka flowers mixed with honey, clarified butter, and milk.
When that incense has been offered, one should perform oblations with a tenth part [of the total], accompanied by the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Thereupon, the Goddess becomes perfected—wondrous and the granter of all desires.
Oṃ vicitre vicitrarūpe siddhiṃ kuru kuru svāhā! The sādhana for the yakṣiṇī Svapnāvatī: one should smear the ground with clay and cow dung and spread kuśa grass upon it.
One should worship the God and Goddess with the five types of offerings and food oblations.
Holding a rosary in one's hand, one should first recite [the mantra] ten thousand times;
having meditated upon her as equal to ten million suns, one should recite it over the palm of the hand at night.
When midnight has passed, the Goddess speaks words concerning what is auspicious and inauspicious.
Oṃ hrīṃ āgaccha āgaccha cāmuṇḍe śrīṃ svāhā. Having entered the interior of the city, one who is pure should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times. This is the *sādhana* of Haṃsī Yakṣiṇī.
An oblation made with lotus petals mixed with clarified butter should be performed in the tenth part [of the total]. || 38 ||
The female swan gives him collyrium by which he beholds the treasure hidden in the earth;
he takes it with ease and is not overcome by obstacles. (39)

Oṃ haṃsi haṃsijane hrīṃ klīṃ svāhā; or: Oṃ namo haṃsini haṃsagate māṃ svāhā. This is the sādhana of the yakṣiṇī Kālakarṇī; one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with fuel from the palāśa tree.
When the oblation is performed with honey and clarified butter, Kālakarṇī becomes propitiated.
She who causes the obstruction of movement shall bind the streams of the army's weapons;
the practitioner of mantra should constantly remember her, the bestower of various sovereign powers. (41)
Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ kālakarṇike ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā. One should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times while remaining pure and steady at the royal gate for the practice of Madanayakṣiṇī.
An oblation of ghee with milk-soaked *mālatī* flowers should be performed one hundred times for every single bite.
The yakṣiṇī Madanā bestows the accomplishment of a pill;
by keeping that in one's mouth, a man becomes invisible and long-lasting.
Oṃ aiṃ, O Madanā, O Madanavidrāvaṇī, grant, grant union with Anaṅga! Krīṃ krīṃ svāhā!
This is the *sādhana* of Lakṣmīyakṣiṇī; established in one's own home, [one should worship] with red *karavīra* flowers.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) consisting of one-tenth that number.
If performed at home, success shall be attained, and the Yakṣiṇī named Lakṣmī bestows mercury, divine elixir, and the ritual procedure. (45)
Oṃ aiṃ lakṣmīṃ śrīṃ kamaladhāriṇīṃ kalahaṃsī svāhā | Oṃ aiṃ lakṣmīṃ śrīṃ kamaladhāriṇīṃ kalahaṃsī svāhā | The Sadhana of Śobhanāyakṣiṇī.
Wearing red garlands and garments, one should recite the mantra on the fourteenth day;
thereafter the goddess becomes perfected, beautiful, and the bestower of enjoyments.
Oṃ aśokapallavākāra karatale śobhanīṃ śrīṃ kṣaḥ svāhā | Oṃ aśokapallavākāra karatale śobhanīṃ śrīm kṣaḥ svāhā | The Sadhana of Naṭīyakṣiṇī.
Having gone beneath a flowering *aśoka* tree, having prepared a beautiful mandala with sandalwood paste, and having worshipped the Goddess by offering a thousand incense sticks; 47.
Then, eating only at night, a man should repeat the mantra for one month;
having performed an auspicious worship at night, he should recite the mantra at midnight.
The actress-goddess, having arrived, bestows the treasure of the essence-ointment, the mantra for the minister, and the certain divine yoga. (49)
Oṃ hrīṃ naṭi mahānaṭi svarūpavati svāhā. This is the sādhana of the yakṣiṇī Padminī. In a fragrant place within the house, one should draw a beautiful maṇḍala with sandalwood paste.
Having made [an image] of the size of a cubit, one should worship the Padminī there.
Having offered incense with guggulu resin, one should recite the mantra one thousand times for one month;
then, having performed worship, one should recite it again at night.
When midnight has passed, the Goddess arrives and bestows a treasure-trove and divine yoga; therefore, the practitioner of mantra shall become happy.
Oṃ hrīṃ (or krīṃ) Padminī svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ Padminī svāhā | Oṃ krīṃ Padminī svāhā | Mahāyakṣiṇī.
Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ, obeisance to Śrī Mahāyakṣiṇī, the bestower of all sovereignty.
O Kāmeśvarī Yakṣiṇī, oṃ, obeisance, come, O Kāmeśvarī, svāhā!
O Jayāyakṣiṇī:
Oṃ aiṃ jaye yakṣiṇī, accomplish all tasks, accomplish them! Svāhā! [This is the mantra of] Kalāvatīyakṣiṇī.
Oṃ hrīṃ kalāvati maithunapriye āgaccha svāhā. Thus ends the fifteenth instruction, titled "The Sadhana of the Yakṣiṇī," in the *Kāmaratna* composed by Śrī Nityanātha. 15.
The Sixteenth Instruction:
Now, for the successful accomplishment of the application of aphrodisiacs and other remedies, the purification of mercury and other substances;
first, the purification of mercury.
One must not perform the supreme consecration of the mercury (rasasaṃskāra) with less than [the prescribed] materials;
the worship of the king of mercury (rasarāja) is performed with the Aghora mantra alone. || 1 ||
Oṃ! To those who are non-terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the most terrible;
to all of them, everywhere, to all those who possess the forms of Rudra—salutations be unto you. || 2 ||
To those who are not terrible, to those who are terrible, to those more terrible than the most terrible,
to all those who are everywhere and are everything— to you who possess the forms of Rudra, let there be homage.
One should grind mercury processed for a day with the ashes of a virgin's hair;
it should be subjected to the *pātana* apparatus, whereby the mercury becomes perfectly purified. (3)
Alternatively, one should cause mercury to be extracted from cinnabar; that process is now described:
cinnabar should be ground with the juice of *pāribhadra* for a period of exactly one *yāma*.

Alternatively, one should cause that mercury to fall using the juices of *jambīra* fruits by means of the *pātālayantra*; then, once freed from the seven coatings, one should employ that mercury in a medicinal preparation.

Having added one-tenth part of sulfur to the mercury, one should rub it together for one watch (yāma) with juices extracted from jambīra fruits, and then subject it to precipitation in a pātālayantra.
It should be kneaded again and poured again seven times for the sake of purification;
thus are the purifications proclaimed, and one should perform at least one of them.
For water is above, fire is below, and the liquid paste is in the middle;
when fire gradually effects that [transformation], it is called the *pātāla* yantra.
Thus ends the purification of mercury.
Now, the killing of mercury is described: for every type of mercury, one should perform grinding in a heated mortar.
One should throw the three—goat dung, husks, and fire—into a pit in the ground.
Indeed, that which stands upon it is the heated mortar;
this mortar is recommended as being made of iron, stone, or even clay. (10)
O Maheśvarī, that man who causes mercury to be killed when it is undigested or seedless is a slayer of a Brahmin, one of very wicked conduct, and a traitor to the mantra.
Asafoetida, the five salts, as well as the four alkalis, the three pungents, ginger, and citron, all saturated with juice. 12.
Having placed the liquid within the middle of the mass, one should subject it to heat for seven days;
in a clay vessel containing a decoction of sāra, it will certainly become desirous of food.
This very essence, mixed with the juice of *jambīra* fruit, should be kept with effort in a clay vessel in the heat for one day; then it becomes dead [inactive]. || 14 ||
The morsel should be given right there; the purification of the gold is done very gradually.
An equal portion of sixty-four [parts] and so forth should be added, and once it has been digested, one should stir it.
First, one-sixty-fourth part; then, thirty-second;
again, twentieth should be taken; and then, in sequence, the eighth and twelfth. (16)
One-eighth, one-fourth, or even half a part, equal in measure; for each morsel, one should grind it with sour gruel in a heated mortar for a day.
One should cast that [mercury] into a *cāraṇayantra* combined with the juice of *jambīra*;
one should keep that apparatus in the heat, and in a day the mercury becomes liquefied (*jārita*). || 18 ||
Having smeared it with goat’s milk, cow urine, snuhī milk, and acidic liquids,
and having bound it securely on the outside with a strong cloth, the wise one should heat it in an earthen pot.
O Goddess, having processed that mercury in a *dolāyantra* for a day and night with sour gruel, alkali, and urine, one should immediately purify it in a mortar.
Having crushed it as before in a mortar and again in a vessel smeared with a *puṭa*,
O Goddess of the Gods, it is digested through these three "bites" by this sequence.
To whatever extent [the substance] is taken from that, to that same extent one should rub it; at each morsel, one should digest it in the heated mortar according to one's capacity. (22)
One should kill that aged mercury with liquid reagents; this is called "killing.
Having ground it with all the juices, one should thoroughly rub it in a mortar. (23)
One should combine the lead with sulfur and restrain it at the end of the day;
one should then roast it in a *bhūdhara* furnace and extract it at the end of the day.
The mercury should be rubbed for two watches (six hours) in oil of black dhattūra; it should then undoubtedly be cooked for one day in the apparatus known as the kacchapa. || 25 ||
The dead mercury becomes active immediately; one should employ it in all diseases.

Having ground equal parts of mercury and sulphur for a day with the juice of *nirguṇḍī*, and having heated them in a *cakramūṣā* crucible, the resulting ash is the impurity-free mercury (*sūta*). || 26 ||
Bitumen, honey, lac, and the juice combined with *kūrṇā* and *guñjā*. || 27 ||
One should rub it with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* for one day and then seal it again;
when blown [in the furnace], it attains the state of ash, pure and resembling crystal. (28)
One should grind two palas of the king of elixirs (mercury) and one pala of sulfur together with the juice of *mārkava* for one day continuously.
Having sealed it in that earthen crucible (bhūdhara-yantre), one should kill [the mercury] by means of a puṭa for one day;
thus, when the mercury has been processed (jārita), the "killing" (māraṇa) is proclaimed.
Alternatively, one should kill the mercury along with the other ingredients that are fit for ingestion;
then, one should grind the sūtaka and the essence of mica (ghanasattva) with the juices of kaṅguṇī.
One should dry that golaka for one day in the intense heat of the sun,
and then cook it inside a crucible apparatus (garbhayantra) for three days over a fire of chaff.

One should cook mercury, gold, mica, and conch-shell in equal parts in a fire of dried cow-dung day and night until they are reduced to ashes; then, one should process them for a day with the juice of plantain.
One should grind it together with the seed in a *carṣicāraṇa* machine;
one should then grind it once with the juice of all the root-herbs (*mūlikā*).
The mercury, having been placed within the "womb-machine" (garbhayantra), should be cooked; it dies as before.
[The ingredients are] brahmadaṇḍī, meghanāda, citraka, and kaṭutumbikā. (35)
Vajravallī, balā, kanyā, trikuṭā, arka, the milky sap of snuhī, kanda, rambhā, nirguṇḍī, lajjā, jātī, and jayantī. (36)
Viṣṇukrāntā, hastiśuṇḍī, dadrughna, bhṛṅgarāja, paṭu, guḍūcī, lāṅgalī, nīrakaṇā, kālī, and mahoragā. (37)
Kākamācī and dantī—these are the purifiers of mercury (pāradamāraka).
Whether used individually or all together, these eighteen [substances] should be administered in the prescribed places for the successful accomplishment of the king of elixirs (rasarāja). || 38 ||
Now, the method for the embryo-furnace (*garbhayantra*):
One should make a firm crucible (*mūṣikā*) made of clay, four finger-breadths in length, with a circular opening three finger-breadths in diameter at its center. (39)
There should be twenty parts of salt and one part of guggulu;
having ground them very finely, water should be added repeatedly.
Then one should apply a coating to the surface and pour the liquid (rasa) therein;
having sealed it, a *puṭa* should be applied—this constitutes the *garbhayantra*. || 41 ||
Thus ends the killing of mercury.
Now, the purification of cinnabar (*hiṅgula*):
cinnabar should be treated with sheep’s milk and the group of acidic substances (*amlavarga*), and then infused with heat.
If practiced diligently seven times, it certainly attains purification. || 42 ||
Thus ends the purification of cinnabar (hiṅgula).
Now, the purification of sulfur (gandhaka):
it has a luster like the bright fortnight and a radiance like fresh butter.
Sulphur that is smooth, hard, and glossy is said to be the best. || 43 ||
Having poured ghee into a vessel and added milk, one should cover the mouth with a cloth;
having first placed powdered fragrant substances, one should set that [mixture] on top of them.
Having placed a single skull-cup, turned face upwards and inseparable from its fragrance, upon a milk-vessel set on the ground, one should quickly apply the "upward-sealed" (ūrdhvapuṭa) method.
Then, one should quickly add the liquefied fragrance to milk during the pure conjunctions;
the fragrance should be cooked in ghee until it becomes like oil.
Having covered it with a cloth, one should shake it in water infused with the three myrobalans (triphalā);
thus the purification of sulphur (gandhaka) is accomplished, after which one may employ it in medicinal formulations.
Thus ends the purification of sulfur.
Now, the purification of mica (*abhraka*): black, yellow, white, or red [mica] should be employed in *yogarasa* and *rasāyana* [therapies].
The Pināka, the Dardura, the Nāga, and the Vajra—thus it is of four kinds. || 48 ||
The three [types of] *pināka* and others should be avoided; one should carefully collect the *vajra*.
When cast into the fire, the *pināka* releases a mass of fragments. (49)
From eating it out of ignorance, it will bring about great suffering;
like a frog cast into the fire, it makes the croaking sound of a frog.
And by merely eating that, it bestows various diseases;
furthermore, the serpent situated within the fire immediately emits hissing breaths. (51)
And that [substance], when situated in the body, would constantly cause the disease of fistula;
however, vajra-ore (vajrābhraka) undergoes no transformation whatsoever even in fire.
Therefore, vajra-iron (vajrābhra) should be employed, for it conquers disease, old age, and death.
One should smelt the vajra-iron in fire until it becomes like fire itself. (53)
Then it should be sprinkled with cow’s milk, and again and again with cow’s milk;
having placed it in a separate vessel, one should saturate it for eight watches (eight hours) with the liquid of meghnāda (blue vitriol), and it becomes free from defects.
Alternatively, one should place two parts of Abhra and one part of Musta together with water in a vessel for three days, and then grind them finely.
This powder of dehusked abhraka, combined with rice,
should be tied in a cloth and macerated within a vessel containing the juice of sāra.
When it comes by itself through the hands until it reaches the state of fine powder, being free from defects and situated in the clouds, it becomes pure, dried *dhānyābhraka*. (57)
One should cook dhānyābhraka with the milk of Calotropis gigantea or with the juices of its roots for one day in an ardha-puṭa; after being processed thus seven times, it becomes dead (mṛta).
One part of *dhānyābhraka* (grain-iron) and two parts of *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax). || 59 ||

Having ground that [substance] and sealed it in a blind crucible (andhamūṣā), one should blow it with a fierce fire; once cooled naturally, the resulting powder should be employed in all formulations. || 60 ||
Thus ends the purification of mica (*abhraka*).
Now, regarding the immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*): listen to the immortalization of all [substances] that have been killed.
Taking sixteen palas of the decoction produced from the three myrobalans (triphalā).
Eight palas of cow’s ghee and ten palas of dead mica,
having combined these together, one should cook them in an iron vessel over a gentle fire.
Having collected that which has been digested by liquids, one should employ it in all yogic practices.
Thus ends the process of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*). Now, for the extraction of the essence (*sattva-pātana*) of mica (*abhraka*):
having ground the mica leaf into powder, one should place it in *āranāla* (sour gruel) for one day, and then dry it over a *sūraṇa* (mountain ginger) fire.
Thereafter, the rasa should be processed with the root-rasa of the plantain (kadali), combined with one-fourth part of ṭaṅkaṇa and together with śapharī.
Having formed it into a mass and dried it thoroughly with buffalo dung in many ways, one should quickly heat it placed in a crucible over a fire of *yavāgni*.
Then, by means of two bellows, the essence (*sattva*) contained within the mineral ore will indeed be emitted; of this there is no doubt. (65)
Thus ends the extraction of the essence of mica (*abhraka-sattva-pātana*).
Now, the purification of realgar (*manaḥśilā-śuddhi*):
one should [process] the realgar with the juice of *jayantī*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, and red *agasti*. (66)
One should cook it in a dolāyantra (swinging vessel) for one prahara at a time with goat’s urine; then wash it with fermented rice-gruel (āranāla) and employ it in all formulations. || 67 ||
Thus ends the purification of realgar (*manaḥśilā*).
Now, for the purification of yellow orpiment (*haratāla*):
one should bind the orpiment in a cloth pouch (*poṭalī*) and immerse it in sour gruel (*kāñjika*) along with its powder.
Then, for one watch (yāma), [it should be processed] in the juice of kūṣmāṇḍa using a dolāyantra (swinging apparatus).
One should cook it for one watch (yāma) in sesame oil and for one watch in the decoction of triphalā;
thus, having been cooked in the apparatus for four watches, the tālaka becomes purified.
Thus ends the purification of haratāla.
Now, the purification of tuttha: one should purify tuttha with the excrement of a cat and a pigeon mixed with wine.
Having added one-tenth part of ṭaṅkaṇa (borax), it should be cooked in a mild fire-pit;
a puṭapāka with curd and a puṭapāka with honey should be applied for the purification of tuttha.
Thus ends the purification of tuttha.
Now, regarding the purification of kāśīśa and conch-shell navel:
kāśīśa is purified by being soaked in jambīra juice for a day in the heat of the sun. (71)
Having thoroughly burnt the conch-navel and treated it with acid seven times, one should wash it and then take hold of it; only then does it attain purity, and not otherwise.
Thus ends the purification of conch shells from Kāśī.
Now, the purification of metals such as gold:
[the metal] should be infused with clay and the acid of *mātuluṅga* for five days.
One should purify gold by means of *puṭapāka* using ashes and salts.
Ant-hill earth, soot, red ochre, brick-dust, and salt—these five types of clay [should be used] with jambīra fruits and sour gruel. 74.
Having ground it, a gold leaf smeared with it becomes completely purified by means of a *puṭa* (herb-enclosure);
likewise, silver is purified by lead and *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax) through sublimation (*dhūma*).
One should grind chalk and salt with buttermilk and sour gruel;
a copper leaf smeared with this should be heated repeatedly and quenched [in the liquid]. (76)
Nirguṇḍī, when consumed with khadira, aralu, and buttermilk, does not lead to purification. || 77 ||
Rohaṇa, rājāvarta, and thirdly puṭīraka—thus the sharp [metal] is threefold; one should purify it for the sake of success in yoga. (78)
Thus ends the purification of gold and other minerals. Now follows the purification of *tuttha*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and iron:
smeared with rabbit blood and heated in fire three times.
Or, when melted with Tuttha, Ṭaṅkaṇa, and Kāca, it becomes pure. || 79 ||
Alternatively, one should cook iron powder with six times its quantity of cow’s urine;
it should then be washed with fermented rice-gruel (āranāla), dried, and thus attain purity.
According to the opinion of all [authorities], one should place purified mercury and an equal amount of gold in a mortar and form a ball;
having added sulfur both below and above—equal in weight to the whole—and having sealed it, [one should proceed]. (81)
One should apply fourteen *puṭas* using twenty pieces of wood;
thus, an ash that leaves no residue (*niruttha*) is produced, and the fragrant substance (*gandha*) should be applied again and again.
One should coat a silver leaf with a fourth part of mercury and a single part of sulfur,
ground together with lemon juice, using twenty-five pieces of vanopalas.
Having bound it in three folds, one should cook it, adding fragrance again and again.
He dies; there is no doubt about this—one should employ him in those respective tasks. || 84 ||
One should smear a leaf that has been perforated at the edge with a paste of copper-colored fragrance ground with sour liquid; then, having covered it, one should cook it in a *puṭa*.
Having extracted [the mercury] and powdered it, one should add a quarter-part of sulphur;
having ground it with jambīra or āranāla juices and formed a pellet, one should cook it in a puṭa.
In this manner, it should be cooked with four *puṭas*, adding fragrance again and again;
having ground it with the juices of *mātuluṅga*, one should administer a single *puṭa*.
Then, for its purification from impurities, one *puṭa* should be administered with white sugar; it will become dead (calcined). || 88 ||
One should grind dead copper with *jambīra* fruits for one watch (*yāma*) in a mortar.
Having placed that mass inside a *sūraṇa* root and sealed it, one should coat everything.
Once dried, it should be cooked in a *gajapuṭa*; thus it becomes free of defects and removes all diseases. (89)
Now, regarding the killing (māraṇa) of iron:
one should not cook [the iron] below five palas, nor above thirteen.
At the outset, the mantra and the ritual procedure must be performed; thus, the mantra is stated: || 90 ||

*Oṃ amṛtodbhavāya svāhā*—this is the mantra for rubbing. With this mantra, protection must be performed for the metal and its practitioner. *Oṃ namaścaṇḍacakrapāṇaye svāhā yakṣasenādhipataye suragurumahāvidyābalāya svāhā*. Having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) with this mantra, one should then perform the ritual action.
At the break of day, one should place iron powder into that [liquid] of dantī leaves;
it should be kept in the sun for a day in a bronze vessel, and the liquid should be added again and again.
Having sealed it at night, one should cook it in a *puṭa* and then saturate it with liquids in the morning;
one should proceed in this manner for eight days, whereby that which is of three kinds indeed dies.
The characteristic of the "dead" [substance]:
one should place honey, clarified butter, dead iron, and silver into a crucible;
having sealed it and subjected it to heat, the silver should be recovered if it retains its original weight.
Then one should know the iron to be dead; otherwise, one should process it again.
Now, for purification:
one should grind equal parts of sulfur and iron together in a mortar.
Having sealed [the substance] for one day with the juices of kanyākā, one should cook it in a gajapuṭa;
in this manner, the nirutthana (recovery from dissolution) of all metals should be performed. 95.
Now, the immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) of this:
one should cook dead iron, equal in weight to ghee, in an iron vessel.
Once the ghee has been absorbed, one should take it up and employ it in those [preparations] that serve as vehicles for the yoga. || 96 ||
Then, having taken fresh earth-snake essence, the wise one should wash it until it becomes loose;
or else, having made a cock the "hero" (vīra) and placed it within the temple [of the body]. 97.
Having taken the first portion of feces and urine along with water, one should stir it together with a ṭaṅka of honey and clarified butter during the summer heat for all purposes; with care,
one should release the essence, which is like that of copper— this is the essence of bhūnāga.
Thus ends the section on the Nagas.
Now, the five salts: sea salt, rock salt, black salt, sochal salt, and suvarcala salt.
Mūlikā, the nine alkalis (navakṣāra), and the five salts (lavaṇapañcaka) should be known [as the ingredients]. || 99 ||
Thus ends the group of five salts. Now, the alkalies:
the three alkalies (trikṣāra), ṭaṅkaṇa-kṣāra, yavakṣāra, and svarjikā. (100)
Thus end the alkalies.
Now, regarding vegetable alkali: sesame, apāmārga, kadala, palāśa, śigru, and pauṇḍraka.
One should cook radish, fresh ginger, and citraka entirely inside a sealed crucible (puṭa).

Having stirred it with water and bound it in a cloth, one should take the water from below; then, having purified that water and boiled it in an earthen vessel over a fire, the remaining alkaline residue should be taken—this is known as *vṛkṣakṣāra* (alkali from trees). || 102 ||
Thus end the alkalies from trees. Now, as for *viḍa*:
the alkali of *mūlikā*, ginger, and *vahnī* combined with cow’s urine.
One should take pure cloth and water, and with that, one should saturate the sulphur.

This seed [mercury] should be subjected to heating seven times in a hot vessel for the purpose of digesting gold; meanwhile, the sulfur should be processed with the juices of kanyā, hayāri, and dhattūra.
This seed is for the digestion of gold in the harsh dharma;
it is sulphur or conch-shell powder saturated a hundred times with cow's urine.
This seed is excellent for the digestion of [metals] and beneficial for the liquefaction of seeds. (105)

Now, the group of sour substances (amlavarga): the citron (jambīra), the orange (nāgaraṅga), the citron (mātuluṅga), the wood-apple (āmbavetasa), the sorrel (cāṅgerī), and the chickpea-flower (caṇaśukra) are proclaimed as the sour group. || 106 ||
Thus ends the section on acidic substances.
Now, regarding the *vajramūṣā* (thunderbolt crucible):
take one part of anthill clay, along with cow bone ash and chaff ash.
Having taken a portion of the essence, they fashioned a vajra-mūṣā crucible for you.
Thus ends the sixteenth instruction, titled "The Purification of Mercury and Other Substances," in the *Kāmaratna* composed by Śrī Nityanātha. 16.
